name: NY CDPAP: New York Medicaid consumer-directed home care paid through a single fiscal intermediary
size_basis: Reported program cost of about $9B a year with about 280,000 consumers (Spectrum News, Jan 2025, quoting the state). Advocates call the PPL contract $11B; that is a characterization, not used for sizing.
money_flow: NY Medicaid (state + federal) pays a fiscal intermediary, which pays personal assistants (often family or friends) chosen by disabled and elderly consumers.
shock: On 1 April 2025 Public Partnerships LLC (PPL) became the sole statewide fiscal intermediary, replacing roughly 600-700 FIs, after a federal TRO on 31 March forced continuity of pay. Hochul claims more than $1B saved by Jan 2026 (FPI says about $500M is clearly admin savings); advocates claim 150k workers and 90k consumers left (contested, unverified).
incumbents: PPL, now the statutory single FI. Advocates allege private-equity control and service failures (unverified). About 700 displaced small FIs lost their model.
incumbent_fragility: A single politically exposed state contract; the state wants savings and a working program at once and cannot quickly swap vendors, so friction builds at the edges. Displaced FIs hold caregiver relationships and data.
funded_startups_already_here: None found at the FI layer, which is closed by statute (no dedicated startup search was run for this pool). Adjacent funded home-care platforms such as Papa and Honor exist, from memory and not verified this session.
wedge_hints: (a) Displaced FIs converting to licensed home care agencies and needing back-office tooling; (b) enrollment, timesheet and benefits-navigation help for caregivers and consumers layered on PPL; (c) the same financial-management-services function in the other ~45 states with self-directed Medicaid programs, which is the only route to $100M.
insider_roles: Former FI owners and compliance leads, independent-living-center staff, Medicaid managed long-term care plan care managers, home-care payroll specialists, elder-law attorneys.

name: England adult social care: council purchases from independent home-care and care-home providers
size_basis: GBP 29.4B gross current expenditure on adult social care in 2024-25 (GBP 23.6B long-term support), converted at 1.30 USD per GBP. Averages: GBP 23.56 an hour external home care; GBP 1,185.55 a week residential or nursing.
money_flow: Councils (council tax, central grants, NHS transfers) pay independent providers at council-set rates; providers pay care workers.
shock: The overseas Care Worker visa route closed to new applicants on 22 July 2025 (in-country switching allowed until 22 July 2028). Skills for Care 2025/26: international arrivals into direct care fell from 105,000 (2023/24) to 50,000 to 30,000; British-national posts fell 40,000 in a year; vacancy rate 6.2% (about 96,000), a decade low. Employer NIC rise in April 2025 added cost (from memory).
incumbents: Thousands of small providers plus groups (HC-One, Bupa, Care UK, from memory); councils as monopsony buyer; staffing agencies.
incumbent_fragility: Providers cannot raise prices (council-set), cannot recruit abroad, and domestic supply is shrinking; the 2028 transition cutoff sets a clock.
funded_startups_already_here: Cera (about $150M combined debt and equity, Jan 2025; reported valuation above $1B from one aggregator), Birdie (GBP 24.7M Series B, older), Florence (shift matching, GBP 28.5M Series B, older).
wedge_hints: Domestic pipeline (UK-born recruits and returners), sponsorship-transfer matching for in-country switchers before July 2028, pay-on-demand and retention tooling, commissioning tools that let councils price the true cost of care.
insider_roles: Registered managers, care-home recruitment leads, council commissioners, immigration solicitors, payroll bureau staff.

name: England social landlords' repairs and maintenance spend (housing associations, Awaab's Law era)
size_basis: GBP 10B repairs and maintenance in the year to 31 March 2025 for private registered providers (GBP 3.9B capitalised), up 13% from GBP 8.8B; forecast average GBP 10.9B a year over five years; at 1.30 USD per GBP. Excludes council housing repairs, so the true pool is larger.
money_flow: Tenant rents, grants and borrowing pay landlords, who pay contractors (Mears, Wates, Kier and similar, from memory) and in-house repair teams, who pay trades.
shock: Awaab's Law phase 1 took effect 27 October 2025: emergency hazards within 24 hours and short deadlines to investigate and make safe damp and mould; more hazards added in 2026 and 2027. The government impact assessment shows only GBP 10.8M a year net cost to business, which the sector and an acknowledging official say vastly understates cost.
incumbents: Large repair contractors and housing-management software vendors (NEC, MRI, Civica, from memory). Nineteen providers with 40,000+ homes hold 42% of units and 47% of turnover.
incumbent_fragility: Schedule-of-rates contracts pay per job rather than per outcome; legacy systems cannot track new legal clocks; landlord margins are already stretched by rent caps.
funded_startups_already_here: Switchee (Mould iQ launched May 2025 with three housing associations covering 92,000 homes), Mobysoft (RepairSense and a damp-and-mould module), Aico (HomeLINK sensors), Made Tech. Funding amounts not found.
wedge_hints: Compliance clock and Ombudsman-ready evidence trail for Awaab's Law cases; dispatch of sub-GBP 500 hazard jobs across small subcontractors; ventilation and mould-remediation crews as a service; contractor performance audit for landlords.
insider_roles: Repairs managers and damp-and-mould leads at housing associations, contractor operations directors, Housing Ombudsman case officers, surveyors.

name: German Mittelstand ownership succession: purchase-price flow plus advisory and financing fees
size_basis: Derived: KfW Nachfolge-Monitoring 2025 reports about 109,000 successions a year planned through 2029 at an average intended sale price of about EUR 499,000, giving about EUR 54B (about $62B at 1.15). This is an upper bound: not all are sales and the price is owners' hope. IfM Bonn expects about 37,200 actual handovers a year (reported, unverified), roughly EUR 18B. The capturable fee and financing layer is about 3-8%.
money_flow: Successors pay retiring owners; Steuerberater, M&A boutiques, banks (Sparkassen) and KfW take fees and interest.
shock: KfW Jan 2026: for the first time, planned closures without a successor (about 114,000 a year) exceed succession wishes (about 109,000). More than 2M owners are 55+; 42% of firms planning closure cite bureaucracy (+12 points); employee and management buy-outs are being considered by 28% and 24%.
incumbents: Tax advisers (Steuerberater), Sparkassen and Volksbanken, IHK/HWK succession advisers, M&A boutiques, nexxt-change (free state-backed board), KfW loans.
incumbent_fragility: Free public substitutes price matching at zero; advisers skip sub-EUR 1M deals; information is hidden and valuations are opaque; many firms are too low-earning to sell.
funded_startups_already_here: None found with a 2023-2026 round in Germany. Historical: Carl Finance (EUR 3M, 2019), Valuedesk (EUR 5M, 2024, valuation SaaS), UnternehmerTUM ETA programme (Sept 2025). US analogs now funded: Baton, Rowan, Iconic.
wedge_hints: EBO/MBO financing with KfW and Bürgschaftsbank guarantees; buy-and-hold vehicles for the roughly 114,000 planned closures; Handwerk trades (about 1M firms); valuation benchmarks. A $100M revenue path needs $1.5-3B of transacted value.
insider_roles: Steuerberater, IHK and HWK succession moderators, Sparkasse corporate-client advisers, notaries, business brokers.

name: German live-in elder care (24-Stunden-Betreuung): household spend on Eastern European live-in carers via agencies
size_basis: Derived and borderline: Federal Health Ministry working group estimates 100,000-210,000 live-in carers on a given day (200,000-420,000 a year with rotation); price above EUR 2,000 a month plus board and agency fees. 100,000-210,000 x EUR 2,000-3,000 x 12 = EUR 2.4-7.6B; midpoint about EUR 5B (about $5.8B). Low confidence, wide range.
money_flow: Households (topped up by Pflegegeld and the EUR 125 a month Entlastungsbetrag) pay a German placement agency plus an Eastern European posting company, which pay the live-in carer.
shock: BMG working group report (Nov 2024) finds working-time, rest-time and minimum-wage rules often not met and false self-employment common, and that even agency placement is no guarantee of a legal model; the Federal Labour Court counts on-call time toward minimum wage with 3-year back-claims. A draft Pflegeneuordnungsgesetz was published 5 June 2026 and a Bundestag lobby-register entry (22 Sept 2026) ties live-in reform to it; what the draft actually requires is unverified.
incumbents: Placement agencies (about 60 in 2009, 266 by 2017, no minimum standards) and posting companies mostly in Poland and Romania; legal models (Entsendung with A1, employer model, self-employed) all carry risk.
incumbent_fragility: A compliant model forces employment, on-call pay and rest time, raising cost sharply; agencies cannot pass it on without subsidy, and the gray market has no registry.
funded_startups_already_here: marta (Berlin, EUR 6.6M seed Aug 2022, over 13,000 families), Pflegehelden (sold to Rigeto 2021, over 3,000 customers), ennie 24h. No 2025 round found.
wedge_hints: Compliant-employment infrastructure (A1 admin, time recording, cross-border payroll); family-side financing bridging Pflegekasse benefits; a certification standard (DIN SPEC exists but does not protect households).
insider_roles: Agency founders and dispatchers, Polish posting-company owners, Pflegekasse caseworkers, care counselors (Pflegeberater), labour-law attorneys.

name: Japan municipal water-supply pipe and facility renewal spend
size_basis: Health Ministry forecast: replacing at the current rate needs an average of JPY 1.8T a year over FY2021-2050 (about $12B at 150 JPY per USD), about JPY 500B more than the prior decade; pipes alone JPY 33.5T over 30 years. Sewers are additional and not sized. Surfaced via search summaries; the decn.co.jp article returned 404 on direct fetch.
money_flow: Water bills and general-account transfers fund municipal waterworks bureaus, which pay contractors, consulting engineers and pipe makers.
shock: The Yashio sinkhole in Saitama (28 Jan 2025) triggered a national inspection of large sewers older than 30 years: 297 of 621 km inspected showed exposed rebar or cracks needing repair within five years, and 72 km needed work within one year.
incumbents: Municipal waterworks bureaus, consulting engineers, pipe contractors, pipe makers (Kubota, Kurimoto, from memory); AI diagnostics from Fracta Japan (with NTT Business Solutions in Kakegawa, 1,062 km, Nov 2025), Hitachi Systems, Marubeni.
incumbent_fragility: Shrinking customer bases and water volumes, aging engineer workforces, and a fixed 40-year legal-life rule that does not match real pipe condition; replacement rate about 0.64% a year implies a roughly 156-year cycle.
funded_startups_already_here: No 2025 venture round found for a Japanese water-pipe AI company (funding amounts not found). Corporate and research players: Fracta Japan, Hitachi Systems, Marubeni, Maeda/Sumitomo Mitsui/University of Tokyo inspection robot; Bwell Technology (Shenzhen) filed for a Hong Kong listing.
wedge_hints: Condition-based prioritization to stretch asset lives; void and cavity detection behind sewer pipes; wide-area utility consolidation back-office; PFI and operator bundles. The buyer is municipal procurement, so a local partner is needed.
insider_roles: Municipal waterworks engineers, sewer inspection contractors, pipe manufacturers' sales engineers, MLIT officials, consulting engineers.

name: Japan shippers' spend on contracted road freight (multi-tier trucking subcontract chain)
size_basis: Derived: about 63,000 truck operators (MLIT, undated) x JPY 264M average 2023 revenue (All Japan Trucking Association management analysis) = about JPY 16.6T (about $110B at 150 JPY per USD). Whole logistics market about JPY 24.2T for FY2023 per a secondary summary of MLIT data. 99.5% of operators have capital of JPY 300M or less.
money_flow: Shippers pay prime carriers and forwarders, who sub-contract down multi-tier chains of small carriers.
shock: On 1 Jan 2026 the Subcontract Act became the Act on Proper Transactions for SME Entrusted Businesses, widening coverage to companies above 300 staff; Trucking Business Act amendments require written contracts itemizing charges (including fuel surcharges) and an actual-carrier register; designated shippers must appoint a Chief Logistics Officer and file a first medium- to long-term plan by end of October 2026.
incumbents: Yamato, Sagawa, NX, Fukuyama (from memory), over 60,000 small carriers, and forwarders earning layered intermediary margins.
incumbent_fragility: The new laws attack intermediary margin and unpaid waiting time; small carriers lack compliance capacity; the driver overtime cap (the 2024 problem) shrinks capacity.
funded_startups_already_here: Hacobu (MOVO; JPY 700M in May 2025, cumulative above JPY 5.6B), T2 (autonomous trucking; JPY 5B pre-Series B Aug 2025, JPY 16.5B-plus cumulative per one July 2026 report). CBcloud not verified.
wedge_hints: Compliance back-office for about 60,000 small carriers (contracts, itemized charges, registers); waiting-time and berth data for shippers' CLO plans due October 2026; accessorial-charge billing and collection.
insider_roles: Transport managers (unko kanrisha), dispatchers at mid-size carriers, forwarder pricing staff, warehouse berth managers, JFTC and MLIT enforcement officers.

name: Japan home-visit long-term care insurance payments to home-help agencies
size_basis: MHLW FY2024 care benefit statistics: home-visit care cost JPY 1,214,189M (JPY 1.21T), up 5.1% year on year, about $8.1B at 150 JPY per USD. All long-term care cost is JPY 11.94T.
money_flow: Municipal long-term-care insurers (half tax, half premiums) plus 10-30% copays pay home-visit agencies, which pay helpers.
shock: The April 2024 cut to home-visit base fees (about 2-3%) was followed by record bankruptcies: 176 care-provider bankruptcies in 2025 (second straight record), 91 of them home-visit (third straight), 87% with fewer than 10 staff (Tokyo Shoko Research, via secondary summary). Villages with zero home-visit offices: 107 at end-2024 (Kyodo), 116 at end-2025, with 285 municipalities down to one office by June 2026.
incumbents: Large chains (Sompo Care, Nichii, from memory), municipal social-welfare councils, thousands of micro-agencies.
incumbent_fragility: Per-visit reimbursement leaves rural travel time unpaid; helpers are aging; a fee cut landed when wages needed to rise.
funded_startups_already_here: CareMaker (about JPY 100M, Feb 2025, visiting-nurse SaaS), CareFran (care-plan platform, Dec 2025), EMC Healthcare (Jan 2026). No large round found for home-visit billing or records.
wedge_hints: Roll-up of distressed micro-agencies with a shared back office; municipality-level shared helper pools and route optimization; claim optimization for treatment-improvement add-ons; foreign specified-skilled-worker caregivers (home-visit allowed from April 2025, from memory). Needs Japanese operator talent.
insider_roles: Care managers, agency service managers, municipal long-term-care section staff, Kokuho-ren billing clerks, social-insurance labour consultants (sharoushi).

name: Northeast US home heating oil retail (fuel, service contracts and installs)
size_basis: Derived: EIA (via Fuel Oil News, Nov 2025) has about 5.0M US households (4.1M in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic) using oil as main heating fuel, spending about $1,390 each per winter at about $3.50 a gallon, about $6.9B; plus service and installs (19% of Star Group revenue) and commercial and multifamily oil, so an estimated $8-10B. Household counts date to EIA's 2020 survey.
money_flow: Homeowners pay local oil dealers for delivery, service contracts and installs; dealers pay terminals and wholesalers.
shock: Star Group FY2025 10-K: net account loss 4.7% (3.6% in FY2023), gross losses 13.5%, with conversions explaining only about 1.3% of lost accounts. NY and CT raised the bioheat minimum from 5% to 10% on 1 July 2025 (RI 10% to 20%). NY's all-electric new-building law start was delayed on 12 Nov 2025 pending appeal. A $450M New England Heat Pump Accelerator began Feb 2026.
incumbents: Star Group (largest, 5.5%-plus share, 406,400 full-service and 63,200 delivery-only customers, bought one oil and three propane businesses for $80.5M in FY2025) and a long tail of family dealers (trade group NEFI represents about 1,100 oil and propane providers).
incumbent_fragility: Fixed route and truck costs against 3.6-4.7% net annual attrition create a density death spiral; owners are aging; trade groups lobby against heat pumps rather than converting.
funded_startups_already_here: Dandelion Energy (geothermal; $40M Series C reported around late 2024; targets NY, CT and MA oil and gas homes). No venture-funded dealer roll-up or dealer-software startup found.
wedge_hints: Buy dealers' customer books and convert them to heat-pump, hybrid and service contracts using the $450M incentives; delivery route and degree-day SaaS; dealer succession brokerage; financing for oil-to-heat-pump swaps at burner failure. A $100M path is about 60,000-70,000 customers via 15-25 acquisitions, with thin margins on a shrinking base.
insider_roles: Dealer owners and office managers, oilheat burner technicians, terminal operators, NEFI and NORA staff, state energy-office program managers.

name: US Main Street business sales: SBA 7(a) change-of-ownership financing and brokerage
size_basis: SBA FY2025 7(a) approvals were $37B across 77,600 loans; change-of-ownership loans were more than $9B (23.6%, Coleman Report) or $8.29B and about 7,003 deals (CT Acquisitions); BizBuySell Q3 2025 had 2,599 closed deals worth $2.13B, about $8.5B annualized on its marketplace. The fee layer (brokers and lenders) is under $1B, so this fails the $100M-revenue test unless a wide stack is captured.
money_flow: Buyers, mostly using SBA-guaranteed bank loans, pay retiring owners; brokers, lenders and closing professionals take fees.
shock: SOP 50 10 8 (1 June 2025): at least 10% equity injection and seller notes count only on full standby, up to 50% of the injection. A citizenship rule effective 1 March 2026 (100% US citizen or national owners; not confirmed against the SBA notice). SOP 50 10 8.1 issued 14 Aug 2026, effective 1 Oct 2026: debt-service coverage on historical earnings only, quality-of-earnings report for deals of $3M or more, and 7(a) Small barred from ownership changes.
incumbents: Live Oak Bank (top acquisition lender), Huntington, First Internet Bank; business brokers and the BizBuySell marketplace.
incumbent_fragility: Lender-side rules now force re-underwriting and add cost and time on larger deals; brokers' listings priced around old financing assumptions may need repricing (my inference).
funded_startups_already_here: Baton ($10M Series A, Jan 2025), Iconic ($6M seed, May 2026), Rowan ($3.3M seed, Mar 2026), DealFlowAgent (about $646K-750K, 2026), Boom ($3.3M seed), Acquire.com (older rounds).
wedge_hints: Lightweight earnings normalization for sub-$3M deals (below the QoE threshold); seller-note standby servicing; non-citizen buyer alternatives. Honest verdict: real shock but small, crowded fee pool.
insider_roles: SBA lender underwriters, business brokers, CPAs who do quality-of-earnings work, SBA closing attorneys.

name: US CRE borrowers' refinancing, extension and transaction costs on the loan maturity wall
size_basis: MBA: $875B of commercial/multifamily mortgages mature in 2026 (17% of $5.0T; $957B in 2025, $652B in 2027). My derivation of the fee pool: ~$700-800B annual originations (MBA ~$706B in 2025; ~$806B forecast 2026) x 1.0-1.5% all-in friction (broker/banker, lender fee, legal, appraisal, reports, title) = $7-12B, plus ~$0.5-1B extension/modification fees on ~$200B extended. Central estimate $9B. Sanity check: Walker & Dunlop booked $1.2B revenue on $54.8B volume in 2025.
money_flow: Borrowers pay capital-markets brokers/bankers, lender origination fees, lawyers, appraisers, title and report vendors to refinance or extend; lenders pay special servicers when loans default. Signers: borrower CFO/principal; bank chief credit officer or workout head.
shock: MBA Feb 2026 survey shows $875B maturing in 2026 and lenders no longer simply extending (First American: extensions fell from $384B in 2024-25 to $200B in 2025-26). Trepp Sept 2026: CMBS delinquency 8.02% (highest since late 2020), office 12.16%, multifamily 8.04%; special servicing 10.86% overall and 16.75% office (May 2026).
incumbents: Capital-markets brokers and bankers (CBRE, JLL, Newmark, Cushman, Berkadia, Walker & Dunlop; only W&D verified in this pass), banks holding $396B of the maturing debt, CMBS servicers/special servicers, debt funds (CRE private credit took 23% of capital raised in Q1 2026, secondary). Fees are mostly success-based commissions.
incumbent_fragility: Low to moderate. Large brokers hold relationships and the fee pool is largely captured by them. Softness is in sub-$10M loans at community and regional banks, which are manual and local; a software-only entrant faces the problem that the lender, not the borrower, controls the decision.
funded_startups_already_here: Atlas Invest (AI-driven CRE bridge lender, $25M led by BlackRock Jan 2026, $38M total); Blooma (AI underwriting for lenders, $15M Series A 2021, older). Found no 2025-26 round for Lev or a refinance marketplace in 3 searches. Private credit capital is heavy even though venture-funded software is thin.
wedge_hints: Sub-$10M loan workflow for community banks (collateral re-underwriting, extension/modification paperwork); borrower-side refinance readiness packages for small owners; special-servicing workout administration for bank-held (non-CMBS) loans.
insider_roles: CRE debt brokers, bank workout officers, special servicer asset managers, receivers, appraisers valuing distressed office.

name: US homeowners-insurer-paid property repair and restoration (claims money flowing to contractors)
size_basis: III (verified): 2025 net premiums earned $152.6B; incurred losses 53.6% of premiums = ~$82B; loss plus LAE 61.1% = ~$93B. ISO 2023: property damage 97.3% of claims (wind/hail 42.5%, water 22.6%, fire 21.6%), so the claim money is overwhelmingly repair/rebuild spend. LA fires alone: CA Dept of Insurance says >$22.4B paid on 42,121 claims (secondary).
money_flow: Insurers pay claim proceeds, often by check jointly payable to homeowner and mortgage servicer (loss draft), which flow to roofers, restoration contractors, GCs and public adjusters; carriers also pay adjusters, TPAs and estimating software. Signers: restoration/roofing contractor owner; servicer loss-draft operations head; carrier claims-ops VP.
shock: Jan 2025 Los Angeles wildfires (largest payout event), plus 2025-26 shift to actual-cash-value/payment-schedule roof settlements. Verisk 2026 roof report (secondary): roof claims fell ~20% in 2025 but average roof replacement hit $17,631 (+33% vs 2021-24). Texas TDI clarified 2026-09-29 that insurers may weigh roof condition.
incumbents: Carriers; Verisk (Xactware/Xactimate) and Cotality for estimating; Sedgwick and Crawford as TPAs/adjusters; restoration franchisors; public adjusters (vendor names other than Sedgwick not re-verified). Mortgage servicers control loss-draft release (Fannie/Freddie thresholds per a Louisiana AG summary: <=$20k to borrower alone, >$20k joint with contractor, licensed contractor at $40k+; verify against Selling Guides). ~60% of owner-occupied homes carry a mortgage (ACS 2022, secondary).
incumbent_fragility: Contractor base is fragmented and cash-constrained; carrier payment rules are changing (ACV roofs, schedules); the servicer loss-draft step is a manual back office. Carriers resist tools that raise payouts, so contractor-side products need to be paid by contractors.
funded_startups_already_here: Rebuild (restoration claims software, $13M Series A Sept 2026 led by Asymmetric Capital Partners; $2.1M seed Jan 2025); NovaData Solutions (carrier-side restoration invoice review, Series A Mar 2024, Activate Venture Partners); Xcelerate (restoration documentation software); T&M Pro (acquired by Sedgwick).
wedge_hints: Contractor cash acceleration against approved claims; recoverable-depreciation holdback recovery on ACV roofs; servicer-side loss-draft disbursement and inspection workflow; contents inventory; post-catastrophe lien and payment tracking.
insider_roles: Restoration estimators and owners, public adjusters, mortgage servicer loss-draft managers, roofing contractor owners, carrier claims-operations leaders.

name: US HOA, condo and co-op association assessments and capital repairs
geography: United States (Florida and California are the largest concentrations)
size_basis: FCAR 2025 Statistical Review (verified PDF): $124.2B of assessments collected in 2025, of which $31.1B contributed to reserve funds; 373,000 associations; 35.2% of US housing; 9,000-10,000 management companies; 30-40% self-managed; Florida 50,600 associations / 4.47M units.
money_flow: Owners pay assessments to associations, which pay management companies, insurers, utilities, landscapers and contractors, and fund reserves for roofs, elevators, structure and pools. Signers: board treasurer/president on owner votes (Florida allows loans and lines of credit with majority owner approval), advised by the management company.
shock: Fannie Mae Lender Letter LL-2026-03 (Mar 18, 2026): minimum reserve allocation rises from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income for loan applications dated on/after Jan 4, 2027; Limited Review ended for established projects >10 units (Aug 3, 2026 per summaries). Buildings that miss the floor lose conventional financing eligibility. Florida: reserves must be funded to 100% of structural-integrity study recommendations from Jan 1, 2026 with no waiver (HB 913, 2025); Miami Realtors found 62% of South Florida associations missed the original Dec 31, 2024 study deadline. Fannie PDF returned 403; five secondary summaries agree.
incumbents: Management companies (9,000-10,000 firms), reserve-study firms (Association Reserves, Reserve Advisors), portfolio banks that lend to associations (e.g. U.S. Century Bank in Miami), insurers writing master policies.
incumbent_fragility: 30-40% of associations are volunteer-run; boards face a hard compliance deadline with six-figure per-unit exposure in some Florida buildings; conventional unit-owner financing is tightening; association lending is bank-local and slow.
funded_startups_already_here: Vantaca (HOA management software, $300M+ growth round at $1.25B Oct 2025, Cove Hill Partners; 500+ management companies, 6M households); PayHOA ($27.5M Series A May 2024); Assembly HOA ($1.8M); Bluejay HOA ($2.0M). Found no venture-scale startup in association capital-project financing or procurement.
wedge_hints: Special-assessment financing and loan servicing for Florida condo associations (lien-secured); 15%-rule budget modeling and lender-eligibility reporting; milestone-inspection repair project procurement; master-policy premium financing.
insider_roles: Community association managers, reserve specialists, condo attorneys, association lending officers at community banks, engineers performing milestone inspections, insurance brokers placing master policies.

name: US third-party property management fees and rent-pricing software
size_basis: Census via FRED: total revenue of real estate property managers (NAICS 53131, employer firms) was $105.2B in 2022 (up from $94.3B in 2021). Includes non-residential managers; no Census residential-only series found. 60,818 residential property manager establishments in 2023 (third-party summary of Census data). A $134.2B figure for NAICS 531311 is unverified.
money_flow: Owners pay property managers (management fees, leasing and maintenance markups) and software vendors (property management systems, revenue management). Signers: regional VP of operations or head of revenue management at an operator; asset manager at an owner.
shock: DOJ-RealPage proposed consent decree (Nov 2025): no real-time use of competitors' nonpublic data, training data at least one year old, no features limiting price decreases. Greystar, Cortland, LivCor and Willow Bridge settled; 10 states still litigating; Maryland HB 434 and Massachusetts H.5222 (2026) pending. Also the Jan 20, 2026 executive order restricting federal financing support for large institutional single-family buyers (build-to-rent carved out; Invitation Homes fell 7.5%).
incumbents: RealPage, Yardi, AppFolio, Entrata and large operators' in-house teams (names from background knowledge, not re-verified). Fragmented small managers underneath.
incumbent_fragility: The dominant revenue-management product is now legally constrained in its core mechanism (pooled competitor data). Small and mid-size landlords lack compliant pricing options.
funded_startups_already_here: EliseAI ($250M Series E Aug 2025 at ~$2.2B; $350M at $4B Sept 2026; reported >$200M ARR by June 2026; secondary); Latchel ($16.7M Series A 2022, Allegion Ventures 2023, single-family maintenance); Belong ($50M total). AI leasing and resident communication is the generic-copilot trap.
wedge_hints: Compliant public-data-only market benchmarking and pricing for small and mid-size landlords; maintenance coordination and turn operations for single-family and build-to-rent operators; audit trails for pricing recommendations.
insider_roles: Revenue managers, regional property managers, antitrust counsel at operators, single-family maintenance operations heads.

name: US building-permit plan review and inspection (government and private providers)
geography: United States (Florida, Texas, California, Tennessee lead on private-provider laws)
size_basis: My derivation: BLS counts ~133,640 construction and building inspectors (May 2023, mean wage $72,880) and ~147,600 jobs in 2024 (OOH, median $72,120) = ~$10-11B in inspector wages alone, excluding plan examiners, permit technicians, software, overhead and private-provider fees. Context: Census Aug 2026 private residential construction $882B SAAR, total $2.2T.
money_flow: Applicants pay permit, plan-review and inspection fees to cities and counties; under private-provider laws they pay licensed third-party reviewers/inspectors directly. Signers: builder/contractor permit coordinator or owner; city building official or CIO.
shock: State laws moving work to private providers when governments miss deadlines: Florida HB 803 (signed May 6, 2026, effective July 1, 2026) sets a 10-business-day clock with private providers (5 for single-trade single-family work), deemed approval on a miss, and reported 50% commercial permit-fee cut when private providers do all review and inspection; California AB 253 (signed Oct 10, 2025) allows third-party review after 30 days; Texas HB 14 (2023) and SB 1450 (2025); Tennessee Public Chapter 771 (2024); Florida HB 683 (2025).
incumbents: Municipal building departments, permitting-system vendors (Tyler Technologies, Accela, Clariti; vendors other than Clariti from background knowledge), code-consulting and third-party review firms.
incumbent_fragility: Public departments are understaffed and statutory clocks now shift volume to private providers faster than departments can hire; permit software vendors sell to the same governments losing volume.
funded_startups_already_here: PermitFlow ($54M Series B Dec 2025 led by Accel; ~$90M total); CivCheck (AI plan review, acquired by Clariti; Honolulu requires it for eligible residential projects from Sept 1, 2026; Denver uses it). No venture-backed licensed private-provider firm combining software and a state inspection license was found.
wedge_hints: Licensed private provider (plan review plus inspection) in FL/TX/CA/TN earning the review and inspection fee with software doing first-pass checks; single-trade permits (solar, HVAC, roofing, electrical) where the shortest clocks apply; inspection scheduling for builders.
insider_roles: Building officials, plan examiners, ICC-certified private providers, permit expediters, builder permit coordinators.

name: US residential construction trade labor (payroll and subcontract labor, plus staffing/payroll/training intermediation)
size_basis: My derivation from BLS (Sept 2026): residential building construction 922.7k + residential specialty trade contractors 2,340.3k = 3.26M jobs; construction average weekly earnings $1,634.25 (~$85k/yr; all-construction payroll ~$710B on 8.364M jobs); at ~$75k for residential trades, payroll is ~$245B. Intermediation layer (staffing, PEO/payroll, workers' comp, recruiting, training) at 5-15% = $12-37B. NAHB (ACS 2024, secondary): immigrants 26.3% of construction workforce; ~1.5M undocumented (Pew via secondary).
money_flow: Builders and remodelers pay framers, drywallers, roofers, concrete and finish crews directly or through subcontractors; intermediaries take a share. Signers: residential contractor owner or builder field-operations VP.
shock: AGC/NCCER 2026 Workforce Survey (released Sept 3, 2026; 1,830 respondents, primary): 87% have craft openings, 50% of those say harder to fill; ~29% report an immigration-enforcement effect in six months (42% in the South); 16% say subcontractors lost workers; 42% say labor shortages delayed projects; >80% raised base pay; 36% increased training spend; 49% expanded online recruiting; data centers pull skilled labor.
incumbents: General staffing firms, union hiring halls and apprenticeship trusts, local labor brokers and informal 1099 crews, PEOs.
incumbent_fragility: Informal labor supply is exposed to I-9/E-Verify risk and enforcement, which is the shock; no incumbent specializes in compliant residential crew supply. Legal premise to check: worker classification, E-Verify duties and joint-employer liability for a platform placing crews.
funded_startups_already_here: Buildforce ($10M Series A July 28, 2026 led by Saepio Capital; commercial electrician staffing). None found for residential framing, drywall, roofing or concrete crews in 3 searches; labor marketplaces have a poor track record (misclassification, thin margins), so 'open' reflects a thin search and a hard model.
wedge_hints: Verified-work-authorization crew staffing for builders; training-to-placement pipelines paid by contractors; payroll, certified-payroll and workers' compensation bundles for small subcontractors.
insider_roles: Residential framing and drywall subcontractors, builder field-operations VPs, union apprenticeship coordinators, immigration and employment counsel, workers' compensation brokers.

name: US manufactured-home sales and chattel (personal-property) finance
size_basis: My derivation: MHI April 2026 report (read): seasonally adjusted annual shipments 103,703; YTD through April 33,054 (-7.3%); 57.7% multi-section. Census prices (secondary): new single-section ~$88-91k, double-section ~$161-164k, excluding land, delivery and setup. Blended ~$131k x ~104k homes = ~$13.6B. FHFA says chattel loans are 70-80% of new manufactured homes, so ~$9-11B chattel originations. Lot rent is a separate stream (MHI: >43,000 communities, ~4.3M homesites), not included.
money_flow: Buyers pay manufacturers, retail dealers and installers; most finance with chattel loans from specialized lenders; many homes sit on leased lots paying lot rent. Signers: buyer via dealer; dealer principal for lender partnerships; chattel lender CEO for servicing/securitization.
shock: June 2026 rule proposals: FHFA proposed replacing Duty to Serve with an outcome framework emphasizing chattel loans (91 FR 37848, published June 24, 2026; final expected effective by Jan 1, 2028); HUD proposed June 12, 2026 to require the permanent chassis only for lowest-floor sections, enabling multistory homes (HUD est. $4,800-6,700 saved per multistory unit; comment closed Aug 11, 2026; not final). ICBA opposes GSE expansion under conservatorship.
incumbents: Clayton (Berkshire; 21st Mortgage, Vanderbilt), Cavco, Skyline Champion (names from background knowledge, not re-verified); chattel lenders; community owners including private equity (Florida, Michigan, Texas heavy).
incumbent_fragility: GSEs do not buy chattel loans, so lenders charge high rates and portfolio their loans; a GSE chattel channel would reprice the market. Lot-rent disputes and state bills pressure community owners.
funded_startups_already_here: Zippy (digital chattel lender, $26M total, last reported July 2023); CoverTree (manufactured-home insurance, $13M Series A May 2024); Tammac Holdings ($60M debt and equity, undated); Apollo manufactured-housing fund ($850M first close late 2025, institutional not a startup). Few venture-funded players found.
wedge_hints: Chattel origination and servicing platform built to GSE standards so loans become securitizable; conversion finance for resident-owned communities; land-lease home insurance and escrow; dealer-side finance workflow.
insider_roles: Manufactured-home retail dealership managers, chattel underwriters and servicers, community operators, state manufactured housing association executives, plant managers, installers.

name: US new-home builder sales incentives and mortgage rate buydowns
size_basis: My derivation: Census 679,000 new homes sold in 2025; Dec 2025 median $414,400; Lennar FY2025 ASP $391,000 => ~$270B annual new-home sales. Lennar said it held ~14% in incentives and price adjustments in Q4 2025 (company release, read); Pulte incentives 10.9% of gross price in Q1 2026 vs 8% a year earlier (secondary); NAHB Sept 2026: two-thirds of builders use incentives, 38% cut prices by avg 6%. At a blended 8-10% the pool is ~$24B (range $16-38B); only the buydown/closing-credit share reaches third parties and I did not find that split.
money_flow: Builders give buyers price cuts, closing credits and rate buydowns; buydown dollars are paid to lenders, often the builder's captive mortgage company. Signers: builder CFOs and heads of mortgage joint ventures.
shock: Incentive intensity rose sharply in late 2025-2026 as new-home inventory built (Lennar ~14%, Dec 16, 2025 release; Lennar guided Q1 2026 gross margin 15-16% vs 18.7% a year earlier). Regulators are watching: Feb 2026 Benesch alert warns promotional rates can mask higher prices; an analysis cited by CUNY coverage found ~20.8% of D.R. Horton and ~30.7% of Lennar FHA loans underwater (secondary, verify).
incumbents: Builder captive lenders: Lennar Financial Services earned $612.5M operating profit in FY2025 (company release); D.R. Horton and Pulte captives (background knowledge). Many incentive packages require the captive lender (Texas buydown guide, secondary).
incumbent_fragility: Incentives are eroding builder gross margins, captive steering faces regulatory scrutiny, and mid-size builders without captives have no neutral buydown capital or administration option. Legal premise to check: seller-concession caps (FHA ~6%, VA ~4%, conventional 3-9% by LTV; from background knowledge, must be verified), RESPA steering, appraisal treatment.
funded_startups_already_here: None found for builder-side buydown pricing, escrow, insurance or hedging (3 searches). Adjacent and older only: Built Technologies (construction lending software), UpEquity (2021 cash-offer rounds).
wedge_hints: Independent buydown pricing and escrow administration for mid-size builders without captives; forward-commitment capital for temporary buydowns; compliance and disclosure audit tooling.
insider_roles: Builder CFOs, captive mortgage heads, builder closing managers, FHA underwriters, settlement agents.

name: US title insurance premiums and settlement
size_basis: ALTA market share analysis (via ALTA release coverage): 2024 title insurance premiums $16.2B, up 7% from 2023; claims paid ~$676M (~4% of premiums). Shares: First American 22.2%, Fidelity National 14.3%, Old Republic 14.3%, Chicago Title 13.4% (Fidelity-owned), Stewart 9.2%.
money_flow: Buyers and lenders pay title premiums through agents, who keep most of the premium and remit a share to underwriters; settlement/escrow fees are additional. Signers: lender secondary-marketing/QC head for waiver-based products; title agent for closing software.
shock: FHFA/Fannie Mae title waiver pilot lets qualifying refinances (LTV under 80%) be sold without a lender title policy or attorney opinion letter; expanded July 2025 with a second vendor (Westcor); Pulte says more expansion coming; pilot scheduled to end Nov 30, 2027. ALTA opposes (fraud ~40% of refinance title claim cost); H.R. 5837 would require title insurance on all GSE loans. No 2026 rule or rate data found.
incumbents: Four underwriter groups hold ~70% of premiums; they own agencies and technology (Endpoint is a First American subsidiary with $220M raised from its parent).
incumbent_fragility: Fragile on lender policies in refinances, not on owner's policies in purchases. The pilot is a regulatory bet that Congress or a new FHFA director could reverse, so the legal premise is weak.
funded_startups_already_here: Qualia (closing platform; $1B-plus valuation in 2020; an unverified aggregator lists a $50M round Sept 2026); Westcor (waiver pilot vendor); Endpoint (parent-funded). Could not verify 2025-26 rounds for Qualia or Pavaso.
wedge_hints: Property-data risk scoring to qualify refinances for waiver; lender-side title quality-control tooling. Honest read: depends on a reversible pilot.
insider_roles: Title agents and escrow officers, underwriting counsel, lender secondary-marketing and QC heads, title claims counsel.

name: US low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC) equity, development and compliance
size_basis: Novogradac estimate of LIHTC equity market ~$25B in 2025, banks ~80% of equity in 2024 (cited in a June 2026 comment letter; secondary, PDF returned 403). Berkadia closed a $100M multi-investor LIHTC fund in Sept 2025.
money_flow: Investors (mostly banks) buy federal tax credits from developers, funding construction/rehab of affordable rentals; property managers then run annual income certifications and compliance for 15+ years. Signers: state housing finance agency allocators, developers, bank CRA/tax-credit officers, owners.
shock: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed July 2025) made permanent from 2026: private-activity-bond test for 4% deals falls from 50% to 25% (bonds issued after Dec 31, 2025) and 9% allocations rise 12%. Novogradac estimates ~1.22M additional affordable rentals over 2026-2035 (~$15.7B added housing credit investment). Open risks: lower equity pricing as volume rises, a June 2026 bank regulatory-capital proposal (details unverified), uncertain HUD rental assistance.
incumbents: Syndicators and investors (Boston Capital, Raymond James, Enterprise; background knowledge), banks, state agencies, compliance monitoring firms and CPA firms such as Novogradac.
incumbent_fragility: Bond-test change creates structuring work incumbents handle by hand; compliance and income recertification are labor-intensive; bank-dominated equity concentrates risk if capital rules change.
funded_startups_already_here: Pronto Housing (affordable housing compliance SaaS, ~$9M total, last round Feb 2024). No LIHTC marketplace or structuring startup found in 2 searches.
wedge_hints: Income-certification and compliance automation for affordable properties; 25%-test structuring and pricing analytics for developers; credit and equity pricing data product; transfer marketplace. Revenue path: 1% of a $25B equity market is $250M, but the market is dominated by bank relationships, so $100M is a stretch.
insider_roles: Syndicator asset managers, state allocators, tax-credit attorneys and CPAs, affordable-housing compliance specialists, bank CRA officers.

name: US personal-auto physical-damage claims (collision + comprehensive): insurer payments for repair, parts, calibration and total-loss payouts
size_basis: NAIC data via trade press: private-passenger physical-damage premiums about $154.3B in 2024 at a 59.9% loss ratio, so about $92B incurred losses (my arithmetic). Includes comprehensive, glass and theft, so the collision-shop revenue slice is smaller and not sized. NAIC report itself not opened.
money_flow: Drivers pay premiums to insurers. Insurers pay repair shops (labor, paint, parts, ADAS calibrations), parts distributors and OEMs, and cash out total losses to owners. Estimating and valuation platforms (CCC, Mitchell/Enlyte, Solera) take per-claim fees.
shock: 25% Section 232 tariff on non-USMCA auto parts effective May 3, 2025. CCC Crash Course 2026 (Mar 31, 2026, covering 2025): record 23.1% total-loss frequency, calibrations on 28.3% of repairable estimates (up from 21.8%), 72% of total-loss valuations on vehicles 7+ years old. Secondary: average repair cost $4,818, repairable claim volume -9.7%. Parts prices +3.8% and repair/maintenance +5% y/y in Apr 2026 (Scripps). NOTE: the widely repeated $3.4B / 2.7% tariff figure is a 2018 PCI projection, not current. An S&P headline claims a one-time $12B+ private-auto tariff hit (page not opened, unverified).
incumbents: CCC Intelligent Solutions (public), Mitchell/Enlyte and Solera/Audatex own estimating, valuation and workflow. Insurers steer volume via direct-repair programs. Large MSOs (Crash Champions, Caliber, Gerber) are consolidating; Crash Champions renewed with CCC and expanded AI estimating in Aug 2026.
incumbent_fragility: Insurer and shop are adversaries paying the same platform vendor, so neither can fix the other's incentives. Total-loss valuation (23.1% of claims) is the one step where the policyholder has no advocate. Each new calibration is a line item nobody in the chain owns. Tariff pass-through is slow and uneven across parts, and shops are squeezed between insurer-set labor rates and rising parts cost.
funded_startups_already_here: Revv ($20M Series A, about late 2024; AI inspections and supplier links for independent shops; lead investor conflicts between sources), ServiceUp ($55M Series B led by PeakSpan, Jul 2025; $70M total; fleet and insurance repair management), Tractable ($65M Series E, 2023; AI damage estimating), VaraFix (AI estimate review launched Aug 25, 2026; no funding disclosed), CrashBay ($1.25M, Apr 2024). Nothing funded found on ADAS-calibration networks or policyholder-side total-loss audit.
wedge_hints: (1) ADAS calibration capacity and scheduling for shops. (2) Tariff-aware parts sourcing and price-lock for independent shops (PartsTrader is the incumbent to check). (3) Missed-operations and supplement audit for shops. (4) Policyholder-side total-loss valuation audit on contingency; check state total-loss rules and public-adjuster licensing. $100M revenue is about 0.11% of loss dollars, so a thin per-claim take works if one channel (large MSO or carrier program) is won.
insider_roles: Collision shop estimators and owners, DRP managers at carriers, total-loss adjusters, ADAS calibration technicians, parts managers, public adjusters, auto-claims litigators.

name: US consumer auto-loan interest and fees, with the subprime servicing, collections and repossession layer under stress
size_basis: NY Fed Q2 2026 auto balances $1.713T times an assumed blended APR of roughly 7.5-8% (my assumption; Experian Q1 2026 originations average 6.39% new, 11.43% used, 21.77% deep-subprime used) gives about $130B interest a year. Subprime was 15.75% of Q1 2026 financing; subprime-only slice probably $40-55B (my estimate). Servicing/collections cost not sized from a source.
money_flow: Borrowers pay interest and fees to banks, captives, credit unions, finance companies and buy-here-pay-here dealers. Lenders pay servicers, collection agencies, repo agents and auctions for servicing, recovery and remarketing.
shock: Tricolor Holdings filed Chapter 7 on Sept 10, 2025 (alleged double-pledged collateral); Vervent took over servicing of about 100,000 loans within days. Fitch subprime 60+ day delinquency 6.9% in Jan 2026, reported as a record since the 1990s (vendor-cited; Philadelphia Fed argues it overstates new distress). NY Fed Q2 2026: 3.00% of balances flowed into 90+ day delinquency, most new serious auto delinquencies since 2010. Cox: about 1.73M repossessions in 2024, highest since 2009.
incumbents: Captives and banks (Ally, Capital One, Santander Consumer, Credit Acceptance, Westlake; from memory), independent subprime lenders and BHPH dealers on legacy servicing systems (Megasys-type vendors), collection BPOs paid on recovery, successor servicers such as Vervent.
incumbent_fragility: Independent subprime lenders have thin operations and fail abruptly (Tricolor), forcing emergency servicing transfers. Collection BPOs are paid on recovery, so they have no incentive to prevent default. Legacy servicing systems cannot do channel-level outreach or fast portfolio onboarding. Regulator enforcement pressure that used to fund compliance vendors has eased (my understanding, not sourced).
funded_startups_already_here: Salient ($60M Series A, Jul 2025, loan-servicing AI; Axios Pro headline only, paywalled), Prodigal (AI collections for subprime auto; funding unverified), Vervent (successor servicer; ownership and funding unverified). No funded startup found focused on post-repo recovery, deficiency balances or a standing backup-servicing utility.
wedge_hints: (1) Warm backup and successor servicing for small subprime lenders and ABS issuers (payers: warehouse lenders, ABS investors). (2) Early-intervention and extension programs priced per saved loan, below expected loss avoided (round 1 failed on this price/value test). (3) Post-repossession recovery and remarketing including deficiency balances. $100M revenue is about 0.08% of interest dollars.
insider_roles: BHPH dealer principals, subprime collections managers, repossession agents and forwarders, auction remarketing managers, ABS investors and rating analysts (Fitch, KBRA), consumer-bankruptcy attorneys.

name: US homeowners' residential HVAC replacement and installation (equipment plus labor)
size_basis: AHRI 2025 shipments: 7.75M central AC and heat-pump units plus 3.25M gas furnaces (about 11.0M). Assuming 75-80% are replacements at about $6.5k average installed (both my assumptions) gives about $55B. Cross-check: Carrier CEO cited about 130M installed systems and about 6% replaced yearly, about 8M (secondary). Range $40-70B.
money_flow: Homeowners pay local contractors (often under duress after a failure). Contractors buy from distributors, who buy from OEMs. Third-party lenders finance many jobs. Lead-gen platforms sit on the front end.
shock: R-410A equipment manufacturing ended Jan 1, 2025 (A2L refrigerant transition; William Blair estimated 8-10% price increases). Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum and copper content. Federal 25C efficiency credit ended for installs after Dec 31, 2025 (contractor source; IRS page not opened). Result: 2025 central AC and heat-pump shipments -20.0%, with Oct and Nov 2025 down 49.4% and 46.4% y/y (partly pull-forward and a strong 2024 base).
incumbents: OEMs (Carrier, Trane, Lennox, Daikin, Rheem and others), distributors, a very fragmented base of local contractors, some private-equity roll-ups (not sourced here), lead-gen platforms.
incumbent_fragility: Homeowners buy with no price visibility and the comfort-advisor model depends on one-visit closes. OEMs cannot sell direct without breaking their dealer networks (channel conflict). Contractors face technician shortages and a post-credit, post-price-hike demand hole. Price opacity is the main thing a new entrant can attack.
funded_startups_already_here: Jetson ($50M Series A, Jan 2026, led by Eclipse; vertically integrated heat-pump installer, 1,000+ systems, CO/MA/NY and California from June 2026), Quilt ($20M Series B, date unconfirmed), Arch ($6.2M seed, date unconfirmed), Tetra ($10.5M seed, 2023), Aira (EU, EUR 150M). Field-service software incumbents such as ServiceTitan exist (not re-verified).
wedge_hints: (1) Instant replace-on-failure quote, financing and install booking for conventional AC and furnace, sold on price transparency (the credit tailwind is gone and heat-pump startups are not focused here). (2) Contractor buy-side tools: price and availability across distributors, A2L compliance and refrigerant documentation. (3) Good-better-best quoting embedded at the distributor counter. $100M revenue is about 0.18% of the pool.
insider_roles: HVAC contractor owners, comfort advisors and sales techs, distributor branch managers and counter staff, OEM territory reps, home inspectors, utility rebate program managers.

name: US title insurance premiums (plus the attached settlement-fee stack)
size_basis: ALTA 2025 market share analysis (published May 22, 2026): $18.5B premium, +13.8%. Claims paid just over $667M, about 3.6% of premium (my arithmetic). Top shares: First American 23.1%, Fidelity National 14.5%, Old Republic 14.0%, Chicago Title 13.1%, Stewart 10.9% (Fidelity and Chicago are both FNF brands, about 27.6% combined by my sum).
money_flow: Buyers, sellers and refinancers pay premiums at closing to title agents and underwriters. The lender's policy is required; the owner's is optional. Agents keep most of the premium (typical split from memory, not verified).
shock: Fannie Mae title-waiver pilot (started Nov 2024 with Doma, Westcor added Jul 2025; refinances under 80% LTV only; test ends Nov 30, 2027). FHFA Director Pulte said Fannie is working to expand it (reported Jun 26, 2026). KBW: pilot 'remains very small' and refinances are under 10% of title revenue. Fannie scrapped an earlier waiver pilot in Aug 2023 after industry pushback. The shock is real but modest so far; the pool matters because of the 3.6% payout ratio.
incumbents: Five-brand underwriter oligopoly with thousands of independent agents; trade group ALTA, which has already defeated one waiver pilot. Rates are filed or, in some states, promulgated (Texas; from memory).
incumbent_fragility: Any move toward pricing near expected loss would cut their premium base by an order of magnitude, and agents, who keep most of the premium, are their distribution. They cannot cut price or embrace waivers without destroying their own economics, so they respond with lobbying and risk arguments (First American study released alongside the expansion news).
funded_startups_already_here: Titl (Miami, $2.5M seed, 2026), Qualia (closing software; Series D-II $40M Apr 2021), Endpoint ($150M corporate minority round, Oct 2021), Blueprint Title ($16M Series B, Sep 2021), Spruce (2018), Doma (pilot's first vendor; prior-wave underwriting-startup economics were poor, from memory). Very little funded in 2023-26.
wedge_hints: (1) Automated title-risk scoring and attorney-opinion-letter workflow for low-LTV refinances, HELOCs and second liens, sold to lenders (budget line: closing-cost reduction and QC). (2) Consumer closing-cost transparency is a distribution wedge, not a revenue line. Check the legal premise first: state title-insurance statutes, rate filing and licensing, and whether the GSEs buy loans without a lender's policy beyond the pilot. $100M revenue is about 0.54% of premium.
insider_roles: Title and escrow officers, underwriting counsel, agency owners, lender QC and closing managers, county recorders, real-estate attorneys in attorney-opinion states.

name: US families' spend on paid child care (centers and family child care)
size_basis: Committee for Economic Development / Conference Board: $68.5B industry revenue in 2022 (86% center-based, 624,300 businesses). Includes subsidy dollars. Child Care Aware 2025 national average price $13,184 per child (about 10% of median two-parent income, 33% for single parents). Parents' out-of-pocket share not found; EPI estimated $42B for under-5s in 2020. Probably higher now.
money_flow: Parents pay (after-tax or pre-tax through dependent-care FSAs) or state subsidies (CCDF) pay about 624,300 providers, mostly small centers and home-based family child care.
shock: Dependent-care FSA cap rises from $5,000 to $7,500 for tax years starting Jan 1, 2026 (law signed Jul 4, 2025). Section 45F employer child-care credit rises from 25% to 40% (50% small business) with cap $500k ($600k small), for 2026 expenses, and payments to intermediaries such as CCR&Rs now qualify. New Mexico began no-cost universal child care Nov 1, 2025, the first state. Supply is shrinking: home-based providers down 17,235 since 2019.
incumbents: Tens of thousands of small providers, large chains (Bright Horizons, KinderCare; from memory), state CCDF subsidy administrators and CCR&Rs, DCFSA benefit administrators.
incumbent_fragility: Razor-thin provider margins and low wages (center-worker average $28,185 in 2022) mean providers cannot raise price without losing families, and state subsidy rates lag cost. Subsidy payments are slow. Benefit administrators have no incentive to push employers toward the new 45F credit.
funded_startups_already_here: Brightwheel ($88.8M total; last round Series C, Feb 2021), Lillio/HiMama (Series B $55.6M, Nov 2021), Kinside ($12M, Jun 2022), Winnie ($9M, 2019), Upwards/WeeCare ($21M Series B, about Feb 2024), Bumo ($67M, Sep 2025; VCBacked only, unverified), Kidola ($2.5M, Jun 2025). Little aimed at employer-credit packaging or subsidy-payment speed.
wedge_hints: (1) 45F intermediary product: an employer buys capacity or subsidies through a managed network and claims a 40-50% credit; payer is the employer's HR or finance head with the tax credit as the budget line (check how 45F treats for-profit intermediaries and whether employers will fund the cash outlay). (2) Fast subsidy reimbursement or payment advances for small providers. $100M revenue is about 0.15% of the pool.
insider_roles: Center directors, family child-care owners, state CCDF administrators and CCR&R directors, employer benefits managers, child-care licensing inspectors.

name: US private-pay in-home care for older adults (non-medical aides, companions, live-in)
size_basis: LOW CONFIDENCE. IBISWorld puts 'elderly and disabled services' at $80.1B in 2025; Home Care Pulse reported agencies at 65% private-pay revenue in 2020 (down from 72% in 2018). 80.1 x 0.65 is about $52B (my derivation mixing scopes). NY DFS cites about $55B of total out-of-pocket long-term care in 2018, including nursing homes, so not like-for-like. Median aide pay $16.78/hour in 2024.
money_flow: Older adults and families pay agencies (franchise and independent) or hire aides directly (household employment). Public payers (Medicaid, VA) draw on the same workforce.
shock: OBBBA (Jul 4, 2025) cuts federal Medicaid by about $911B over 10 years (KFF); Medicaid pays about two-thirds of home- and community-based services; nearly one in three home care workers is an immigrant. DOL proposed (Jul 2, 2025) restoring the FLSA companionship/live-in exemptions for agencies and on Jul 25, 2025 halted enforcement of the 2013 rule (final status unconfirmed; many states require overtime anyway). TPS for Haitians ended after a Supreme Court ruling (reported Jul 2026), about 330,000 people, Haitians about 7% of the workforce per LeadingAge. CMS GUIDE dementia model: Papa joined Jun 2026.
incumbents: Franchisors and independents (Home Instead, Right at Home, Visiting Angels and similar; from memory), thousands of local agencies, gray-market direct hires.
incumbent_fragility: Labor supply is the binding constraint: immigration enforcement shrinks the pool as demand rises, and agencies cannot raise wages without pricing out families. Private-pay share is falling as public programs grow. Agencies run on referrals and local reputation with little tech.
funded_startups_already_here: Papa ($242M total; last big round Nov 2021; GUIDE partnership Jun 2026), Hera ($27M Series A, Jun 26, 2026, Bain Capital Ventures; coordination), Carallel (Series A-II about $2M, Jan 2025), Cariloop (Series C, Apr 2024), Wellthy ($25.5M Series C, May 2023), Hometeam and ConcertoCare (undated). Honor's $140M Series D appears to be 2021 (pre-window).
wedge_hints: (1) Household-employer payroll and compliance for families that hire directly, cutting the agency markup (labor law varies by state). (2) Caregiver supply: training, credentialing, visa-eligible pipelines, backup-coverage pools. (3) VA Aid and Attendance and LTC-insurance claim filing for families. $100M revenue is about 0.20% of the pool, but unit economics depend on take rate against very tight labor supply.
insider_roles: Agency owners and administrators, geriatric care managers, elder-law attorneys, hospital discharge planners and social workers, VA benefits advisors, state Medicaid HCBS program managers, immigration attorneys, aides themselves.

name: US estate settlement (post-death administration) fees paid by estates and heirs
size_basis: LOW CONFIDENCE; no authoritative national total exists. CDC provisional: 3,094,593 deaths in 2025. Assuming about half need formal administration (my assumption) at professional fees above $8,500 (WealthManagement) gives about $13B; the same article estimates North American hidden costs at $15-16B (author's estimate). Consumer guides cite 3-6% of estate value. Executor time is excluded: about 570 hours and 16 months average (EstateExec survey of about 1,200 adults); Alix cites 12-18 months and up to 900 hours. Realistic range $12-25B.
money_flow: Estates and heirs pay probate and trust attorneys, CPAs (final 1040, 1041, 706), appraisers, real-estate agents, corporate trustees and courts. Funeral spend is a separate flow.
shock: Cerulli projects $124T of wealth transfer through 2048 ($105T to heirs), with about $2.5T a year already inherited. The federal estate-tax exemption is $15M per person for 2026 deaths (OBBBA), indexed from 2027, so work shifts from tax planning to plain administration. Wealth managers are buying in to retain inherited assets: Alix's $20M Series A (Jul 2025, Acrew) included Charles Schwab and Edward Jones Ventures.
incumbents: Fragmented small-firm probate bar billing hourly, bank trust departments, online will companies (LegalZoom, Trust and Will; from memory), state courts.
incumbent_fragility: 50 state probate regimes and paper-based courts, and nobody owns the end-to-end job. Hourly billing rewards the 12-18 month timeline, so lawyers cannot easily productize. Banks, brokerages and insurers each handle thousands of death claims a year with no good intake process.
funded_startups_already_here: Alix ($20M Series A, Jul 2025; $30.65M total; Schwab and Edward Jones backing), EverSettled ($5M seed led by Emergence, reported Jul 17, 2026; CB Insights only, unverified), ClearEstate (Canada, CAD 16.8M Series A, 2021, pre-window). Empathy, Lantern and Cake not found in this search. Only Alix is well funded, and it owns the wealth-manager channel.
wedge_hints: (1) Executor operating system with a flat-fee attorney network in high-volume states (CA, FL, TX, NY). (2) Deceased-account intake for banks, brokerages and insurers (payer is a servicing-cost budget line, not the grieving heir). (3) Real-estate disposition as the monetizing step. Legal premise to check: unauthorized-practice-of-law rules (Arizona ABS and Utah sandbox allow non-lawyer ownership). $100M revenue is about 0.67% of the pool and likely needs a channel partner rather than direct-to-heir marketing.
insider_roles: Probate attorneys and paralegals, probate court clerks, bank trust officers and deceased-accounts ops staff, recent executors, funeral directors, estate-sale liquidators, fiduciary-return CPAs, life-insurance claims adjusters.

name: US pet owners' spend on veterinary care
size_basis: APPA 2026 State of the Industry: 'vet care and product sales' $41.0B in 2025 inside a $158B US pet industry (2026 projection $165B). Private equity spent $45B on vet deals 2017-2022 (PitchBook via Stateline); PBS reports vet costs up about 60% since 2014.
money_flow: Owners pay mostly out of pocket (pet insurance is small) to clinics, increasingly corporate (Mars, NVA, Thrive; from memory and Stateline). Clinics buy drugs and diagnostics from Zoetis, IDEXX and distributors.
shock: UK CMA final report (Mar 24, 2026): vet prices +63% over 2016-23 vs 31.3% inflation; remedies include price lists, prescription fee caps and a comparison site; online pharmacies 50-60% cheaper on common medicines (foreign precedent, not US law). In the US, Chewy closed its roughly $400M purchase of Modern Animal on May 21, 2026 (clinics 18 to 47), and telehealth VCPR laws are loosening (Rhode Island signed Jun 23, 2026; Arizona effective Sep 12, 2026; about 8 states). No US FTC action on vet consolidation found.
incumbents: Mars Petcare (VCA, Banfield, BluePearl), NVA, Thrive and other PE-backed groups; Petco; Chewy Vet Care; Zoetis and IDEXX upstream.
incumbent_fragility: Corporate groups earn margin on drugs, diagnostics and bundled pricing, which is exactly what price-transparency and prescription-portability rules attack (as the CMA is doing). Debt-funded roll-ups cannot cut price, and a vet shortage limits capacity.
funded_startups_already_here: Modern Animal ($46M, Sep 2025; then acquired by Chewy for about $400M), Supertails (India, $30M Series C, Feb 2026), Vetster ($30M Series B, 2022, pre-window), Invetx ($60.5M Series B, undated), PetPharm (Korea, Series B 2025), Chewy Vet Care (incumbent entrant).
wedge_hints: (1) Buying group and services for independent clinic owners resisting or exiting a roll-up (valuations were 2-10x per Stateline). (2) Price-comparison and estimate-transparency layer on the model the CMA mandated. (3) Written-prescription portability to online pharmacies (check state law). $100M revenue is about 0.24% of the pool.
insider_roles: Independent clinic owners, practice managers, vet techs, veterinary M&A brokers, compounding pharmacists, pet-insurance claims adjusters, emergency-hospital managers.

name: US individuals' tax-preparation fees (paid preparers; DIY software not in the sourced figure)
size_basis: IBISWorld: $15.0B for US tax preparation services in 2026. About 54% of individual returns for tax year 2021 were paid-prepared (GAO 2024, quoted secondhand). H&R Block FY2026 (June 30, 2026) revenue $3.95B, +4.9%; FY2027 guidance $4.11-4.16B. DIY software (Intuit and others) adds an unsourced amount; total probably $20B+ (my estimate).
money_flow: Taxpayers pay paid preparers (H&R Block, Jackson Hewitt, CPAs, enrolled agents, independent shops) or DIY software (Intuit and others). Bank products (refund transfer fees) ride on top.
shock: The IRS told the 25 participating states in Nov 2025 that Direct File will not run in the 2026 season, with no launch date set. It accepted 296,531 returns in 2025, more than twice 2024. Free File remains (AGI $89,000 or less). The 2025 budget law directed a task force on public-private partnerships to replace it. New 2025-law deductions (tips, overtime, seniors, car-loan interest) add complexity (not separately sourced). Honest read: the shock helped incumbents; H&R Block assisted revenue rose on higher net average charge and volume.
incumbents: Intuit (TurboTax) and H&R Block hold the consumer layer along with the Free File partnership; Jackson Hewitt; CPAs and enrolled agents; thousands of independent shops.
incumbent_fragility: Not fragile on price; the gaps are segments they under-serve (1099 and gig filers, multi-state filers, ITIN filers, simple filers who paid because the free option was hard to find). The IRS-built free option is gone, so a state-level or privately funded free/low-cost option is now an open lane.
funded_startups_already_here: Filed ($17.2M seed, May 2025; pro-facing), Fifteenth ($8.25M seed, Feb 2025; founders and tech employees), TaxGPT ($4.6M seed, Feb 2025), Taxwire ($25M seed or Series A, Jun 2026; single aggregator, unverified), TaxScouts (UK Series A). Column Tax: funding not confirmed. Funding clusters in pro-side AI tools, not consumer filing.
wedge_hints: (1) White-label state free-filing (the Direct File architecture) sold to state revenue departments; budget line is the state DOR e-file program, and the federal task force may add demand. (2) Embedded filing inside payroll, gig-platform and banking apps for 1099 filers, sold per return. (3) Enrolled-agent network for simple-but-not-DIY returns. $100M revenue is about 0.67% of the sourced $15B pool.
insider_roles: Enrolled agents, seasonal preparers and franchise owners, VITA coordinators, state DOR e-file managers, Free File Alliance participants, refund-transfer bank product managers.

name: SNAP benefits redeemed at US grocers, plus state administration and retailer compliance spend
size_basis: USAFacts: federal government spent $101.7B on SNAP in FY2025. Average benefit $188 per person per month. Participation about 39.5M in Dec 2025, down from about 43M a year earlier (unlabeled USDA table). The revenue pool for a vendor is administration plus retailer compliance, a small fraction of this figure.
money_flow: Federal government funds EBT cards. Recipients spend at about 250,000 authorized retailers (count not verified). EBT processors (for example FIS in South Dakota) and POS vendors sit in the middle. States pay administration costs.
shock: OBBBA (Jul 4, 2025) cuts SNAP by about $186B over 2025-2034 (CBO). States pay up to 15% of benefits from FY2028 scaled by payment-error rate, and their share of administration rises from 50% to 75%. Food-restriction waivers began Jan 1, 2026 in IN, IA, NE, UT and WV, about 18 states approved, and a National Grocers Association letter (Apr 2026) cites 22 state pilots with thousands of unresolved product-classification questions. Retail trade groups estimate $1.6B initial losses. In Jun 2026 a federal district court ruled USDA exceeded its authority approving waivers for five states (appeal status unknown).
incumbents: EBT processors, POS vendors, grocers' IT teams, product-data firms.
incumbent_fragility: There is no single national SKU-level eligibility dataset; each state defines categories differently and retailers update systems themselves. State agencies face a new hard cost line (75% admin share and error-rate-based benefit share) with no tooling budget. Federal court ruling adds legal uncertainty for restriction-based products.
funded_startups_already_here: Propel (Fresh EBT) raised a $4M seed in 2017 and $12.8M Series A in 2018; no 2023-26 rounds found. No funded startup found on SKU-level eligibility or state error-rate reduction.
wedge_hints: (1) SKU-level SNAP eligibility data service (UPC denied-product lists by state) sold to retailers, POS vendors and EBT processors. (2) Payment-error-rate reduction tooling (income and asset verification, duplicate-participation checks) for states that now pay up to 15% of benefits. Caveat: retailer ARPU is small and the buyer is government with long procurement cycles, so $100M realistically needs the state-agency payer.
insider_roles: Grocery front-end and IT managers, convenience-store compliance leads (NACS), POS and EBT-processor product managers, state SNAP quality-control directors, USDA FNS retailer-management staff, food-bank benefits navigators.

name: US data centers' spend on onsite / behind-the-meter power (engines, turbines, fuel cells, batteries, backup) and the services around it
geography: United States (global figure ~$18B in 2026 shown for reference)
size_basis: DERIVED. Enverus forecasts 22.5 GW of behind-the-meter generation for data centers in 2026-2030, about 4.5 GW/yr; at an assumed blended installed cost of $1.5-2.5M/MW (my assumption: recips low end, turbines and fuel cells high end) that is $7-11B/yr, midpoint ~$9B. Cross-checks: MarketsandMarkets (paid) global onsite/BTM data-center power ~$18B in 2026 rising to $87B by 2032; Baker Hughes >$25B BTM/off-grid opportunity by 2030. Reality check: Cleanview counts ~90 GW in the pipeline but only ~2 GW operating mid-2026 (mostly xAI Memphis), 5-13 GW by end-2027, so the pool is large on paper and slow in practice.
money_flow: Hyperscalers, neoclouds and colos (or developers like Crusoe on their behalf) pay engine/turbine/fuel-cell OEMs, EPC and electrical contractors, gas suppliers and pipeline-lateral builders, and increasingly 'power-as-a-service' owners who finance and operate the plant (Bloom/Brookfield model). Utilities lose the load or the rate-base growth.
shock: Heavy-duty gas turbine and grid-interconnection scarcity pushes buyers onsite. GE Vernova's gas backlog plus slot reservations hit 116 GW at Q2 2026 with 2031 delivery slots being sold; Caterpillar power generation grew 72% on data-center demand (per MarketsandMarkets). DOE asked FERC for a large-load interconnection rule by 2026-04-30; FERC instead opened six FPA 206 show-cause proceedings on 2026-06-18 (only confirmed at that level of detail). Texas SB 6 (2025-06-20) requires large loads >=75 MW to disclose backup generation and accept emergency curtailment.
incumbents: Caterpillar, Cummins, Wartsila, GE Vernova (aeroderivatives), Siemens Energy, Solar Turbines, Bloom Energy (Brookfield financing framework expanded to $25B in June 2026; a framework, not booked revenue), EPC firms and gas midstream capture the money by selling equipment and installation.
incumbent_fragility: OEMs are supply-capped, not demand-capped, so they cannot absorb more orders; utilities cannot deliver power on a data-center timeline. The scarce inputs are permits, engineering hours, commissioning crews and fuel supply, not money. Air-permit exposure is real: EPA reportedly found (Jan 2026, secondary report) that xAI's 'temporary/portable' Memphis turbines are not exempt; the county permit for 15 turbines expires 2027-01-02.
funded_startups_already_here: Crusoe (Series E $1.375B Oct 2025; Series F ~$3B+ at ~$30B valuation, reported closed Sept 2026), Bloom Energy (public), ProEnergy (private; repurposed CF6 jet-engine cores, 21 turbines sold for >1 GW of data-center bridging power), Emerald AI ($150M Series A at $1.05B, 2026-08-25; makes data centers flexible loads), DG Matrix ($60M Series A, Feb 2026; ~90% of pipeline is data centers). VoltaGrid is a named private provider but its funding was not verified.
wedge_hints: Air-permit and emissions-compliance engineering for onsite turbines/engines; commissioning and controls integration (islanded microgrids with grid-forming batteries); gas supply and lateral procurement; bridging-power rental fleets; secondary-market and refurbished-core brokerage; replacing diesel backup under tightening air limits. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): permitting + commissioning + controls is ~300 campuses x $300k = ~$90M; reaching $100M+ most plausibly means owning assets or financing, which is the crowded layer.
insider_roles: Data-center development VPs of power; utility large-load account managers; air-permit consultants; OEM dealer application engineers; interconnection consultants; midstream gas marketers.

name: US purchases of power and distribution transformers (utilities, developers, data centers, industrials)
size_basis: Commercial (paid) estimates disagree: MarketsandMarkets $13.76B in 2025 rising to $19.0B by 2030; Arizton $16.5B (2024); GMI $12.2B (2024); narrow-definition outliers $0.7-3.4B. I used the broad definition (~$14B). Cross-check: EEI transmission capex $39.9B (2025 projected) and distribution capex $50.9B (2023), so $14B is plausibly 10-15% of grid capex. Wood Mackenzie: imports ~80% of power-transformer and ~50% of distribution-transformer supply in 2025.
money_flow: Utilities (close to half of distribution-transformer demand in one global forecast), IPPs/developers, data centers and industrials pay manufacturers and electrical distributors; most units are imported.
shock: Section 232 tariffs took effect 2025-08-18 (50% on the non-US steel/aluminum content of transformers). Wood Mackenzie projected 2025 supply deficits of 30% (power) and 10% (distribution); generator step-up lead times passed 160 weeks by Q1 2026; DOE cites >30 months for distribution units; ~40M US distribution transformers are past expected service life; only one US grain-oriented steel producer (Cleveland-Cliffs).
incumbents: Hitachi Energy (>$1B US investment announced 2025-09-04; $457M Virginia large-power-transformer plant broke ground June 2026, operating 2H 2028), Siemens Energy, GE Vernova (closed $5.3B buyout of Prolec GE on 2026-02-02; Prolec 2025 revenue ~$3B), Eaton, Hubbell and regional makers; distributors resell.
incumbent_fragility: New capacity does not arrive until 2027-2028; grain-oriented steel is single-sourced; every utility has custom specs, which blocks standard-unit mass production; utilities hold spares in silos. Manufacturers have cyclical-capex scars and no reason to over-build, so they cannot respond quickly.
funded_startups_already_here: All solid-state-transformer hardware: Heron Power ($140M Series B, Feb 2026, a16z American Dynamism + Breakthrough; $38M Series A in 2025; 40 GW plant, production 2H 2027), DG Matrix ($60M Series A, Feb 2026), Amperesand ($80M Series A, late 2025), Hyperscale Power (EUR 5M seed, Mar 2026). None found funded on repair/refurbishment, spares pooling or spec standardization (searched solid-state and general terms only; 'none found', not 'none exist').
wedge_hints: Transformer repair/rewind and life extension for the ~40M units past service life; mutualized spares pool or group purchasing for ~2,000 public-power utilities and ~800+ co-ops (approximate counts, unverified); standard-spec consortium to aggregate orders into factory slots; condition-monitoring analytics; certified used-transformer marketplace with test data; tariff/import-compliance brokerage. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): a consortium brokering ~$2-3B/yr of co-op and muni purchases at 3-4% is $60-120M.
insider_roles: Utility transformer asset managers; co-op and muni procurement directors; transformer repair-shop owners; distributor reps (Graybar/Wesco type); transformer test labs; NRECA/APPA purchasing staff.

name: US electric utilities' vegetation management (line clearance and tree trimming)
size_basis: Power Magazine (post-LA fires, Jan 2025) estimates ~$7B/yr; Harris Williams (2022 report) via Middle Market Growth estimates ~$8B/yr and calls it often the largest utility O&M line item; midpoint ~$7.5B. Cross-check (DERIVED): Davey Tree's utility segment grew $54.2M (+5.4%) in 2025, implying ~$1.06B segment revenue; Asplundh is private (~$4.7B revenue in 2021 per Wikipedia, single-source, low confidence). Other reports claim $8.2B (US-ish) to $30B (global) and are paid-report quality.
money_flow: Utilities pay line-clearance contractors (Asplundh, Davey, Wright Tree, Lewis, ACRT and others) by unit price, crew-hour or per-mile; costs are recovered from ratepayers as O&M. Inspection and LiDAR vendors sit on top.
shock: Wildfire liability became existential and visible: Xcel agreed to pay ~$640M for the Marshall Fire (2025-09-24); SCE booked $1.6B of Eaton Fire losses by 2026-06-30 and exhausted self-insurance on 2026-02-11 (outside Jefferies estimate of exposure: $13.5B); PacifiCorp was found grossly negligent for Oregon's 2020 fires. California SB 254 (Sept 2025) requires cost-per-avoided-ignition reporting, pushing utilities from fixed-cycle trimming toward risk-based trimming.
incumbents: Asplundh (private), Davey Tree (public), Wright Tree, Lewis Tree, ACRT, plus engineering/LiDAR firms, capture the money by selling crew-hours and unit-priced work.
