incumbent_fragility: They sell crew-hours, so analytics that cut crew-hours threaten their revenue (business-model conflict); little software culture; utility foresters often manage work in spreadsheets and GIS exports. Spend verification is weak (who trimmed what, to which clearance, at what price), and cycle-based schedules are indefensible after Marshall/Eaton while regulators want cost-effectiveness proof the incumbents' data cannot supply.
funded_startups_already_here: Overstory ($43M Series B, Nov 2025, Blume-led with Energy Impact Partners and B Capital; $14M Series A in 2023). Adjacent: Pano AI (camera detection, $44M Series B, $89M total, 15 utilities incl. Xcel) and Gridware ($55M Series B 2025-11-17; $26.4M Series A Jan 2025, Sequoia). Nobody found funded on work verification, invoice audit, crew marketplaces or small-utility foresters.
wedge_hints: Work-verification and unit-price invoice audit for utility VM spend; crew scheduling and subcontractor marketplace with storm-surge staffing; hazard-tree identification for the highest-risk circuits; herbicide-program verification; co-ops and munis with no staff forester. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): audit/verification software at 1-2% of a $7.5B pool is $75-150M only if it reaches most large IOUs; a crew marketplace taking 5% of subcontract flow is bigger but operationally harder.
insider_roles: Utility vegetation managers and ISA-certified utility arborists; line-clearance general foremen; contractor estimators; wildfire-plan regulatory staff; forestry GIS analysts; insurance risk engineers.

name: US utility wildfire mitigation programs (undergrounding, covered conductor, sensing, inspection, PSPS), California-led
geography: United States (California-led; also CO, OR, UT and other Western states)
size_basis: DERIVED. PG&E alone: 2025 wildfire mitigation spending estimated >$6B (PNNL May 2025, citing PG&E). The two California IOUs' wildfire mitigation plans were reported to detail >$23B of expenditures through 2025 (about $7.7B/yr over 2023-25 combined; source is a Buchalter title I could not open). Add Xcel ($1.9B proposed 2025-27 in Colorado alone), Berkshire Hathaway Energy (wildfire capex rising from $188M in 2022 to $797M in 2027), PacifiCorp, SDG&E and others to reach ~$9B. Capital is 55-86% of the spend across four utilities that split it.
money_flow: Ratepayers fund utilities (capex into rate base); utilities pay EPC/line contractors, equipment makers (covered conductor, fast-trip protection), sensor/software vendors and vegetation contractors; the California Wildfire Fund backstops liability.
shock: California SB 254 (signed Sept 2025) adds an $18B Wildfire Fund continuation account (half ratepayer via an extended charge, half shareholders; PG&E 47.85%, SCE 47.85%, SDG&E 4.3%), bars $6B of wildfire-mitigation capex from earning a return in rate base, requires cost-per-avoided-ignition reporting, and exempts undergrounding plan approvals from CEQA. Utilities lose return on part of the spend, so cheaper and provably effective measures win.
incumbents: The utilities themselves, EPC contractors (Quanta, MasTec), equipment OEMs and engineering firms capture the money.
incumbent_fragility: Regulation now demands a metric (cost per avoided ignition) that nobody has a standard methodology or data for, and return on $6B of spend was removed, flipping incentives toward cost-effective options. Liability rules can still move: an August 2026 tentative ruling declined to hold SCE liable without a trial (trial set for 2027).
funded_startups_already_here: Pano AI ($44M Series B, $89M total, 15 utilities), Gridware ($55M Series B, Nov 2025), Overstory ($43M Series B, Nov 2025). Other fire-modeling vendors exist but were not verified. Detection/sensing is the busy layer.
wedge_hints: Cost-per-avoided-ignition analytics and wildfire-plan compliance reporting; PSPS customer notification plus medical-baseline backup-power logistics; inspection QA (drone/ground); covered-conductor install productivity; wildfire plans for Western co-ops and munis that must now file them. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): analytics/compliance software at 1% of $9B is only ~$90M, so reaching $100M needs a services or logistics layer.
insider_roles: Utility wildfire-mitigation program managers; PSPS incident commanders; fire-weather meteorologists; state energy-safety regulators; insurance brokers; covered-conductor crew leads.

name: PJM capacity payments passed through to utilities' and large customers' bills
size_basis: PJM's 2028/29 delivery-year Base Residual Auction (results 2026-07-14) cleared at the $325/MW-day cap, procuring 138,318 MW for a total cost of $16.4B. Without the cap PJM estimated ~$555/MW-day, roughly $30B. The independent market monitor attributes $6.3B (38%) to data centers. Each verified megawatt of flexibility is worth ~$118k/yr at the cap (325 x 365, DERIVED).
money_flow: Generators and demand-response providers are paid at the clearing price; load-serving entities (utilities and retail suppliers) charge customers. For large customers the share is set by their peak load contribution, which (from my knowledge of PJM rules, not re-verified here) is based on load at the system's summer coincident peaks, so curtailing at the right hours cuts the capacity charge.
shock: Auction results released 2026-07-14: third straight year at the cap, 6,831 MW short of PJM's reliability target. The price collar (cap $325, floor $175) was extended through the December 2026 auction for 2029/30; PJM planned to ask FERC in September for a backstop procurement (outcome not confirmed).
incumbents: Demand-response aggregators (CPower and others), retail energy suppliers, utilities, and brokers/consultants paid on commodity commissions capture the pass-through and DR fees.
incumbent_fragility: Legacy DR products are mostly emergency-only on fixed contracts, and market rules on DR performance and ELCC derating keep shifting, which punishes fixed portfolios. Brokers earn on volume, not on demand reduction. Most mid-size customers (1-20 MW) do not manage their peak at all even though a managed megawatt is worth ~$118k/yr at the cap.
funded_startups_already_here: Voltus ($225M Series D, 2026, Vitol; claims 8.1 GW of flexible capacity managed, a 100 MW Google deal in PJM, acquired Brightfield AI in June 2026), Emerald AI ($150M Series A at $1.05B, 2026-08-25). EnergyHub, Renew Home and Base Power are plausible competitors but their funding was not verified.
wedge_hints: Mid-market C&I peak-tag management with batteries and controls; coincident-peak prediction and alerts; capacity-pass-through audits of large customers' supplier contracts; school, hospital and muni aggregation; data-center flexible-load contracting. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): 5,000 PJM customers each avoiding $50-100k of annual capacity cost with the vendor keeping 25-30% gives $60-150M; needs software plus storage financing.
insider_roles: C&I energy managers; retail-supplier pricing desks; PJM market-monitor analysts; DR dispatch operators; utility rate analysts; data-center power procurement leads.

name: Gas-turbine fleet services and aftermarket (maintenance, repair, parts, upgrades, LTSAs)
geography: Global (US share ~$4.5B per GMI); the US fleet is central to the shock
size_basis: GMI (paid report): $27.1B in 2025 and $30.2B in 2026, US $4.5B. Other paid reports range $10-25B depending on scope (Future Market Report $10.25B; MarkNtel all-turbine services $25.3B in 2026, gas ~46%). Filing cross-check: GE Vernova's Power services revenue was $13.07B in 2025 (gas, steam, nuclear and hydro together; not split) against $6.42B of equipment. Siemens Energy Gas Services ~EUR 1.6B in FY2025 (unconfirmed whether revenue or profit). Treat as a $10-30B range, ~$30B at the top.
money_flow: Plant owners (utilities, IPPs, industrials, data-center BTM operators) pay OEMs through long-term service agreements (LTSAs), parts and outage services; independent service providers and repair shops take a minority (top 5 firms hold ~39% of global services per MarkNtel).
shock: GE Vernova's gas equipment backlog plus slot reservations rose from 100 to 116 GW in Q2 2026 (target >=125 GW by year-end), it is selling 2031 slots, and output is 20 GW/yr rising to 24 GW in 2028 and 30 GW in 2030. New heavy-duty units are unavailable for years, so owners must keep old frames running, defer retirements and lengthen overhaul cycles, while BTM data-center adds enlarge the fleet needing service.
incumbents: GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi, Solar/Baker Hughes, Ansaldo capture the money via LTSAs, proprietary hot-gas-path parts and outage services; a thin layer of independent service providers.
incumbent_fragility: OEMs prioritize scarce factory and field-service capacity for new equipment (business-model conflict with servicing old units cheaply); outage labor is short; parts lead times are long; owners have little price transparency on LTSAs. Proprietary designs lock parts, but also leave gaps where owners cannot get service slots.
funded_startups_already_here: None found focused on turbine MRO/parts after two broad searches (treat as open but confirm with named-company checks before building). Adjacent: ProEnergy (private) selling repurposed CF6 jet-engine cores for data-center power.
wedge_hints: LTSA and parts-price benchmarking and audit for owners; condition-based outage planning (borescope AI, digital twins); a certified marketplace for surplus frames, aeroderivatives and spare parts including slot transfers; outage-technician staffing and credentialing; rotable inventory pooling among IPPs and co-ops; independent hot-gas-path repair (capital intensive). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): benchmarking/audit at 1% of a ~$20B accessible pool is $200M but early capture is a fraction; surplus-equipment brokerage at 3-5% of a few $B/yr of trades reaches $100M+ only if scarcity persists.
insider_roles: Plant O&M directors at IPPs and utilities; outage managers; combustion engineers; LTSA contract managers; ex-OEM field service reps; independent service-provider shop owners; insurer engineering surveyors.

name: US oil and gas operators' produced-water gathering, disposal, recycling and treatment
size_basis: DERIVED. Rystad's 2022 outlook put US onshore produced water at 22.9B bbl in 2022 and 23.8B bbl in 2026; times an assumed blended all-in cost of $0.40-0.65/bbl (B3 Insights says Delaware-basin gathering plus disposal will reach $0.75-1.00/bbl; Aris reports $0.31-0.46/bbl margin on top of its own costs) gives ~$9-15B, midpoint ~$12B. Broader benchmark: Bluefield (Oct 2025) sizes US midstream water at $156B over 2025-2030 (~$26B/yr, Permian $101.8B), which includes freshwater sourcing and frac-water logistics.
money_flow: E&P operators pay water-midstream companies per barrel for pipeline gathering and saltwater-disposal (SWD) injection, and trucking firms for spot loads; a small and growing fraction goes to treatment and recycling.
shock: The Texas Railroad Commission widened the area of review for new SWD permits from a quarter mile to half a mile (from 2025-06-01), added injection-pressure and volume limits tied to reservoir pressure, and barred deep injection below the top of the Strawn in the Gardendale seismic response area; at least one-third of Permian SWD wells have lost injection capacity since 2016; B3 sees 20-30% cost increases in parts of the Delaware. In 2026 the escape valve (treated-water discharge) is still blocked: TCEQ has issued no discharge permits since accepting applications in 2024, and the early-2026 land-application rule drew ~450 comments with over two-thirds opposed (Aug 2026).
incumbents: Aris Water, WaterBridge (raised $345M equity), Texas Pacific Water Resources, NGL, Select Water; many E&Ps run their own SWD systems. The business is acreage dedication plus fixed pipes and wells.
incumbent_fragility: Disposal capacity is constrained by physics and regulation, not by capital; pipes and wells cannot be software-updated; treatment is energy-hungry (the Orla plant needs 5.5 MW for 10,000 bbl/d) and has no outlet permits. Wood Mackenzie projects $3-6 of water cost per barrel of oil over time, so incumbents cannot escape the regulatory ceiling.
funded_startups_already_here: Axine Water Technologies ($5.6M Series A, Oct 2025), Sourcewater ($7.2M Series A, water data/market; date unverified), Clean Chemistry ($2.2M; date unverified), WaterTectonics + Clearvale's WT Oil & Gas (launched Oct 2025). All small compared with the infrastructure incumbents.
wedge_hints: SWD pressure-front and seismic-risk analytics for operators and regulators; disposal-capacity and recycled-water marketplace; trucking dispatch and verification; SWD integrity monitoring; permitting service for reuse; matching treated water to data-center cooling or agriculture once discharge rules open. Bottom-up sketch (assumption): a capacity marketplace/software layer taking 2-3% of a $12B pool is $240-360M at full share, but traction needs operators to give up self-disposal; a data/compliance product alone is likely under $100M. Legal premise to check: induced-seismicity rules and produced-water ownership (Texas moved land-application authority from RRC to TCEQ in 2025).
insider_roles: E&P water and completions managers; water-midstream commercial managers; RRC/TCEQ permit consultants; SWD operators; hydrogeologists and seismologists; surface-use landmen; water-trucking dispatchers.

name: US nuclear fleet operating, fuel and capital spend (and the outsourced supplier/services ecosystem behind it)
size_basis: DERIVED. 816 TWh generated in 2024 (World Nuclear Association) x $31.76/MWh total generating cost (NEI/EUCG 2023 dollars: fuel $5.32, capital $7.06, operating $19.38 per MWh) = ~$25.9B; operating cost alone is ~$15.8B. Uses 2023 cost data with 2024 generation; no newer NEI edition was found.
money_flow: About two dozen owner-operators (Constellation, Vistra, Duke, Southern, Dominion, Entergy and others) pay fuel suppliers, O&M labor, outage-services firms (Westinghouse, Framatome, BWXT, Curtiss-Wright, Jacobs, Bechtel and specialists), engineers (Sargent & Lundy is ENR's #1 nuclear-plant design firm), compliance and NRC fees. Hyperscaler PPAs now fund uprates and restarts.
shock: Executive Order 14300 (2025-05-23) sets 18-month limits for new-reactor decisions and 12-month limits for license renewals, with NRC final rules due ~November 2026 and an NRC reorganization. Follow-through: NRC approved TVA's Clinch River BWRX-300 construction permit on 2026-09-29 (14-month review), TerraPower's Natrium permit in March 2026, four DOE pilot test reactors reached criticality by 2026-07-04, and Palisades began fuel loading (~2026-08-31) after repeated slips.
incumbents: Owner-operators' in-house staff plus the OEM/outage-services oligopoly capture the money; documentation, quality assurance (NQA-1) and condition-report workflows are largely manual.
incumbent_fragility: Aging workforce; regulatory documentation (licensing responses, 10 CFR 50.59 screenings, condition reports) is mostly hand-written; very few shops hold nuclear quality certifications, so the new-build and uprate wave hits a supplier base that cannot scale; commercial-grade dedication is slow and expensive. QA sign-offs cannot be waived by software.
funded_startups_already_here: Nuclearn ($10.5M Series A, Sept 2025, Blue Bear; claims >65 reactors; per-reactor annual subscription) and Atomic Canyon ($7M seed, May 2025, Energy Impact Partners; Diablo Canyon customer). Both target documentation/AI search, not supplier qualification, staffing or outage services. Reactor developers (Valar, Aalo, Antares, Deployable Energy) are funded but do not attack fleet spend.
wedge_hints: Nuclear supplier qualification and commercial-grade dedication marketplace; outage workforce staffing and credentialing (radiation-worker portability); counterfeit/suspect-item detection; procurement of nuclear-grade valves and pumps; uprate engineering at scale; restart and decommissioning services; licensing documentation (contested). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): if outsourced services and supplies are ~40% of the pool (~$10B), a staffing/qualification marketplace taking 5% is ~$500M at full share; $100M needs ~20% of that, a stretch without a standard or certification role.
insider_roles: Plant licensing engineers; outage managers; procurement and commercial-grade dedication engineers; NQA-1 lead auditors; radiation protection technicians; fuel reload engineers; former NRC resident inspectors.

name: Utilities' and developers' outsourced transmission and distribution engineering and line-construction contracts
size_basis: Floor figure, annualized from one contractor. Quanta Services' Electric segment booked $7.84B revenue in Q2 2026 (+44% y/y), ~$31B annualized (DERIVED); this excludes MasTec, MYR, Primoris, Henkels & McCoy, Asplundh's utility work and engineering firms. Payer budget: EEI projects $208B of investor-owned-utility capex in 2025 (>$1.1T for 2025-2029), with transmission $39.9B (2025) and distribution $50.9B (2023). Engineering/design is a smaller slice; no sourced engineering share was found (an NYISO independent estimate puts a mixed bucket of mobilization, engineering, permitting, testing, project management and indirects at ~28% of one line's subtotal).
money_flow: IOUs, co-ops, munis, RTOs and data-center/renewable developers pay line contractors (Quanta, MasTec, MYR, Primoris, Henkels) and engineering firms (Burns & McDonnell is ENR's #1 power design firm, Sargent & Lundy #3; also Black & Veatch, POWER Engineers, Ulteig, Kimley-Horn). Utility capex is recovered through rates.
shock: Quanta's Q2 2026 revenue was $9.56B (vs $6.77B a year earlier), total backlog $53.4B, 2026 guidance raised to $39.3-39.7B, and it added ~7,400 employees through four acquisitions in the quarter and July; more meaningful field activity on some newly booked projects is expected from 2H 2027. EEI's capex plan and data-center load growth are the drivers; the lineworker and engineer shortage is widely cited but no 2026 source was found.
incumbents: Quanta, MasTec, MYR on construction; Burns & McDonnell, Sargent & Lundy, Black & Veatch on engineering. They bill by the hour or unit and design still runs on utility-specific standards and desktop tools.
incumbent_fragility: Growth is gated by hiring, not demand; automation reduces billable hours (business-model conflict); every utility's design standards differ; small utilities cannot compete for contractor crews.
funded_startups_already_here: Piq Energy ($5M seed, 2026-07-08; automates interconnection/grid-planning studies), Pearl Street Technologies (acquired by Enverus, Mar 2025), envelio (German; Eversource uses it). Nothing funded found on distribution design, estimating, crew productivity or lineworker workforce.
wedge_hints: Distribution design automation for new-load service requests on utility GIS; estimating and bid tools for line contractors; crew scheduling, materials staging and yard logistics; mutual-assistance storm-staffing marketplace; lineworker apprenticeship and credentialing pipeline (a network/standard asset); outsourced 'engineer-in-a-box' for ~2,000 public-power utilities and ~800+ co-ops (approximate counts, unverified). Bottom-up sketch (assumption): design automation plus engineering-as-a-service for 200 mid-size utilities at $500k each is $100M; a workforce marketplace taking 3% of $30B+ is ~$1B at full share but a thin-margin labor business.
insider_roles: Utility distribution planners and designers; line-construction superintendents; contractor estimators; T&D engineering managers; storm-response coordinators; IBEW/NECA training directors; project-controls managers.

name: US banks' and credit unions' spend on core, digital-banking and processing vendors (Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry)
size_basis: Sum of segment revenues: Fiserv Financial Solutions FY2025 $9,664M; FIS Banking Solutions FY2025 $7,285M; Jack Henry FY2026 about $2.55B (my derivation: 10-K says revenue rose 7.1% or $169M). Ceiling for US bank/CU spend since it includes some non-US and card-issuer processing revenue; other vendors (nCino, Q2, Alkami) not counted. US share not verified.
money_flow: About 4,400 banks and 4,300 credit unions (rounded, from memory) pay the big three multi-year per-account and per-transaction fees for core ledgers, digital banking, card/payments processing and ancillary software, with termination and deconversion fees on exit.
shock: Fiserv stock fell about 44-48% after its Oct 2025 miss and guidance reset; Q2-2026 (reported 2026-08-06): banking organic revenue -10%, total revenue -3%, 2026 guide cut to -1% to flat organic and EPS $7.20-7.40, head of Financial Solutions resigned in July 2026, product mix under review. At the same time bank M&A approvals fell to about 4 months (shortest since 1990), the FDIC proposed easing merger review in Sept 2026, and Q4-25/Q1-26 deal value hit multi-year highs. Every merger forces a core/data conversion.
incumbents: Fiserv (about a third of community-bank cores per one analyst), FIS, Jack Henry. They capture money through 5-10 year contracts, deconversion fees and decades of lock-in.
incumbent_fragility: Fiserv is distracted (guidance reset, executive departures, product review) and its DNA core is reportedly the most disliked and least likely to be renewed (consultant survey, secondary). Counter: management says attrition is stable and core contracts run for decades, so churn will be slow. Fragility is real but a decade-scale migration, not a sudden break.
funded_startups_already_here: Core/BaaS layer (named from memory, funding years not re-verified this session): Nymbus, Thought Machine, 10x Banking, Mambu, Narmi; Finxact was bought by Fiserv in 2022; public peers nCino, Q2, Alkami. Services/middleware layer (conversion, contract benchmarking): none found, but no dedicated funding search was run.
wedge_hints: (1) Core-contract benchmarking and renegotiation for $1-10B banks and CUs on a savings success fee. (2) Merger-conversion toolkits (data mapping, deconversion, parallel testing, vendor-exit project management) sold to the acquirer, a named buyer with a deal-driven budget. (3) Real-time data/API layer over legacy cores so banks can add products without a core swap. (4) Third-party risk management for bank-vendor oversight.
insider_roles: COOs/CIOs of $1-10B community banks; core-conversion project managers; bank M&A integration officers; vendor-contract negotiators at bank consultancies; credit union CEOs; former core-vendor account managers.

name: US mortgage servicers' operating cost (call centers, escrow, collections, loss mitigation, foreclosure, systems)
size_basis: My derivation from MBA Servicing Operations Study: fully loaded cost 2024 was $176 per performing loan and $1,573 per non-performing loan. Assumed 50-55M first-lien loans (NOT verified; consistent with Valon's claim that 1 in 6 US mortgages is under contract to it): about 52M x $176 = $9.2B plus about 2.6M loans 30+ days late or in foreclosure (4.37% + 0.67%) x $1,573 = $4.1B. Range $11-14B. MBA's 2025 direct cost is $185 per loan, about 75% of it non-default.
money_flow: Investors/MSR owners (Fannie, Freddie, Ginnie, banks, non-banks) pay servicers via the servicing-fee strip; servicers spend it on operations. The operating cost is the addressable pool.
shock: Pandemic-era FHA loss-mitigation options expired end of Sept 2025 and trial payment plans keep loans delinquent until a permanent workout. MBA Q2-2026: total delinquency 4.37% (+44 bps YoY), FHA 11.79% (+122 bps YoY), VA 4.89%, foreclosure inventory 0.67% (+19 bps); FHA foreclosure inventory highest since Q4-2018, VA highest since Q2-2017; VA partial-claim program still awaiting guidance. Default cost is about 9x performing cost, so delinquency growth moves the pool fast.
incumbents: Platforms: ICE Mortgage Technology (MSP; expanded Wells Fargo servicing deal) and Sagent. Servicers: large non-banks (Rithm/Newrez, Carrington, ServiceMac) and banks, running on decades-old systems plus offshore call centers.
incumbent_fragility: Agency rules (FHA loss mitigation, VA, Ginnie) change faster than legacy vendors ship, and cost per loan keeps rising (systems $36, customer service $33 per loan in the MBA 2025 breakdown). Valon claims over $200M contracted ARR from servicers covering 1 in 6 US mortgages, so the legacy lock is cracking, though large migrations (Newrez) start only in 2027.
funded_startups_already_here: Valon: $150M Series D at $2.3B valuation on 2026-10-05 (Ribbit, a16z); earlier $50M Series A (2021) and $100M Series C (2024); sold its own servicing ops to Carrington in 2026 and now sells ValonOS plus AI agents (customers Newrez, Carrington, ServiceMac). Competitors are incumbents ICE and Sagent. No funded startup found focused specifically on FHA/VA default operations.
wedge_hints: FHA/VA default operations: loss-mitigation packet assembly, trial-payment-plan tracking, partial-claim processing, and avoiding Ginnie/FHA curtailments (investor penalties for late or wrong claims); subservicing for small non-bank servicers; REO/property preservation and foreclosure-timeline management; escrow/insurance-shortfall handling as homeowner premiums climb; priced per resolution or per loan below the $1,573 default cost.
insider_roles: Heads of default servicing at subservicers; loss-mitigation negotiators; FHA/Ginnie compliance officers; MSR traders; property-preservation vendor owners; foreclosure attorneys.

name: US title insurance premiums and settlement fees paid by home buyers and refinancers
size_basis: ALTA 2025 full-year: $18.5B premiums written, +13.8% vs 2024; net income $1.168B; claims paid $667M. Q2-2026 premiums $5.3B vs $4.5B in Q2-2025. Settlement/escrow fees come on top and are not counted. Agents keep most of the premium (about 80% per older estimates).
money_flow: Buyers and refinancers pay lender's and owner's policy premiums plus settlement fees at closing; independent agents retain most of the premium and underwriters keep the remainder and pay claims. Rates are state-filed, so there is no price competition.
shock: Weak shock: Fannie Mae's title-waiver pilot lets certain refinances (LTV under 80%) skip the lender's title policy and attorney opinion letter using automated title review. Launched Nov 2024 with Doma, second vendor Westcor added July 2025, FHFA's Pulte wants it expanded, pilot end date Nov 30, 2027. KBW says refis are under 10% of title revenue so the earnings effect is small; ALTA says fraud/forgery is about 40% of refinance claim costs. Premiums are actually rising. I could not confirm any 2026 expansion to purchases (about 75% of mortgage volume), which is the real prize.
incumbents: Underwriters 2025 share: First American 23.1%, Fidelity National 14.5%, Old Republic 14.0%, Chicago Title 13.1% (an FNF brand), Stewart 10.9%; thousands of independent agents do the local search/exam/closing work.
incumbent_fragility: Revenue is priced as a percentage of loan or sale price while the work is a records search and an exam, so a waiver is a direct price attack. Counter: strong lobbying (ALTA, bipartisan legislators), fraud-claim data, and healthy margins mean incumbents are not under financial pressure.
funded_startups_already_here: Qualia (closing software), Spruce, Snapdocs-type e-closing; Doma (first Fannie waiver vendor; I recall its 2024 sale to Title Resources Guaranty, from memory, not re-verified); Endpoint is a First American subsidiary after about $70M of investment (2020). My searches surfaced only 2018-2020 rounds and no 2023-26 venture rounds, a sign of a hard-to-disrupt, incumbent-friendly market.
wedge_hints: Title-risk scoring data asset for lenders weighing waivers (path to a third waiver vendor with an insurance-backed product, like Westcor); automated county-record search and exam for agents; wire-fraud and closing-fund controls; curative (defect-fixing) outsourcing; payoff and lien verification.
insider_roles: Title agency owners and escrow officers; underwriting counsel; title plant operators; lender secondary-market and QC staff; Fannie/Freddie title policy staff; title claims examiners.

name: Creditors' contingency fees to US third-party debt collection agencies (medical, card, student and other defaulted debt)
size_basis: First Research (Nov 2025): about 3,900 establishments, about $15B combined revenue, top 50 hold about half. A 2026 roundup citing IBISWorld says $21.4B across about 7,000 agencies, which I could not verify. Debt-buyer income (Encore, PRA) and creditors' in-house collection costs are on top. Used the conservative $15B.
money_flow: Creditors (hospitals and physician groups, card issuers, telecoms, utilities, lenders) pay agencies roughly 20-40% of recoveries on contingency; debt buyers purchase defaulted paper at cents on the dollar.
shock: Medical debt is 68.9% of furnished collections by contingency collectors (CFPB, 2018-2022). The CFPB rule to remove about $49B of medical debt from credit reports was finalized Jan 2025 then vacated July 2025; about 15 states now restrict medical-debt credit reporting (one mid-2026 blog count, verify with NCLC; Oregon SB 605 effective 2026-01-01) and at least 8 states considered limits on medical-debt wage garnishment in 2026. Federal student loans: collections restarted May 2025 but wage garnishment and Treasury offset were paused 2026-01-16 with no end date (about 5.3M borrowers in default). CFPB debt-collection complaints nearly doubled to about 207,800 in 2024. Net: the credit-report leverage that makes medical collections work is eroding state by state.
incumbents: Debt buyers and agencies (Encore Capital, PRA Group, Conduent, Performant, Alorica, healthcare revenue-cycle firms; names from memory), with the 50 largest holding about half of revenue. The number of contingency-fee collectors fell 18% (815 to 672) from 2018 to 2022.
incumbent_fragility: Call-center and letter workflows are expensive to adapt to 50 sets of state rules and to bans on credit reporting; the federal backstop (CFPB) is weakened, so the rules are a state patchwork. Counter: scale players have compliance staff and creditor relationships.
funded_startups_already_here: From memory, rounds not re-verified: TrueAccord (digital-first collections), Symend (behavioral collections), Collectly (healthcare patient payments). No dedicated funding search was run for this pool.
wedge_hints: Hospital-side product converting medical balances into payment plans or financing before collections, aimed at states with reporting bans; state-law rules engine (licensing, call limits, reporting bans, garnishment limits) licensed to agencies and small creditors; chain-of-title/documentation for debt-buyer portfolios ('debts I don't owe' is 45% of complaints); deceased-account and bankruptcy handling (overlaps with estate settlement); skip tracing and contact-consent management.
insider_roles: Collection-agency compliance officers; hospital patient-financial-services directors; debt-buyer portfolio managers; FDCPA defense attorneys; state licensing specialists; student-loan guaranty-agency staff.

name: US and Canadian financial institutions' financial-crime compliance operations (AML, KYC, sanctions screening, fraud)
size_basis: Forrester/LexisNexis Risk Solutions survey (Feb 2024): US and Canada total cost of financial crime compliance $61B; labor is the largest line; 99% of institutions reported rising costs. Survey base was 160 US/Canada respondents out of 1,181 global; vendor-commissioned, so treat as upper-ish. Not a US-only number.
money_flow: Banks, credit unions, broker-dealers, fintechs and money-service businesses pay in-house analysts, offshore operations centers, and software and data vendors for AML/KYC/sanctions/fraud work.
shock: FinCEN's April 7, 2026 proposal replaces the 2024 proposal: defines an 'effective' AML/CFT program for the first time, shifts effort from low-risk to high-risk customers, reserves enforcement for systemic failures, standardizes four pillars (internal controls, independent testing, US-based compliance officer, training); comments closed June 9, 2026, effective 12 months after the final rule; FDIC/OCC/NCUA issued a companion bank proposal (Fed did not join). The investment-adviser AML rule was delayed to Jan 1, 2028. GENIUS Act adds AML duties for stablecoin issuers from Jan 2027. Mayer Brown reads the structure of obligations as largely unchanged, so the shock is how spend is allocated and examined, not a big cut.
incumbents: Per-alert and per-seat vendors (NICE Actimize, Oracle, SAS, Fenergo, LexisNexis, Nasdaq Verafin; names from memory) plus BPO/offshore labor.
incumbent_fragility: Effectiveness-based exams threaten alert-volume pricing because fewer alerts are acceptable if risk is covered; no FinCEN cost estimate was in the proposal summaries I read, and the final rule has not been confirmed.
funded_startups_already_here: Sardine ($70M Series C Feb 2025, $660M valuation per third-party profile), Greenlite ($15M Series A May 2025, Greylock), Flagright ($12.5M Series A, undated), Castellum.AI ($8.5M Series A, undated), AiPrise ($12.5M Series A, undated), Diligent AI ($2.5M, March 2026), Marble (EUR 6.5M Series A, Sept 2026), Unit21 (latest round I saw was 2022). Hawk AI, Alloy, Parcha, Feedzai not verified this session.
wedge_hints: Not copilots: (1) independent testing and 'effectiveness' validation for $1-5B banks, since the proposal makes independent testing a named pillar; (2) US-based BSA officer-as-a-service for fintech sponsors and foreign-owned US entities; (3) investment-adviser AML program build-out ahead of the 2028 date (about 15,000 RIAs, from memory); (4) sponsor-bank oversight for BaaS programs.
insider_roles: BSA/AML officers at $1-5B community banks; former OCC and FDIC BSA examiners; SAR QA leads at offshore centers; sponsor-bank compliance heads; AML consultants and independent testers.

name: Businesses' cross-border B2B payment fees and FX spread (stablecoin disruption after the GENIUS Act)
size_basis: About $193B a year of international payments revenue, about 80% B2B, from a 2024 Visual Capitalist chart citing McKinsey (I did not find the 2025-report figure). McKinsey 2025: total payments revenue about $2.5T. For scale, one third-party estimate puts real stablecoin payment volume at about $390B a year (B2B about $226B), tiny against the pool.
money_flow: Businesses pay banks, FX providers, correspondent networks and payment firms fees plus FX spread to send money across borders; fees are highest on small-ticket and emerging-market corridors.
shock: GENIUS Act became law July 18, 2025. Agencies missed the July 2026 rulemaking deadline; the OCC said on 2026-08-19 it aims to finalize by November; effective date expected Jan 18, 2027 (draft rules: $5M capital floor, 10% same-day redeemability). Stablecoin market cap $317B on 2026-04-06 (Fed, secondary). Networks are buying in: Mastercard agreed to acquire BVNK for up to $1.8B (March 2026).
incumbents: Correspondent banks, SWIFT, Wise, Payoneer, Airwallex, card networks, Circle, Ripple.
incumbent_fragility: High fees on long-tail corridors are exposed to cheaper rails, but the networks are acquiring the winners (BVNK) rather than being displaced, so the rail itself is commoditizing and value moves to balance sheet, licenses and distribution.
funded_startups_already_here: BVNK (Mastercard deal up to $1.8B after Coinbase's roughly $2B talks collapsed), Bridge (bought by Stripe for $1.1B; announced Oct 2024, my recollection is it closed early 2025 though one search summary implied Feb 2026), Zerohash (independent, reportedly raising $250M at $1.5B), Rain ($250M Series C Jan 2026), Noah ($38M seed Oct 2026), Cybrid ($10M Series A), Kast, Arq, Levl, VelaFi, Almond, Mesta.
wedge_hints: All narrow, and most are dead ends without a lending balance sheet: corridor-specific working capital/trade finance for SMB importers, AR and treasury reconciliation for businesses receiving stablecoins, contractor payroll into specific emerging markets, GENIUS comparable-regime compliance for foreign issuers.
insider_roles: Treasury managers at importers/exporters; freight-forwarder finance staff; correspondent-banking operations heads; MSB compliance officers; regional-bank FX desks.

name: Merchant and issuer cost of card disputes and chargebacks (Visa VAMP monitoring)
size_basis: LOW CONFIDENCE: about $33.8B of global chargeback value in 2025 rising to $41.7B by 2028 (Chargeflow blog; not confirmed in Mastercard pages). Mastercard/Datos: about 261M chargebacks in 2025 projected to reach 324M by 2028, issuer processing cost $9.08-10.32 per dispute (about $2.4-2.7B for issuers). This is value reversed from merchants, not fees; the vendor-addressable part is the portion merchants recover or avoid.
money_flow: Card-not-present merchants lose the sale value on chargebacks, pay dispute fees and now network program fees; issuers spend about $9-10 per dispute; representment vendors take a share of recoveries.
shock: Visa's VAMP (effective 2025-04-01) merges fraud and dispute counts into one ratio. Sources conflict on dates; most consistent account: merchant 'Excessive' enforcement from Oct 1, 2025, merchant threshold cut from 2.2% to 1.5% on April 1, 2026, fees about $4-8 per flagged transaction, acquirers graded on portfolio ratios so they cut or reserve risky merchants. Confirm against Visa rules before relying on any number.
incumbents: Chargebacks911, Kount (Equifax), Riskified, Signifyd, Forter, and PSPs' own dispute tools (names from memory).
incumbent_fragility: Networks keep changing rules and evidence formats and mid-size merchants have no dedicated dispute staff; acquirers now carry portfolio-level penalties and must police merchants.
funded_startups_already_here: Chargeflow ($25M Series A Nov 2025, about $46M total per CB Insights), Justt ($30M Series C Dec 2024, about $100M total, targeting profitability by 2027), Chargebacks911; overlapping fraud platforms.
wedge_hints: VAMP-ratio early-warning and deflection for mid-size merchants and ISOs/PSPs (before the TC40/TC15 count); acquirer-side merchant monitoring tooling; evidence packages for subscription, travel and digital-goods merchants; performance-fee models.
insider_roles: Risk managers at PSPs and ISOs; acquirer merchant-risk analysts; dispute-operations managers at subscription and travel merchants; network-rules consultants.

name: US fees paid to outside tax preparers and small-business accountants (capacity squeeze plus PE and AI roll-ups)
size_basis: IBISWorld 2025 tax-preparation services revenue about $14.5B (seen via a search summary; VerticaIQ shows about $9.4B). Top 8 firms hold almost 40%. The full small-business bookkeeping, payroll and accounting services pool is larger but I found no primary Census or BLS number, so this undercounts.
money_flow: Individuals and small businesses pay CPAs, enrolled agents, chains (H&R Block) and software (TurboTax) for returns, bookkeeping and advisory.
shock: Labor: first-time CPA exam takers fell from 48,004 (2016) to 32,188 (2021) (AICPA via secondary source), the 75% retirement-eligible figure is an AICPA estimate from about 2020, and 150-hour-rule alternatives took effect in Ohio, Virginia and Georgia on Jan 1, 2026, and Iowa and Utah on July 1, 2026. Capital: IFAC counts 1,052 PE-linked accounting transactions 2015-2025 and Capstone a record 194 deals in 2025. Government: IRS Direct File is unavailable for the 2026 season (296,531 returns in 2025); OBBBA added tips, overtime and senior deductions, and H&R Block expects complexity to push filers to assisted prep (its own claim).
incumbents: H&R Block (about 9,000 offices), Intuit TurboTax, independent CPAs and enrolled agents, PE-backed roll-ups (Crete Professionals Alliance, Thrive-backed, over $300M revenue, planned $500M+ of acquisitions in mid-2025).
incumbent_fragility: Highly fragmented sole-proprietor supply that is aging out with a shrinking pipeline; roll-ups are consolidating, but most acquisitions target small firms and the labor constraint binds them too.
funded_startups_already_here: Basis ($100M Series B, Feb 2026, $1.15B valuation), Rillet ($100M Series C, Aug 2026, $1B valuation), Crete (AI roll-up), plus Pilot, Fieldguide and Juno-type AI tax tools (from memory). Bench collapsed Dec 2024 (from memory).
wedge_hints: Not copilots: financing and brokerage for retiring solo-CPA practices (buyers use SBA 7(a) loans, a lending or marketplace path); seasonal and overflow prep capacity networks of enrolled agents; succession and client-transition services; multi-state small-business compliance.
insider_roles: Solo and small-firm CPAs and enrolled agents; practice brokers; PE-platform deal teams; state CPA society executives; IRS practitioner-liaison contacts.

name: US estate settlement fees (probate, trust administration, fiduciary tax) during the great wealth transfer
size_basis: My derivation: IBISWorld US estate-lawyer revenue $18.2B (2026); I assumed 30-50% is administration (probate and trust administration) rather than planning, giving $5.5-9B, midpoint 7; corporate trustee/executor fees excluded. Large uncertainty, treat as a floor. Context: Cerulli projects $124T of transfers through 2048 ($105T to heirs), about $2.5T a year to heirs now, above $3T by 2030 and above $4T about 2036. Third-party 'estate administration services' reports range from $1.5B (North America) to $15.8B (global) and are low quality.
money_flow: Heirs and estates pay probate/estate attorneys, corporate trustees and executors, CPAs for final and fiduciary returns, appraisers and other providers during a 12-18 month settlement; financial advisors compete to keep or win the inherited assets (Cerulli: more than 70% of heirs likely to change their parents' advisor).
shock: Alix raised a $20M Series A in July 2025 (Acrew, with Charles Schwab and Edward Jones Ventures), showing custodians and advisors paying to own settlement; Empathy has raised about $162M including a $72M Series C and distributes through insurers and employers. From memory, not re-verified: OBBBA set the estate and gift exemption at $15M per person from 2026, indexed, which cuts estate-tax planning urgency for most families and shifts value to administration.
incumbents: Fragmented solo and small-firm probate attorneys (hourly or percentage fees, county-court processes), bank trust departments, and advisors whose revenue leaves when heirs do.
incumbent_fragility: Process is manual, document-heavy and different in every state; banks hold the deceased's accounts but typically offer no service to heirs. Counter: distribution is being locked up by the funded players and courts set the pace.
funded_startups_already_here: Empathy (about $162M total, $72M Series C), Alix (about $30.65M total, $20M Series A July 2025), plus planning-side players Trust & Will and Wealth.com (from memory).
wedge_hints: White-label settlement operations for credit unions and community banks that hold the deceased's accounts but offer heirs nothing; inheritance-advance lending to heirs during probate (balance-sheet path); probate real-estate sale and retitling; account-closure and asset-retitling automation across institutions; unclaimed-asset search for estates.
insider_roles: Probate attorneys and paralegals; trust officers; advisors who track heir attrition; probate court clerks; funeral directors; bank deceased-accounts teams.

name: Indonesia: free-meals programme (MBG) money flowing from BGN through ~27,000 community kitchens (SPPG) to ingredient suppliers
size_basis: 2027 draft budget Rp240T = $15.09B for 60.6M beneficiaries (finance minister, 14 Aug 2026; fetched). 2026 allocation Rp335T (~$21B), Rp153.2T disbursed by end-Sept 2026 (search summary only). Derived: Rp240T / 27,000 kitchens = ~$560k per kitchen per year; ~70% on ingredients (BGN-cited, search summary) = ~$10B/yr of ingredient purchasing. Private capital already sunk in kitchen buildings ~Rp54T.
money_flow: Treasury -> National Nutrition Agency (BGN) -> per-meal payments to ~27,000 privately financed kitchens run by partners (foundations, police-linked groups, businessmen, Kadin) -> ~70% of kitchen budget buys eggs, chicken, rice, vegetables, oil, milk from farmers, traders, cooperatives and village firms (BUMDes; BGN requires purchasing via cooperatives/BUMDes) -> meals to schoolchildren, pregnant women, toddlers.
shock: Aug-Sept 2026 crackdown and re-plumbing: 13 Aug 2026 BGN directive after Berastagi school poisoning (rapid test kits for every kitchen, teachers must reject unfit meals, negligent kitchen heads face dismissal); 12 Sept 2026 BGN announced its own raw-materials marketplace (beef, chicken, eggs, rice, cooking oil, milk) launching late Sept/Oct 2026 with association-vetted sellers; July 2026 pause on new kitchens (partners say up to Rp8.7T investment at risk, ~13,000 kitchens could stall); 1,276 kitchens shut for lacking hygiene certificate (SLHS); a 2026 IPB study found only 44% of sampled kitchens had SLHS. Programme scaled from Jan 2025 to ~57M beneficiaries.
incumbents: No incumbent buyer; the state is a new payer. Money is captured by kitchen partners (many politically or institutionally connected), local wet-market traders, cooperatives and BUMDes, and banks financing kitchens (e.g., BSI Rp181B for 127 kitchens). BGN itself is now building a government commodity marketplace.
incumbent_fragility: BGN is a young agency inspecting 27,000 sites manually with paper reporting; disbursement runs behind budget (~46% spent by end-Sept 2026); policy swings (pauses, new certificates, mandated suppliers) strand kitchen owners who carry bank loans; supply-chain readiness and hygiene compliance are admitted gaps. Rules are being added faster than monitoring capacity exists. Risk to any entrant: the state marketplace and mandated cooperative layer can squeeze private intermediaries, and the programme itself could be cut (2027 draft below 2026 allocation).
funded_startups_already_here: None found for MBG-specific kitchen operations, food safety or procurement (searched English and Indonesian; found no startup names or VC rounds). Government is building its own marketplace. Adjacent Indonesian food-supply-chain startups (Sayurbox, Eden Farm, Chickin) exist from background knowledge, not verified this run.
wedge_hints: (1) Kitchen operating system: menu costing to BGN cost cap, inventory, daily reporting in BGN format, SLHS certificate tracking. (2) Food-safety testing/certification/audit service for kitchens. (3) Working-capital finance for kitchens waiting on BGN disbursements, underwritten on the BGN payment stream. (4) Cold-chain and last-mile ingredient logistics to rural kitchens. (5) Tooling for cooperatives/BUMDes that kitchens are now forced to buy from. Bottom-up: $10B ingredient flow x 1% = $100M but needs near-universal kitchen coverage; SaaS $150/month x 27,000 = $49M at 100% share; testing $1,500/kitchen-year = $40M at 100% share; a $100M path needs 2-3 stacked layers or a balance sheet.
insider_roles: SPPG kitchen heads and nutritionists (ahli gizi), BGN regional coordinators, school principals/UKS officers, village cooperative and BUMDes managers, egg and chicken traders, Puskesmas sanitarians, BPOM/Dinkes inspectors, BSI/BRI kitchen-loan officers.

name: India: interest and fees households and small businesses pay on gold-backed loans (banks, NBFCs, informal)
size_basis: Outstanding gold loans ~INR18.6 lakh crore in Mar 2026 (Experian/CRIF bureau data, +50% y/y), ~INR20 lakh crore by Sept 2026 (RBI governor sees no overheating) = ~$200-215B; blended yield ~10% (conservative; NBFC rates far higher than bank rates, 13% blend gives ~$26B) = ~$20B/yr interest. Figures conflict by definition: RBI bank-only series was only ~INR4 trillion ($43B) in Jan 2026. Mostly search-summarized, not fetched.
money_flow: Borrowers (farmers, shopkeepers, small traders, households pledging family jewellery) pay interest and fees to banks and NBFCs (Muthoot, Manappuram, IIFL, SBI, HDFC, ICICI, Federal, South Indian) and informal pawnbrokers/jewellers; lenders vault the gold, value it with in-house appraisers and auction on default.
shock: RBI 'Lending against Gold and Silver Collateral Directions, 2025' (notified 6 Jun 2025) had to be adopted by 1 Apr 2026: LTV caps 85% (to INR2.5 lakh) / 80% (to INR5 lakh) / 75% above, LTV must hold through tenor; bullet consumption loans capped at 12 months; gold handled at lender's own branches by own employees with secure facility; assaying/purity standards; formal auction SOP with empanelled auctioneers; INR5,000/day compensation for late release. Plus a gold price run-up (one outlet: peak ~$5,595/oz on 29 Jan 2026, then ~27% fall; single commentator, unverified) and NBFC share of retail gold loans rising from 28% to 40% in a year.
incumbents: Muthoot Finance (market cap crossed INR1 trillion in Jun 2025), Manappuram (Bain Capital approved to take up to ~41.7%), IIFL, plus banks (SBI, HDFC, ICICI, Federal, South Indian) and informal pawnbrokers. They earn on branch networks, local trust, vaults and high NBFC yields.
incumbent_fragility: Incumbents are strong, not fragile. The fragility is in the manual process underneath: staff appraisal, physical vaults, paper auctions, fake/under-carat gold fraud, and a thin price buffer if gold falls (one commentator says 7-8%). The own-branch/own-employee rule blocks doorstep and outsourced sourcing models, so incumbents' physical networks become a moat and startups must serve lenders rather than compete with them.
funded_startups_already_here: Rupeek (Peak XV-backed, >$164M raised; 2024 down round at ~INR1,785 crore valuation; profit after tax INR15 crore in H1 of the current FY; reportedly seeking $50M in 2026; works with Federal Bank, South Indian Bank, Axis; co-lending with Indian Bank). IndiaGold could not be verified. No 2025-26 closed rounds confirmed. Search summaries only.
wedge_hints: (1) NPA/auction disposal marketplace built to the new RBI auction SOP. (2) Purity/appraisal tech (handheld XRF assaying, appraiser certification, evidence capture) which the Directions make mandatory. (3) Compliance tooling for banks' rural branches adding gold lending (secure-facility certification, continuous LTV monitoring). (4) Loan-takeover/balance-transfer rails as borrowers move from NBFCs to banks. (5) Cross-lender fake-gold and fraud intelligence. Bottom-up is assumption-heavy: if annual disbursals are ~2x stock (~$430B), a 0.25% service take is ~$1B and a 10% share is ~$100M.
insider_roles: Branch gold appraisers at Muthoot/Manappuram, NBFC auction and collections heads, rural bank branch managers, small-town jewellers and pawnbrokers, BIS hallmarking-centre operators, lender internal-audit and compliance heads, gold refiners.

name: Brazil: annual tax-compliance spend of companies (accountants, ERP/fiscal software, consultants, in-house teams) during the rebuild around the dual VAT (CBS/IBS)
size_basis: Soft. Estimates conflict: FEA-USP 'over R$30B/yr'; IPEA-hosted study 0.75% of GDP = 'about R$50B' (~$9B) on older GDP (at current GDP 0.75% would be higher, maybe $15B+); Deloitte R$181B outlier not verified; FIESP says industry spends 1.2% of revenue on tax computation and payment. I use ~$9B (R$50B) as a floor-ish figure. Needs a primary source before any pitch.
money_flow: Millions of Brazilian firms pay accountants (contadores), ERP and fiscal-document vendors (TOTVS, SAP, Senior, Sankhya, Omie, Conta Azul), tax consultancies and in-house tax teams to compute, invoice and file taxes; from 2026 they must re-engineer systems for CBS (federal) and IBS (state/municipal) VAT replacing PIS, Cofins, IPI, ICMS, ISS by 2033.
shock: LC 214/2025 set IBS/CBS rules; 2026 is a test year with symbolic rates (CBS 0.9%, IBS 0.1% shown on invoices and offset against PIS/Cofins) and NF-e/NFS-e must carry new fields; full CBS charging from 2027; old and new regimes run in parallel until 2033 so every ERP must support both. One ERP vendor claims invoices without the fields are rejected from 3 Aug 2026 (unverified). Sources are vendor and law-firm blogs with commercial bias.
incumbents: ERP vendors (TOTVS, SAP, Oracle, Senior, Sankhya), SME software (Omie, Conta Azul), accounting offices (contabilidade), Thomson Reuters, Wolters Kluwer, Avalara, Sovos; big firms use in-house tax teams.
incumbent_fragility: Not a 'cannot respond' pool; incumbents will ship updates. Openings come from parallel regimes to 2033, regulations still being written (Comitê Gestor, Receita), and credit-tracking under the new non-cumulative VAT (a buyer's credit depends on the supplier having paid), which legacy customised ERPs and per-hour accountants handle poorly. Mid-market firms with no in-house tax team are the underserved segment.
funded_startups_already_here: Spedy (e-invoicing; revenue +33% in Q1 2026 on reform demand), Omie, Conta Azul, Contabilizei, Arquivei, Dootax, Avalara, Sovos (several from background knowledge). Found no 2025-26 funding rounds for reform-specific tax tech; not verified on Crunchbase.
wedge_hints: (1) Tax-rules engine as an API for mid-market ERPs lacking one. (2) IBS/CBS supplier-compliance and credit-tracking monitoring. (3) Transition audits and credit recovery on contingency fees. (4) Distributors/retailers with heavy ICMS-ST complexity. (5) Simples Nacional/hybrid-regime optimisation. Bottom-up: if ~1M mid-market firms paid $1,000-2,000/yr, pool is $1-2B and $100M needs 5-10% share; risk that ERP vendors bundle it free.
insider_roles: Tax controllers at mid-market distributors, SME accountants (contadores), ERP implementation consultants (TOTVS/SAP partners), state tax auditors (auditores fiscais), tributarista lawyers, Comitê Gestor/Receita working-group members.

name: Brazil: farmers' annual crop-input purchases (seeds, fertiliser, crop protection), 72% bought on credit from retailers, manufacturers and cooperatives
size_basis: Input-industry revenue R$112.7B in 2024 (~$20B at ~R$5.5/$), of which R$80.8B (72%) involved credit; resale channel R$44.3B of credit, direct sales R$22.7B, cooperatives R$13.8B; barter R$13B (CropLife Brasil/Markestrat mapping, Jul 2025). Distributor view (Andav, 2025): R$171B total revenue, R$105B inputs, different scope. CPR stock R$565B (year uncertain). Search-summarized, not fetched.
money_flow: Farmers buy inputs from retailers (revendas), directly from manufacturers (Syngenta, Bayer, BASF, Nutrien, Yara, Corteva) and from cooperatives; repay at harvest in cash or grain (barter/CPR). Retailers fund themselves from manufacturer terms, banks and capital markets (FIDCs, CRAs).
shock: Record agribusiness judicial-recovery (bankruptcy-protection) filings: 1,990 in 2025 (+56.4%, Serasa Experian) and 474 in Q1 2026 (+21.9%); retailers' own filings up 32.4% in a year (RGF); Agrogalaxy, Lavoro and Belagricola restructuring with ~R$5B creditor losses; private Plano Safra resources ~20% below last year; drivers are high interest rates, dollar-linked input costs, weaker soy/corn prices. Physical CPRs are shielded from recovery proceedings (Law 14.112/2020); a 2026 CNJ provision reportedly reinforces this (commentary, unverified).
incumbents: Input retail chains and cooperatives (the real decentralised lenders, R$44.3B of credit through resale), manufacturers' direct sales, banks (Banco do Brasil, Sicredi), traders (barter).
incumbent_fragility: Retailers lend without bank-grade data on a farmer's total debt, collateral and planted area, and are now both victims and transmitters of farm stress; they cannot fund more risk, and banks are pulling back. Credit is the centre of the market, so any tool that improves loss rates is directly monetisable.
funded_startups_already_here: Traive (~$48M raised; $20M round with Banco do Brasil CVC and Astella; ~$84M post-money; credit analytics/registry sold to input supply chains), Agrolend ($21M; works via resellers; applied for central bank licence). Others not verified. Rounds found are 2023-24; no 2025-26 raise found. Search summaries only.
wedge_hints: (1) Farm-level credit and collateral monitoring (satellite plus registry cross-checks) sold to retailers/distributors as a risk tool. (2) Physical-CPR/barter origination and registry compliance to move retailers to legally safer structures. (3) Workout/recovery services for defaulted farm debt. (4) Receivables-purchase/FIDC infrastructure for mid-size retailers shut out of bank credit. Bottom-up: 1% of R$80.8B credit sales is ~$150M, but $100M needs a risk-product or spread on roughly R$30-40B volume, a large share, and balance-sheet lending into a defaulting sector is dangerous.
insider_roles: Input-retailer credit analysts, cooperative agronomists, agribusiness bankruptcy lawyers and judicial administrators, FIDC managers, rural-credit officers at Banco do Brasil/Sicredi, grain-trading originators.

name: Mexico: freight, customs-brokerage and trade-compliance spend on US-Mexico truck trade
size_basis: Derived, assumption-heavy. US-Mexico trade was $872.8B in 2025 (+3.9%, BTS annual via AJOT). BTS shows ~$46.1B of US-Mexico truck freight in Sept 2025 alone, ~$550B annualised. Door-to-door cross-border logistics plus brokerage at 3-5% of goods value (my assumption, not sourced) = $16-28B; I use $20B. Needs a real freight-revenue source.
money_flow: Importers/exporters (autos, electronics, appliances, agriculture) pay truckers, drayage carriers, freight forwarders (C.H. Robinson, Kuehne+Nagel, DHL, Expeditors, Uber Freight/Transplace) and licensed customs brokers (agentes aduanales, patente holders) for line-haul, border crossing, clearance, bonds and insurance.
shock: Mexico put tariffs of up to 50% on Chinese and other Asian imports from 1 Jan 2026; a 2026 customs-law overhaul adds duties and steep liabilities to licensed brokers; US 25% tariff on goods not qualifying under USMCA; USMCA joint review (July 2026; no outcome found). Rules-of-origin/substantial-transformation scrutiny rising; carriers reported near-zero freight growth in 2025 and flat rates early 2026.
incumbents: Fragmented licensed customs brokers (patente guild, mostly paper/phone workflows), thousands of small carriers and owner-operators, large 3PLs and forwarders (C.H. Robinson, Kuehne+Nagel, DHL, Expeditors, Uber Freight/Transplace).
incumbent_fragility: New broker liability and origin rules raise compliance load on exactly the segment least able to automate. But the broker patente is a legal moat: a startup must partner with or acquire a broker rather than replace one, and big 3PLs have the volume. Fragmentation of brokers and carriers is the opening.
funded_startups_already_here: Nuvocargo (digital forwarder + customs broker; $5.3M seed, $12M Series A, $20.5M Tiger-led Dec 2021, $36.5M Series B 2023 at >$250M valuation; unverified $10M convertible June 2025; acquired YC-backed Mentum Nov 2025; launched Nuvo AI Mar 2026). Flexport and big 3PLs sell cross-border services. Search summaries only.
wedge_hints: (1) USMCA origin-qualification and certificate management for mid-sized exporters and IMMEX plants. (2) Broker-liability, classification and audit-record tooling for agencies post-reform. (3) Drayage and border-capacity marketplace for small Mexican carriers. (4) Duty/tariff-engineering analytics for importers. (5) Financing for duties, bonds and freight at the border. $100M is ~0.5% of the $20B pool if revenue is gross freight margin, more if software fees only; take rates not yet mapped.
insider_roles: Agentes aduanales and their pedimento clerks, IMMEX trade-compliance managers at maquilas, Laredo/Nuevo Laredo freight forwarders, drayage dispatchers, customs attorneys, plant logistics managers, bonded-warehouse operators.

name: Nigeria: household and business spend on petrol and diesel for self-generation (generators)
size_basis: Most-cited: $14B/yr on generator fuel (attributed to AfDB's Adesina / IMF in Nigerian press); $10B/yr (SEforALL, possibly Lagos-only); ~N16 trillion in 2023 on self-generation fuel. Excludes generator purchases, maintenance, downtime. I use $12B mid-range. Press quoting older estimates; verify at source. Search-summarized.
money_flow: Households, shops, hospitals, factories and bank branches buy petrol/diesel and gensets (Mikano, Sumec Firman, Perkins distributors, local dealers) because grid supply from DisCos is unreliable.
shock: NERC Net Billing Regulations published 3 June 2026 let prosumers sell surplus solar to DisCos; Electricity Act 2023 lets states run own markets; Band A tariff ~N220-225/kWh for a promised 20 hours with a Feb-Mar 2026 shortfall compensation directive; $300M Distributed Renewable Energy Fund (NSIA/Africa50, $25M World Bank) launched 21 Sept 2026; a solar-panel import ban was proposed and remains unsettled; fuel dollar-linked and volatile.
incumbents: Fuel retailers and depots, genset importers/dealers, DisCos.
incumbent_fragility: DisCos are financially weak and cannot deliver reliability; genset economics only held while solar plus batteries were expensive. Fuel suppliers cannot respond to a customer who no longer buys fuel.
funded_startups_already_here: Arnergy ($18M Series B incl. $15M extension, 2025), Starsight ($15M BII mezzanine, Mar 2026; 500+ sites, 36MW), Daystar, Rensource, Westa Solar; Sun King and CrossBoundary not verified in this run. Nigeria installed ~803 MW solar in 2025, second in Africa.
wedge_hints: (1) Small-business (10-50 kW) solar+battery lease for pharmacies, cold rooms, print shops, clinics, underwritten on prior diesel spend. (2) O&M and monitoring across heterogeneous installs. (3) Embedded financing via banks and genset dealers. (4) Net-billing metering/settlement software for DisCos and prosumers. 1% of $12B = $120M, so ceiling is high; the real constraint is naira-risk asset finance, not market size.
insider_roles: Facility managers at banks and hospitals, genset technicians, solar EPC installers, DisCo metering engineers, NERC tariff analysts, estate managers in Lagos and Abuja.

name: Emerging markets: fees and FX margin migrants pay to send money home (US to Mexico; Gulf to South Asia, Philippines, Egypt)
geography: Global South corridors (US-Mexico, Gulf-South Asia, Philippines, Egypt)
size_basis: Remittances to low- and middle-income countries ~$685B in 2024 (World Bank); average cost 6.49% (Q1 2025, probably $200 benchmark). 6.49% x $685B = ~$44B at face; large transfers and digital players are cheaper, so I use ~$30B for the fee-plus-FX pool. Mexico received $61.79B in 2025 vs $64.75B in 2024, the first annual fall since 2013. Search-summarized.
money_flow: Migrant senders pay a fee plus FX spread to remitters (Western Union, MoneyGram, Ria, Remitly, Wise), Gulf exchange houses, banks and wallets; recipients get the net.
shock: US 1% federal excise tax on remittances funded by cash, money order or cashier's cheque (IRC section 4475; bank-account and US-card funded transfers exempt) effective 1 Jan 2026; proposed regs April 2026, comments closed 12 June 2026, no final rule found. Direct effect looks small (98.6% of Mexican remittances were electronic in Jan 2026; only ~1.2% cash/in-kind); larger drivers are US immigration enforcement. Mexico inflows fell 3.6% in Aug 2026.
incumbents: Western Union, MoneyGram, Ria/Euronet, Gulf exchange houses, banks, PayPal/Xoom. Earn on cash-in agent networks and FX spread.
incumbent_fragility: Not fragile in aggregate; cash-agent incumbents are being undercut by app-based players, and the cash-funded excise tax adds a small cost to the most cash-heavy flows.
funded_startups_already_here: Remitly, Wise, LemFi, Felix Pago, Nala, Wave and many others (background knowledge; not re-verified in this run).
wedge_hints: Weak. Possible: cash-to-digital conversion in stores serving cash-heavy corridors; payout rails and compliance for Gulf-to-South-Asia worker wage-to-wallet flows; B2B payouts for platforms paying migrant workers. Recommend deprioritising.
insider_roles: Exchange-house branch managers (UAE, Saudi), MSB compliance officers, corner-store remittance agents in Mexico, correspondent-bank relationship managers, Gulf labour-recruitment agents.

name: India: health-insurance claims that insurers pay to hospitals and patients
size_basis: IRDAI annual report, FY2024-25: 32.6M claims settled, INR94,248 crore paid (~$10-11B at ~INR90-92/$), up from INR83,493 crore; 87% settled, 8% repudiated, 5% pending; average payout INR28,910; cashless ~66% of claim value; TPAs handled ~69% of claims by number (fetched, IndiaMedToday citing IRDAI). Govt said INR26,037 crore of claims rejected in FY2023-24 (search summary).
money_flow: Policyholders pay premiums to general and standalone health insurers (Star Health, Niva Bupa, Care, HDFC Ergo, Bajaj Allianz, ICICI Lombard); insurers, often via third-party administrators, pay hospitals (cashless) or patients (reimbursement).
shock: Aug-Sept 2025: AHPI told North India hospitals to suspend cashless treatment for Bajaj Allianz from 1 Sept over unrevised tariffs, unilateral deductions and delayed settlements; truce in September with cost dispute unresolved. IRDAI pushing to 100% cashless with pre-authorisation in one hour and discharge approval in three. Bima Bharosa complaints rose 47,658 (FY24) -> 64,365 (FY25) -> 73,729 (FY26 to Feb). GST removed on individual health premiums 22 Sept 2025 (background knowledge, not verified).
incumbents: Insurers, TPAs (Medi Assist and others), hospital insurance desks.
incumbent_fragility: Adjudication runs on PDFs, call centres and hospital-by-hospital rate cards; hospital-insurer relations are adversarial and disputes are public. Risk: the public National Health Claims Exchange (NHCX) could commoditise the plumbing; I did not find its current status.
funded_startups_already_here: Medi Assist (listed TPA), Plum, Loop, Onsurity, Even (background knowledge, not verified this run). Hospital-side claims/RCM automation startups exist but were not named or sized.
wedge_hints: (1) Hospital-side claims desk for 10-100-bed hospitals with no revenue-cycle team: pre-auth packaging, discharge documentation, dispute appeals. (2) Contingency-fee recovery of disallowed/short-paid claims. (3) Rate-card and deduction analytics for hospital chains/associations negotiating with insurers. Bottom-up is thin: disallowed + repudiated claims ~INR26,000 crore (~$3B); 20% recovery at 15% fee = ~$90M at 100% penetration. Medium-quality pool.
insider_roles: Hospital billing and insurance-desk managers, TPA claim adjudicators and medical officers, insurer claims heads, hospital CFOs, NHA/state PM-JAY agency officers, IRDAI grievance staff.

name: Saudi Arabia: construction contracts issued by the state and PIF to contractors, now collapsing (distress and working-capital pool)
size_basis: Saudi Contractors Authority: contracts issued under $30B in 2025, almost 60% below $71B in 2024 (and $113B in 2023); PIF share fell from ~38% (~$27B) to 14%. MEED Projects shows a different level ($164B in 2024 to $84.5B in 2025), so level depends on source, direction does not. Knight Frank: construction/transport/power/industrial output $148B in 2024. I use $30B (2025 awards ceiling) as the live flow. The pool is shrinking. Search-summarized.
money_flow: Project owners (PIF and giga-projects such as NEOM, ministries, Aramco, private developers) pay main contractors (Webuild, Hyundai, Saudi Binladin, Nesma and others) who pay subcontractors and materials suppliers (steel, cement, MEP) and labour camps housing migrant workers.
shock: PIF cut spending across its portfolio from early 2025 and giga-project schedules slipped; NEOM terminated large contracts (a ~$1B tunnel contract in March 2026; Hyundai and Webuild rail terminations); one report says NEOM's 2026-30 budget includes SAR60B ($16B) for contractor termination payouts vs SAR40B for new infrastructure (single source, unverified); Saudi bank lending growth reportedly slowed by more than half in Jan-May 2026; an Aug 2026 AGBI piece links Gulf contract disruption to an Iran war (details not verified).
incumbents: Main contractors and banks hold the exposure; PIF/government as payer; subcontractors paid only after main contractors collect.
incumbent_fragility: History repeats: in 2016-17 late government payments exceeded SR100B (~30% of government project volume) and contractors cut staff. Banks are cutting construction credit lines. But the state is also the platform operator (PIF's Tawrid supply-chain finance platform), a structural competitor to any private entrant, and SAMA is rewriting supply-chain-finance rules.
funded_startups_already_here: SILQ (Sary + ShopUp merger; $20M structured debt from Gemcorp Jul 2026; 50,000 businesses), BRKZ ($31M Series B, $18M debt line), Comfi ($65M pre-Series A Apr 2026, expanding to Saudi), Project Suppliers (SAR3.75M pre-seed Oct 2026, targeting MEP suppliers' delayed payments), Lamaa; plus PIF's state-owned Tawrid. Search summaries only.
wedge_hints: (1) Claims and termination-settlement preparation for contractors (delay analysis, quantum, evidence). (2) Redeployment marketplace for idle equipment, modular camps and labour. (3) Receivables financing for tier-2/3 subcontractors on state obligors once SAMA rules settle. (4) Procurement for contractors trading down to cheaper materials. Money is mostly one-off settlements and working capital, not recurring spend; I found no path to $100M recurring revenue without balance-sheet risk on state counterparties. Know about, probably do not build.
insider_roles: Contractor claims managers and quantity surveyors, project controls and planning engineers, construction arbitration lawyers, subcontractor owners, MEP suppliers' finance heads, bank project-finance officers.

name: US health plans' and self-funded employers' out-of-network payments through No Surprises Act arbitration (IDR awards)
size_basis: About $15B of IDR payouts in 2025, more than triple 2024's $4.08B, per a WSJ analysis of CMS data (read via Healthcare Dive). Georgetown/Health Affairs estimates cumulative cost 2022-25 at $22.4B ($15.6B above-benchmark payments, $4.2B admin, $2.7B arbiter fees), which I only saw second-hand. Volume ~1.2M disputes H1 2025 and ~1.4M H2 2025 vs 17,000/yr expected by government.
money_flow: Plans and self-funded employers (via TPAs) pay out-of-network emergency, radiology, anesthesia and hospital-based physicians the offer an arbiter picks, plus a $115 admin fee per party and arbiter fees. Providers and billing intermediaries start ~99.9% of disputes; providers win ~85% with median award ~445% of the plan's in-network benchmark (QPA).
shock: En banc Fifth Circuit (TMA III, 2026-08-11) held the federal QPA rules unlawful on 'ghost rates' and excluded bonus/risk-share payments, so every payer's benchmark methodology is defective and past QPAs may need recomputation; agencies also finalized an IDR Operations Rule in May 2026; insurers are lobbying Congress to overhaul IDR while volume keeps rising 16% half over half.
incumbents: Provider side: PE-backed physician groups (Team Health, SCP Health, Radiology Partners) and contingency billing intermediary HaloMD (~56% of H1 2025 disputes among the top four). Payer side: Claritev (ex-MultiPlan), Zelis, Cotiviti, Fair Health benchmarks, big-carrier in-house teams (UnitedHealthcare, BCBS Texas, Aetna are 57% of disputes).
incumbent_fragility: Payers lose ~85% of disputes and, per physician-group analysis of CMS data, default on roughly 1 in 4 line items; self-funded employers who ultimately fund awards have no defense tooling; the QPA, the legal anchor of the system, was just ruled defective; arbiters are throughput-constrained. Risk: Congress could cap awards and shrink the pool.
funded_startups_already_here: Daffodil Health (payer-side OON pricing/payment integrity, $16.3-16.6M Series A, Flare Capital, ~$20.9M total, 2025-26); Radix Health (software IDR, provider side); Pivotal Health (provider-side IDR, success fee); HaloMD has no disclosed funding I could find. None found for TPA/self-funded-employer IDR defense.
wedge_hints: (a) IDR defense and default-prevention for hundreds of mid-size payers and TPAs with no in-house team; (b) QPA recomputation/audit service after TMA III; (c) pre-IDR negotiation and OON carve-outs for self-funded employers; (d) software for the arbitration entities themselves.
insider_roles: Payer OON/NSA compliance directors, TPA claims-operations VPs, ED and radiology group revenue-cycle directors, IDR-entity reviewers, benefits attorneys.

name: State Medicaid program administration, esp. the H.R.1 work-requirement and six-month-renewal build-out
geography: US (41 expansion jurisdictions for work requirements)
size_basis: State program administration was $41,325M in FY2024 ($25.3B federal, $16.0B state) of $957B total Medicaid (MACPAC Exhibit 16, read). The shock-affected slice is far smaller: CMS estimates ~$15M average systems cost per state ($660M nationally) excluding ongoing verification, notices and appeals; AP counted >$1B across 25+ states; federal implementation grant is only $200M.
money_flow: States (federal match 90% system build, 75% operations, 50% general admin) pay IT integrators, eligibility vendors, call centers, enrollment brokers and data brokers; Medicaid managed-care plans separately pay for member outreach and retention because each disenrollment loses premium revenue.
shock: H.R.1 requires 80 hours/month of work, service or education for expansion adults 19-64 from 2027-01-01 plus six-month redeterminations; CMS issued the interim final rule 2026-06-01 (effective 2026-07-31), projecting ~2.3M fewer enrollees in FY2027; good-faith exemptions expire by 2028-12-31.
incumbents: Deloitte, Gainwell, Maximus, Accenture, Conduent, GDIT, Optum, Acentra, Merative (Curam), RedMane (pledged $600M+ of free/discounted services in Jan 2026); Equifax Work Number (used by ~half of states per Warren/Wyden/Sanders letter).
incumbent_fragility: State eligibility systems are patchworks never built to pull and track data from many sources; integrators are discounting under White House pressure; the employment-data layer is a near-monopoly under political fire; Arkansas's earlier trial dis-enrolled people for paperwork failure, so errors carry legal risk. Buyer is state procurement (slow); $100M needs ~20 states at ~$5M or per-verification pricing across millions of people.
funded_startups_already_here: None found specifically for Medicaid work-requirement verification (searched Nava, Propel, Benefit Kitchen, Truss, Gridwise, Truv, Argyle, Pinwheel; no relevant 2026 hits). Field is dominated by giant integrators giving services away.
wedge_hints: (a) Alternative income/employment verification (payroll APIs, state UI wage records, gig platforms) priced per verification; (b) plan-paid member documentation and retention outreach; (c) volunteer/community-service hour verification; (d) medical-frailty exemption documentation for FQHCs and providers.
insider_roles: State Medicaid eligibility directors and MMIS project managers, managed-care government-programs VPs, county eligibility workers, FQHC enrollment staff, legal-aid attorneys.

name: 340B Drug Pricing Program covered-entity purchases (the spread and the rebate transition)
size_basis: HRSA reports covered entities bought $100B of outpatient drugs in CY2025, up ~22% from $81.4B in CY2024; hospitals ~87%. The contestable money (spread, administration, compliance) is a fraction and I could not source it.
money_flow: Manufacturers sell outpatient drugs at statutory ceiling prices to ~50,000 covered-entity sites; entities bill Medicare and insurers at full rates and keep the spread, increasingly via contract pharmacies run by third-party administrators.
shock: First HRSA rebate pilot was enjoined (D. Maine 2025-12-29) and withdrawn Feb 2026; D.C. Circuit (Novartis v. Kennedy, 2026-07-21) held rebate models lawful only with HHS approval; HRSA published a revised pilot 2026-08-03 effective 2027-01-01 (pay full price, submit claims data, get rebate); AHA sued again 2026-10-09; Congress has competing drafts (Cassidy draft allows rebates or a claims repository, House SECURE 340B Act pauses rebates, Senate SUSTAIN 340B Act moves to a data clearinghouse).
incumbents: Third-party administrators and contract-pharmacy networks (Sentry/Wellpartner, Walgreens, CVS, Verity, Second Sight's 340B ESP) and Kalderos (duplicate-discount and rebate platform).
incumbent_fragility: A rebate model forces hospitals and safety-net clinics to front full price and prove claims-level eligibility: a working-capital and data problem for thin balance sheets and weak data teams. The data standard (clearinghouse vs manufacturer platforms) is unresolved. Risk: outcome splits three ways (rebates, discounts-with-data, pause) and depends on courts and Congress within ~12 months.
funded_startups_already_here: Proximity ($3M seed, Feb 2025, LRVHealth/Commonweal; 340B revenue automation); Pillr Health (Water Street Healthcare Partners investment Jan 2026, size undisclosed; split billing, contract pharmacy, rebate readiness); Kalderos ($7M Series A 2019, $28M Series B 2020, Bain Capital Ventures; no 2023-26 round found).
wedge_hints: Advance financing against 340B rebate receivables; claims-data scrubbing and rebate-submission service for small covered entities and FQHCs; duplicate-discount prevention; a neutral claims clearinghouse if Congress picks that model.
insider_roles: 340B program directors at DSH hospitals and FQHCs, hospital pharmacy directors, manufacturer 340B-integrity leads, TPA compliance staff, health-system treasurers.

name: Medicaid home- and community-based services (personal care, home care agencies, fiscal intermediaries)
size_basis: CMS: 7.8M HCBS users and $129.4B of Medicaid spending in 2022 (+12.5% y/y); narrower personal-care slice ~$46.4B in 2024 (nearly double 2019) per RealClearInvestigations, New York alone $15.67B.
money_flow: State Medicaid agencies (and managed-LTSS plans) pay thousands of small home care agencies and fiscal-intermediary payroll firms per care hour; most revenue passes through as aide wages.
shock: H.R.1 cuts federal Medicaid by $911B over 2025-34 (KFF), and states historically cut HCBS enrollment and rates; immigration enforcement hits a workforce that is >40% foreign-born for home health aides; New York consolidated ~600 fiscal intermediaries into one statewide FI (PPL) on 2025-04-01 for ~250k consumers; the 80/20 wage pass-through rule (effective ~2030) remains unrescinded.
incumbents: Fiscal intermediaries (PPL, GT Independence, Acumen/Tempus), agency chains (Addus, BrightSpring, Amedisys), software (HHAeXchange for EVV, WellSky, AlayaCare, AxisCare, Axxess, ClearCare).
incumbent_fragility: Thousands of agencies under $20M revenue on thin margins, paid late by states, squeezed by rate cuts and a shrinking labor supply, with EVV compliance burdens and no access to working capital; states are willing to restructure the whole market (New York).
funded_startups_already_here: AlayaCare (C$225M Series D 2021; debt financing Feb 2026), Enzo Health ($20M Series A May 2026, home health/post-acute AI), MochaCare (~$1M accelerator round Mar 2026). No venture-funded Medicaid FI/payroll challenger found.
wedge_hints: Working-capital advances against Medicaid receivables (balance-sheet business); fiscal-intermediary/payroll platform for states that bid statewide FIs after New York; EVV-to-claims reconciliation; caregiver pipeline products for agencies.
insider_roles: Agency owners and administrators, state long-term-care program managers, FI operations VPs, EVV compliance leads, waiver case managers.

name: Clinical laboratory testing (independent, hospital-outreach and reference labs)
