size_basis: US clinical lab services ~$99.7B revenue in 2024, projected $122.5B by 2029 (Hyde Park Capital, secondary). Medicare Part B lab spend $8.4B in 2024 per HHS OIG as cited by MarkNtel (secondary), 43% genetic tests. Narrow ~$10B market-research figures are not comparable.
money_flow: Medicare, Medicare Advantage, commercial plans and Medicaid pay labs per test; Medicare's rate is set from a private-payer rate survey under PAMA, so Medicare cuts propagate to billing and contracting.
shock: CMS's preliminary 2027 clinical lab fee schedule (week of 2026-09-25) applies the maximum 15% cut to ~775 tests (~1,200 tests total per ACLA) with more cuts in 2028-29, after Congress delayed cuts a seventh time in the Feb 2026 appropriations act; CMS says it saves ~$1B a year; the RESULTS Act (claims-database rate setting) is pending and analysts expect another delay.
incumbents: Quest and Labcorp (buying hospital outreach labs), thousands of regional and specialty/genetic labs; billing systems XIFIN, Sunquest, Orchard, offshore RCM shops.
incumbent_fragility: Independent labs run thin margins, depend on payer coverage decisions (MolDX) and the PAMA rate, and hospitals are selling outreach labs; billing is legacy or offshore. Risk: Congress may delay cuts again, weakening urgency.
funded_startups_already_here: None found that are lab-specific revenue-cycle companies (general RCM adjacent: Candid Health $120M Series D, Silna Health $27M). Only three searches; low confidence.
wedge_hints: Lab-specific underpayment and denial recovery on contingency; payer-rate benchmarking for labs in the 2025 PAMA data cycle; outreach-lab transition services for health systems.
insider_roles: Independent-lab CFOs and billing managers, hospital outreach-lab directors, MolDX/coverage consultants, lab sales managers.

name: Rural Health Transformation Program state grants
size_basis: $10B a year for FY2026-FY2030 ($50B total) under H.R.1; FY2026 awards range $147M (NJ) to $281M (TX), avg ~$200M. Funding-notice limits (via Texas DSHS summary and AHA letter): provider payments capped at 15%, infrastructure 20%, EHR 5%, so roughly 60%+ goes to programs, technology, workforce and care-model pilots.
money_flow: CMS to 50 states (half split equally, half by CMS-scored plans), then to state agencies, providers, vendors and workforce programs.
shock: CMS announced first-year awards 2025-12-29; states must obligate year-one funds within ~10 months and spend within one more year or face claw-back and redistribution, with RFPs posting from July 2026 through Q1 2027; KFF frames it as an offset to Medicaid cuts.
incumbents: State agencies, large consultancies (Deloitte, Guidehouse, Accenture), EHR vendors, telehealth vendors, rural hospital associations.
incumbent_fragility: Spend-fast pressure creates many isolated pilots; no standard vendor for outcome tracking and subgrant management; rural hospitals lack grant-writing and IT capacity (AHA asking for technical-assistance centers). Risk: five-year grant then a cliff; vendor-addressable share is not public; slow state procurement.
funded_startups_already_here: None found aimed at this program (searches returned only advisory and vendor-blog content).
wedge_hints: Grant-management, compliance and outcome-reporting platform sold to 50 state RHT offices; subgrant application help for critical-access hospitals; shared IT/cyber/revenue-cycle services paid from program funds.
insider_roles: State RHT program directors, rural hospital CFOs and CEOs, state hospital association staff, rural health clinic managers.

name: Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment (coding-intensity) payments
size_basis: MedPAC March 2026: Medicare pays ~14% more for MA enrollees than for the same people in fee-for-service, a projected $76B in 2026, from favorable selection (~11 points) and coding intensity (~4 points); MA plans were paid ~$537B in 2025. Coding slice ~4 points of ~$540B = ~$22B (my arithmetic, consistent with an outside analysis). Vendor spend on risk adjustment is not publicly sized.
money_flow: CMS pays MA plans risk-adjusted capitation; plans spend on chart review, coding vendors, in-home assessments and encounter capture, and pay value-based provider groups.
shock: CY2027 final rate notice (2026-04-06) gives +2.48% base but excludes diagnoses from unlinked chart reviews (CMS-estimated -1.53%) and audio-only encounters and keeps the 2024 model; RADV extrapolation rule was vacated 2025-09-25 and the Fifth Circuit heard the appeal ~2026-10-05, panel reportedly leaning to affirm.
incumbents: Optum, Cotiviti, Episource, Inovalon, Lumeris, plan in-house teams.
incumbent_fragility: Retrospective unlinked chart review, the core of the vendor business, is being excluded from payment; in-home assessment vendors face DOJ scrutiny; RADV enforcement is legally unstable. Strong incumbents and abundant startups limit openings.
funded_startups_already_here: RAAPID (Series A extension Mar 2026 from UPMC Enterprises; earlier M12 and CareFirst's Healthworx); Keebler Health ($6M seed, $7.8M total, date unclear); list is partial.
wedge_hints: Encounter-linked prospective documentation at the point of care; RADV defense and record retrieval for plans; compliance tooling for value-based groups.
insider_roles: MA risk-adjustment directors, value-based group CMOs and coding managers, RADV appeals attorneys, certified coders.

name: Hospital and post-acute claim denials, including Medicare Advantage prior-authorization denials
size_basis: Premier survey of 516 hospitals (claims from 2022): hospitals spend ~$19.7B a year fighting denied claims (15% of private-payer claims denied, 54.3% eventually overturned, $43.84 per denial). Unverified secondary figures: AHA $43B spent on payer collections in 2025 incl. ~$18B on denials; vendor claim of $26B.
money_flow: Providers spend labor and vendor fees to appeal payer denials; the money at stake is revenue recovered (skilled-nursing and hospital revenue from MA and commercial plans).
shock: HHS OIG report OEI-09-24-00331 (2026-06-08): 19 MA parents denied 12% of skilled-nursing admission requests, 18% were appealed and 95% of appeals overturned; naviHealth (UnitedHealth) denied 14%; nursing-home residents denied 40%; Senate HSGAC letters to Humana, UnitedHealth, CVS on 2026-07-14.
incumbents: R1 RCM, Waystar, Optum, Ensemble, Cotiviti; payers' automated utilization-management tools.
incumbent_fragility: A 95% overturn rate on appeal means initial denials are a volume game, and providers under-appeal (11-18%); payer denial systems now face political scrutiny. But hospital denials are heavily funded and crowded.
funded_startups_already_here: Amperos Health ($16M Series A Apr 2026, Bessemer); Candid Health ($120M Series D, Sixth Street); RapidClaims ($11M, Accel); Basalt Health ($20M Series A, NEA, post-acute); ExaCare AI ($30M Series A, Insight, SNF referrals); Willow (YC, long-term-care RCM); Clinware ($4.25M seed); Cascala ($8.6M seed); R1 bought Humata Health.
wedge_hints: Contingency appeals for skilled-nursing and home-health operators against MA denials (95% overturn rate gives a high win rate); payer-contract compliance audit for long-term-care operators.
insider_roles: Hospital denial-management directors, SNF administrators and business-office managers, MA appeals nurses, payer medical directors.

name: GLP-1 obesity and diabetes drug spend
size_basis: Conservative, sourced floor: Lilly's US Q4 2025 revenue was $4.1B Mounjaro + $4.2B Zepbound = $8.3B in one quarter (~$33B annualized) for tirzepatide alone; Lilly FY2025 worldwide Mounjaro $22.97B and Zepbound $13.54B. Novo's US semaglutide adds more but I did not source it. IQVIA: GIP/GLP-1 drugs added $14B to US net medicine spend ($606B) in 2025.
money_flow: Payers (Medicare Part D, Medicaid, employers, commercial plans) and cash-paying patients pay manufacturers via PBMs and pharmacies.
shock: Nov 2025 Trump-Lilly-Novo pricing deal; TrumpRx.gov live 2026-02-05 (oral semaglutide $149/month cash, injectables at or below $350 trending to $245); Medicare GLP-1 obesity bridge from 2026-07-01 ($245 price, $50 copay) through Dec 2027; employer obesity-GLP-1 coverage fell from 72% to 60% (BGH survey) with Cigna and Starbucks dropping coverage.
incumbents: Lilly and Novo (LillyDirect, NovoCare direct-to-consumer), PBMs, telehealth firms.
incumbent_fragility: Manufacturers can now sell direct, shrinking PBM and middleman economics; employers retreating leaves a care-management gap, but manufacturers can also bypass any new intermediary.
funded_startups_already_here: eMed ($200M Series A Mar 2026, Aon-led, >$2B valuation); knownwell ($25M Oct 2025); Form Health ($38M Series B 2024); 9amHealth; Waltz Health.
wedge_hints: Thin: employer purchasing/aggregation of cash-price channels; Medicare bridge enrollment navigation; weak because manufacturers can bypass intermediaries.
insider_roles: Employer benefits directors, PBM clinical pharmacists, obesity-medicine physicians, Medicare Part D plan product leaders.

name: US businesses' spend on uniform, linen and workwear rental (incl. healthcare linen)
size_basis: TRSA/Oxford Economics industry economic output $27.7B in 2024 (304,000 jobs). Narrower First Research definition ~$14B. Bottom-up: Cintas Uniform Rental and Facility Services $8.62B (FY2026), Vestis ~$2.6-2.7B (quarterly ~$660M), UniFirst ~$2.4B (from memory, unverified); top 3 ~$13.7B before Alsco, Elis, healthcare linen and regional laundries.
money_flow: About 1.5M US businesses (restaurants, auto shops, hospitals, factories, hotels) pay route-based rental companies weekly/monthly for uniforms, mats, towels, linen, restroom and first-aid supplies under 3-5 year evergreen contracts with loss/damage charges and annual price escalators.
shock: Cintas agreed 2026-03-10 to buy UniFirst (~$5.5B EV; $155 cash + 0.7720 Cintas shares per share; ~$375M claimed synergies; ~1.5M combined customers). FTC Second Request 2026-06-11; both certified substantial compliance 2026-10-02; timing agreement bars closing before 2026-12-11. Meanwhile Vestis fiscal Q3 2026 revenue -1.8% with pounds processed -4.5%.
incumbents: Cintas, UniFirst, Vestis (Aramark spin-off 2023), Alsco, Elis NA. Route-and-plant model: capture money through weekly rental routes, evergreen contracts, damage/loss charges and price escalators.
incumbent_fragility: The two biggest rivals are merging, so 12-24 months of route consolidation and repricing put a large customer base up for re-bid; Vestis is losing volume and in a $75M cost-cut plan rather than hunting customers; FTC review limits Cintas's aggressiveness before close; asset-heavy laundries and trucks mean they cannot easily go after small accounts profitably; customers dislike auto-renewals and damage charges but have no neutral price benchmark.
funded_startups_already_here: None found attacking US route-based uniform rental (searched uniform/linen startup funding). Adjacent and tiny: bnbkit (Geneva, $1.6M, short-term-rental linen), Quick Smart Wash (India, $5.15M), White Plains Linen (NY, PE-backed by Surge Aug 2025, amount inconsistent, unverified).
wedge_hints: Buyer-side contract audit/exit and re-bid service for SMB renters (auto-renew traps, loss charges, escalators), then a supplier-commissioned marketplace; roll-up/franchise of regional laundries inheriting customers during Cintas/UniFirst route consolidation, especially healthcare and hospitality linen; RFID garment tracking and billing-dispute software for regional operators; any FTC-forced divestiture would be a sudden supply of routes to buy.
insider_roles: Route sales reps and district managers (ex-Cintas/UniFirst), laundry plant GMs and engineers, TRSA member operators, hospital linen/EVS directors, restaurant-group procurement heads, antitrust counsel.

name: US building owners' spend on fire and life-safety inspection, testing, maintenance and monitoring (POTS copper cutover)
size_basis: IBISWorld US fire protection and security system installation contractors $22.1B (2026 label; page text says 2025, year uncertain); fire protection consultants $8.1B. No clean US ITM-only figure exists; my assumption is that recurring ITM, monitoring and code-driven repair is $8-12B of the total. Fragmentation: more than 118,000 privately owned potential acquisition targets (Grata 2026).
money_flow: Commercial building owners pay licensed fire-alarm/sprinkler/extinguisher contractors annual inspection, testing, monitoring and repair contracts mandated by NFPA 25/72 and local fire codes; fire marshals (AHJs) enforce and approve changes.
shock: FCC adopted the Network and Services Modernization order 2026-03-26 (FCC 26-19, WC Dockets 25-208/25-209): ends network-change disclosure filings, 31-day automatic grant for all copper discontinuance applications, blanket grandfathering of legacy copper voice, preempts state/local rules that delay retirement. AT&T stopped taking new copper orders Oct 2025 and targets retiring most copper outside California by end-2029 (vendor trackers). Fire alarm communicators and elevator cab phones on POTS must move to listed cellular/IP communicators. Caveat: the FCC text I read does not name fire alarms; that link is from vendors.
incumbents: Johnson Controls (Tyco), Siemens, Honeywell (panels), Convergint, Securitas, Pye-Barker (57 acquisitions in 2025, 9,000 staff, 47 states), Summit Companies (BlackRock), many PE-owned regionals. Money is annual ITM contracts, monitoring and repair.
incumbent_fragility: Roll-ups are digesting dozens of acquired shops with different paper workflows; licensing is state-by-state; NICET-certified technicians are scarce; inspection reports are still PDFs/paper filed to AHJs; the POTS cutover is a one-time forced retrofit across millions of lines with no standard program, and monitoring contracts carry per-line recurring revenue that incumbents price opaquely.
funded_startups_already_here: Ember Software (ex-Fire Inspect, $10M led by 8VC and Menlo Ventures, Jan 2025); Inspect Point ($28M Mainsail growth equity, Jan 2022); Life Safety Inspection Vault (reported $28.7M, last round Aug 2025, unverified); ServiceTrade and other field-service software. No funded startup found running managed POTS-replacement programs.
wedge_hints: POTS-cutover-as-a-service for multi-site owners (retail chains, school districts, REITs, hospitals): inventory every copper line, replace with listed cellular communicators, file AHJ paperwork, bill monitoring monthly; inspection-report filing network to AHJs (compliance records as data asset); small-commercial sprinkler/extinguisher ITM in metros roll-ups have not reached.
insider_roles: NICET-certified alarm technicians, fire marshals/plan reviewers, central-station operators, telecom managers at national retail chains, insurance loss-control engineers, fire-sprinkler contractors.

name: US community associations' (condo/HOA) reserve and capital-repair funding, Florida structural mandate first
geography: United States (Florida first, then other states adopting reserve mandates)
size_basis: CAI/Foundation: about $96B/yr in assessments (2019-20 edition) and $26.6B/yr contributed to reserves (2021-22 edition); ~358,000 associations and 74.2M residents. Pool defined as the reserve/capital stream ($26.6B). Florida: ~28,250 condo associations with 1.2M+ units (unverified newsletter); no statewide dollar shortfall found.
money_flow: Unit owners pay assessments to associations; volunteer boards (advised by managers, reserve-study firms, engineers, attorneys) spend on operations and capital repairs; shortfalls become special assessments, bank lines of credit, or owner-level loans.
shock: Florida HB 913 (signed May 2025, effective 2025-07-01) set the Structural Integrity Reserve Study deadline at 2025-12-31 for existing associations, raised the non-specified item threshold to $25,000, and lets associations fund reserves through special assessments, lines of credit or loans. The deadline has now passed; catch-up bills are hitting owners (example: Orlando building proposing up to $22,105 per owner). Realtor sources say 2026 bills to soften the mandate failed (unverified).
incumbents: Managers (FirstService Residential, Associa), software (Vantaca, AppFolio), reserve-study and engineering firms (Reserve Advisors, Association Reserves), condo law firms, regional banks with community-association lending desks. Money: management fees per door, study fees, loan spread.
incumbent_fragility: Boards are untrained volunteers with personal liability (SIRS affidavit); association loans are unsecured apart from assessment-lien rights; fixed-income owners cannot pay lump sums; the licensed-engineer bottleneck delays studies; lenders ration credit to buildings with weak reserves, which is exactly who needs it.
funded_startups_already_here: Vantaca (association software) raised $300M+ at $1.25B valuation in Oct 2025 (Cove Hill-led, JMI). No funded startup found doing special-assessment or association financing (searched fintech/loan startups); Miami-Dade runs a county loan program for owners 62+.
wedge_hints: Unit-owner special-assessment installment financing collected through association billing and secured by assessment-lien rights; association credit marketplace; SIRS/milestone-inspection and repair project coordination for boards; insurance premium finance; replicate state by state as mandates spread. Legal premise on lien rights and lending licensing must be checked per state.
insider_roles: Community association managers (CAMs), Florida condo attorneys, structural engineers doing milestone inspections, association-banking officers, board treasurers, insurance brokers.

name: US building owners' spend on elevator, escalator and moving-walk maintenance, repair and modernization
size_basis: Estimate, low-medium confidence: secondary reports put US elevator maintenance at $5.6B (2023) and US installation+service at $5.7B (2024); installed base ~1.3M elevators/escalators in North America (unverified); maintenance $3.5-5k/unit/yr (NEIA-attributed aggregator, unverified). Adding repair and modernization gives ~$8B. Cross-check: Otis alone booked $4,997M Service sales globally in H1 2026.
money_flow: Building owners (CRE, condos, hospitals, hotels, transit) pay OEMs or independents monthly maintenance contracts plus repair and modernization projects; state inspectors and union (IUEC) labor gate the work.
shock: Otis Q2 2026 (reported 2026-07-22): organic Service +9% (post-spin high), modernization backlog +24% (+26% constant currency), double-digit repair growth, but Service margin 23.2% and profit outlook cut on labor/material costs. Otis took majority control of venture-backed WeMaintain on 2026-04-13. FCC copper order (2026-03-26) also hits elevator cab phones on POTS. No 2026 elevator right-to-repair bill found.
incumbents: Otis (45,000 field staff, ~$10B annual Service sales globally), Schindler, KONE, TK Elevator; independents for the rest. Capture money via long maintenance contracts on proprietary controllers, then repair and modernization upsell.
incumbent_fragility: Aging installed base creates repair/modernization backlog but mechanics (5-year apprenticeships, licensing) are the bottleneck and margins compress as OEMs ramp; owners complain about service quality (Otis spending $50M on it); proprietary diagnostics lock customers in but also create independent demand; union labor pools limit new entrants and OEM scaling alike.
funded_startups_already_here: WeMaintain (Paris, ~$40M raised, now Otis-controlled), Mainteny (Berlin, seed), Uptime (France, EUR 7M), Datahoist (Austin, tiny). No US venture-funded independent elevator service company or roll-up found.
wedge_hints: Independent service roll-up in secondary metros with a software-led dispatch and parts layer; owner-side contract audit and benchmarking for CRE portfolios (OEM contracts are opaque); modernization financing and project management for condo boards; cab-phone cellular conversion programs; legacy-controller parts brokerage.
insider_roles: IUEC elevator mechanics, QEI-certified inspectors, state elevator inspection supervisors, CRE building engineers and property managers, parts distributors, elevator consultants.

name: US school districts' spend on student transportation (own fleets and contractor-run yellow bus)
size_basis: Getting Smart (Feb 2026): national pupil transportation exceeds $28B/yr; pre-COVID EdChoice figure >$25B. ~25-26M students ride daily; contractors own/operate roughly a third of buses (NSTA estimate; counts range 6.5-35% by definition). Kansas example: $186M spend, ~$1,459 per pupil.
money_flow: Districts pay contractors fixed-price multi-year contracts or run own fleets; states reimburse part of the cost, with local districts carrying 60-70%; special-ed and homeless-student transport is bought separately (vans/rideshare).
shock: Stacked: EPA on 2026-02-19 cancelled the 2024 Clean School Bus rebate program and is restructuring ~$2.3B of unspent funds (statutory money ends FY2026); tariffs and cumulative bus price increases (Blue Bird FQ3 2026; legacy units -7.2%); ESSER expired in 2024; Mobico sold its North American school-bus arm (14,000+ buses) to I Squared Capital, closed 2025-07-14, and the successor (Summit School Services) lost 3,000 buses.
incumbents: First Student (~52,000 vehicles, 1,300 contracts, 4.6M students/day), Student Transportation of America (~19,000), Summit School Services (~18,500), Beacon Mobility; routing software from Tyler, Transfinder, Edulog. Capture money through fixed-price contracts with escalators.
incumbent_fragility: Fixed-price contracts collide with new 5-year Teamsters national wage contract (22,000+ First Student workers), driver shortage and tariffed $50-200k+ buses; PE owners need growth while districts face enrollment decline, so route consolidation and RFP churn rise; federal bus subsidies just disappeared so small districts and contractors cannot refresh fleets.
funded_startups_already_here: HopSkipDrive ($25M Series C 2021 + $37M Series D; 400+ districts; special-needs niche), BusPatrol (GI Partners Jan 2024, Weatherford Capital Jun 2024; stop-arm cameras financed by violator fines), Via Transportation (NYSE IPO 2025-09-15 at $46), Zum (earlier large raises, no 2025-26 news found). Routing incumbents already entrenched.
wedge_hints: Equipment finance/leasing and pooled purchasing for small districts and independent contractors cut off from EPA subsidies; contract benchmarking and RFP service for districts (signers: transportation director and business official); school-bus CDL training and driver staffing pipeline; maintenance shop/parts network; special-ed/IEP transport coordination.
insider_roles: District transportation directors, contractor regional managers, bus-shop mechanics, school business officials, state pupil-transport directors, bus dealers.

name: US growers' spend on H-2A guest-worker agricultural labor (wages, housing, transport, agent and contractor fees)
geography: United States (about 50% of demand in FL, GA, CA, WA, NC)
size_basis: DOL OFLC FY2025: 398,258 positions certified of 415,496 requested. My derivation: ~400k positions x ~1,000-1,100 hours x ~$17-19/hr = ~$7-8B wages, ~$9B with housing, transport and fees. Hours and AEWR level are my assumptions, not sourced.
money_flow: Growers (directly or via associations/farm labor contractors) pay H-2A workers at state Adverse Effect Wage Rates plus mandated housing and transport, and pay agents, attorneys and foreign recruiters for DOL/USCIS filings and recruiting.
shock: DOL interim final rule 2025-10-02 replaced USDA Farm Labor Survey-based wage rates with BLS OEWS state wages in two skill levels plus a housing adjustment (some wages fall); UFW sued 2025-11-21. Demand keeps climbing past 400,000 requested positions while the wage regime is legally unstable.
incumbents: Grower associations and farm labor contractors that top DOL filings (NCGA 10,398 positions, Foothill Packing 6,959, WAFLA 4,913, Temp.Labor LLC 4,891, Fresh Harvest 4,375, Ag Labor LLC 3,335), plus immigration attorneys/agents (92% of Missouri positions filed through agents or attorneys; one-state sample) and foreign recruiters.
incumbent_fragility: Filing is manual and long-lead (workers often arrive late; a Seso claim says 72% of farms), rule changes and litigation reprice wages mid-stream, housing is the binding constraint, and small agents cannot absorb compliance risk or offer payroll/banking; contractors compete on relationships rather than software.
funded_startups_already_here: Seso (agri workforce/HR platform; $25M Series A 2022 led by Index; $26M led by BOND Apr 2024; claims 27 of top-100 US ag employers); Croft (H-2A software, $700k seed, undated). No 2025-26 rounds found.
wedge_hints: H-2A filing/compliance plus payroll plus worker banking and remittance bundle for mid-size growers; farmworker housing build-to-rent or leasing; extension to H-2B (landscaping, seafood, hospitality); workers' comp and bonding for contractors.
insider_roles: Grower HR managers, farm labor contractor owners, H-2A attorneys, Mexican recruiters, DOL OFLC analysts, packinghouse managers, farm-housing inspectors.

name: US households' and businesses' spend on structural pest control services
size_basis: NPMA/Specialty Consultants: $12.654B total service revenue in 2024 (+7.9% vs $11.723B in 2023); 17,000+ firms. IBISWorld's broader estimate is ~$24B; used the NPMA figure as the defensible floor.
money_flow: Homeowners and commercial sites pay recurring route-based service fees (monthly/quarterly) plus one-off termite and wildlife jobs; food plants and hospitals pay for audit-ready monitoring and documentation.
shock: Rentokil H1 2026 results (2026-07-30): North America pest organic growth slowed to 2.4% in Q2 (guidance 2.6-3.4%), management retired its 20% 2027 North American margin target, shares fell 16%, residential weakness continued into July, and an extra $47M was provided for termite damage claims.
incumbents: Rollins (Orkin), Rentokil Terminix, Anticimex (EQT), PE platforms (Certus, Hawx, PestCo). PE accounted for ~60% of 2024-25 pest M&A per a broker tracker (directional). Money: recurring route subscriptions, termite warranties.
incumbent_fragility: Terminix integration drag and technician churn; termite-warranty liabilities; PE platforms bought at 8-15x EBITDA and need growth; 17,000 small owner-operators aging into succession; commercial customers want digital compliance records incumbents deliver on paper.
funded_startups_already_here: Pest Share (Boise, $28M Series A Sept 2025 per VCBacked, unverified); Zepta (Germany, seven-figure 2025); Spotta (UK seed); Scoutlabs (Budapest, $2M); WorkWave/PestPac and FieldRoutes software already entrenched.
wedge_hints: Termite warranty underwriting/insurance and claims management; commercial compliance monitoring-as-a-service for food plants; owner-succession marketplace and roll-up financing; technician training and recruiting.
insider_roles: Branch managers, route supervisors, QA directors at food plants, state pesticide regulators, PMP owners, M&A advisors.

name: US fines, court fees and automated-enforcement citations (the citation lifecycle)
size_basis: Tax Policy Center citing Census: fines and fees revenue $17.8B in 2024, $15.5B in 2023; Fines and Fees Justice Center $13.9B in 2022. Honest caveat: the vendor-captured slice is far smaller (Verra Mobility's entire 2026 revenue guide is $945-965M), so the monetizable pool is more likely $2-4B.
money_flow: Drivers and defendants pay state and local governments fines, court fees and surcharges; private vendors (camera operators, payment processors, collectors, probation providers) take per-ticket fees, convenience fees or contingency.
shock: Automated enforcement is expanding: Verra Mobility Q2 2026 (released 2026-08-05) Government Solutions revenue $128.5M (+20%); NYC red-light camera contract ~$998M over 5 years for 600 intersections; Los Angeles picked Verra for California's largest speed program (125 locations); New York authorized statewide work-zone cameras in its 2026 budget; ~300 related bills introduced in 2025; Colorado SB26-152 would cut the speed threshold to 6 mph over (outcome unknown).
incumbents: Verra Mobility, Conduent, Tyler Technologies (courts and payments), bill-pay vendors, collection agencies. Capture money via per-citation fees, convenience fees on payments, contingency collection.
incumbent_fragility: Five-year municipal contracts, political backlash over cameras as revenue machines, ability-to-pay reforms, legacy court case-management systems, high convenience fees; Verra itself flags NYC payment timing as a risk and its Government margin fell from 28% to 24%.
funded_startups_already_here: No funded court-payments startup found in 2025-26. Older/small: Ticket Avengers (court-debt installment wallet), Court Innovations/Matterhorn (online dispute resolution, $1.8M Series A 2017). Adjacent: BusPatrol stop-arm cameras.
wedge_hints: Ability-to-pay payment plans and lower-fee payment rails for courts; online adjudication/dispute for camera tickets; unpaid-citation collections analytics; fee-reform compliance reporting. Warning: reputational and political risk, slow municipal procurement.
insider_roles: Municipal court clerks and administrators, city finance directors, public defenders and legal-aid lawyers, traffic engineers, city attorneys, collections managers.

name: US donations to congregations and the payments, software and treasury stack around them
size_basis: Giving USA 2026 (2025 data): giving to religion $151.58B, 23% of $617.2B total; +2.4% nominal, -0.2% real; ~1% real growth since 2005. Addressable fee pool is far smaller than the flow (my estimate: digital share x ~3% processing plus software, roughly $1.5-2.5B), so the pool is the giving flow with weak capture.
money_flow: Donors give to ~350k congregations by check, cash and increasingly online; giving platforms take ~2-3% processing plus monthly software fees from churches.
shock: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 2025) changes charitable tax rules from tax year 2026: deduction up to $1,000 ($2,000 joint) for cash gifts for non-itemizers (direct gifts only, not DAFs), 0.5%-of-AGI floor and ~35% benefit cap for itemizers. Effect on church giving is unmeasured; no projection found. Weak shock.
incumbents: Pushpay (private since 2023 under Sixth Street and BGH; 53.6M gifts in 2025), Tithely, Subsplash, Planning Center (on Stripe), Givelify, Gloo (Nasdaq IPO Nov 2025 at $8, ~$73M raised, 57,000 paying customers, ~$41M LTM revenue). Money via processing fees and bundled church-management software.
incumbent_fragility: Low: bundled platforms with high switching costs; the real constraint is flat real giving and a shrinking congregation count.
funded_startups_already_here: Pushpay, Tithely, Subsplash, Planning Center, Givelify, Gloo and Engiven all attack giving/software; platform consolidation is under way.
wedge_hints: Treasury/banking, church mortgage lending and property sale/lease-back for shrinking congregations (not another giving app); tax-receipt workflows for the new non-itemizer rule.
insider_roles: Church administrators and business managers, denominational finance officers, church-lending credit unions, CPAs for churches.

name: US spend on vending, micro-markets and office coffee (convenience services)
size_basis: NAMA Foundation/Technomic State of Convenience Services census: $31.1B projected 2025 (from $26.6B in 2023). Narrower IBISWorld vending-operators figure: $7.9B in 2026, -0.5%.
money_flow: Workplaces, hospitals, schools and venues host machines and markets; operators stock them and pay site commissions; consumers pay by card.
shock: 365 Retail Markets (Providence Equity) announced completion of its Cantaloupe acquisition on 2026-05-11 (~40,000 customers added), consolidating cashless payments, telemetry and micro-market software; a 10% tariff surcharge on HTS 8476.89 vending machines ran 2026-02-24 to 2026-07-24 (extension unconfirmed). Weak shock.
incumbents: Canteen (Compass), Aramark Refreshment, Sodexo, thousands of small operators; 365+Cantaloupe now owns the payments/telemetry rail for ~40,000 customers.
incumbent_fragility: Operators have thin route margins, labor-heavy servicing and now one fewer payments/telemetry vendor option; otherwise not especially fragile.
funded_startups_already_here: Many smart-fridge and micro-market startups (Farmer's Fridge, Byte, Yo-Kai Express named from background knowledge, not verified this session); 365 Retail Markets is PE-backed consolidator.
wedge_hints: Independent payments/telemetry rail for operators uneasy about 365 owning Cantaloupe; route finance; inventory and spoilage optimization.
insider_roles: Route drivers, operator owners, college and hospital food-service directors.

name: US industrial MRO and indirect-supplies spend by plants, contractors and facilities (industrial distribution)
geography: United States (North America for Grainger's sizing)
size_basis: Grainger's own 2022 investor-day estimate of its North American high-touch addressable market (about $165B; Grainger about 7% share or $11B) [secondary, via search summary, not re-verified]. Earlier 10-K sizing put US MRO at about $127B in 2017 and said no player has double-digit share. Cross-check from actuals [primary]: Grainger FY2025 net sales $17,942M at 39.1% gross margin and its 10-K calls MRO 'large and fragmented'; Fastenal 9M-2026 sales $7,051.9M (about $9.4B annualised, my derivation); MSC fiscal Q3-2026 sales $1,047M (about $4.2B annualised, my derivation). Top three are about $31B, a minority of the pool.
money_flow: Plants, contractors and facilities pay industrial distributors (Grainger, Fastenal, MSC, Motion, Applied, Amazon Business, thousands of regional independents) for fasteners, safety gear, cutting tools, bearings, electrical and janitorial supplies. Distributors buy from thousands of suppliers (Grainger: 5,000+ primary suppliers, none above 5% of purchases) and earn roughly 39-45% gross margin.
shock: Tariff regime churn plus spend consolidating to the largest distributors. IEEPA tariffs were struck down 2026-02-20; Section 232 metals tariffs were restructured 2026-04-02 (effective 2026-04-06); the 10% Section 122 surcharge expired 2026-07-24 and was replaced by Section 301 duties of 10%/12.5% on goods from 60 economies. Fastenal Q3-2026 (reported 2026-10-14): net sales $2,463.3M, +15.5%; pricing added about 240bp; customer sites fell to 90,759 from 98,823 while $50k+/month sites rose to 3,288 from 2,771; manufacturing daily sales +17.2%, heavy manufacturing +20.2%; gross margin helped by direct sourcing savings, supplier rebates and tariff refunds. Grainger said underlying MRO demand was muted in 2025.
incumbents: Grainger, Fastenal, MSC, Applied Industrial, Motion, Amazon Business, Home Depot's SRS/HD Supply, plus a long tail of local and regional independent distributors. They capture the money through product margin (39-45% gross) plus inventory-management services (vending, bin stocking, onsite).
incumbent_fragility: The big three are healthy, so they are not the fragile layer. The fragile layers are mid-size independent distributors (losing national accounts to Fastenal and Grainger, per the site-count shift, and repricing slowly while tariffs change every few months) and plants' own storerooms (large stocks of slow-moving spares they cannot find, cross-reference or sell). Amazon Business and Zoro compete on the low-touch tail.
funded_startups_already_here: Partium (Philadelphia, AI industrial spare-parts search, $15M Series A led by Trestle Partners, 2024-09); Eezee (Singapore, MRO e-commerce, $5M raised 2026-02, $18.7M total); Moglix (India, B2B industrial marketplace); GoExpedi (Houston, last round $25M Series B in 2019, so old). Amazon Business and Grainger's Zoro are the real competition. No US startup with a 2025-2026 round targeting independent distributors was found.
wedge_hints: (a) Repricing and sourcing-substitution software for independent industrial distributors under tariff volatility; (b) plant-side spare-parts data cleanup, cross-reference and surplus resale; (c) distributor roll-ups where the acquirer supplies software and buying scale. Bottom-up hypothesis: about 2,000 independent distributors at $50k a year of software is $100M (count not verified).
insider_roles: Plant storeroom and MRO buyers; inside sales reps and branch managers at independent distributors; Fastenal onsite managers; distributor pricing analysts; reliability and maintenance planners; indirect-spend category managers.

name: US OEM spend on outsourced custom machined parts from independent machine shops
size_basis: IBISWorld machine-shop services (NAICS 33271), updated Feb 2026: about $47.8B 2026 revenue, 16,619 businesses, about 224,000 employees, 0.4% five-year revenue CAGR [secondary, via search summary]. My derivation: about $2.9M revenue and 13.5 employees per business. Excludes captive in-house machining and fabricated-metal job shops. Xometry management's $275B custom-parts opportunity is a global company claim and was not used.
money_flow: Aerospace, defense, energy, medical, machinery and automotive manufacturers buy custom machined parts from about 16,600 independent shops, mostly by RFQ and relationships; marketplaces (Xometry, Protolabs) take the prototype and low-volume end.
shock: Section 232 metals tariffs restructured by proclamation 2026-04-02 (effective 2026-04-06): most derivatives moved from 50% on metal content to 25% on full entered value, the derivative-inclusions process was terminated, and Commerce/USTR can add products on a rolling basis; Section 301 duties of 10-12.5% added 2026-07-23/24. This changes landed cost of imported machined and fabricated parts and makes domestic quotes competitive, while NTMA surveys show recruitment is the top constraint for every respondent. Capital is flooding the defense niche (Hadrian $1.37B Series D in 2026).
incumbents: Thousands of owner-operated machine shops; buyer-side OEM procurement and supplier-development teams; marketplaces Xometry (public) and Protolabs (public, in-house production); Fictiv and Hubs (acquired, per memory, not re-verified).
incumbent_fragility: Shops quote by hand over days, are owner-led with an aging workforce, and cannot easily finance automation or absorb surge demand; skilled-machinist recruitment is the top NTMA concern. Marketplaces fit prototypes and low volume, not mid-volume production runs.
funded_startups_already_here: Xometry (public; Q3-2025 revenue $181.0M, +28%; a critic argues marketplace revenue flat since Q3-2022); Protolabs (public); Fictiv and Hubs (no recent round found); Hadrian ($260M in 2025-07, then $1.37B Series D in 2026 at $7.87B valuation, automated US factories for defense/space CNC parts); Isembard (London, reported $50M Series A led by Union Square Ventures in 2026, unverified); Standard Bots ($200M Series C June 2026, sells robots to machine shops). Crowded for defense/aerospace CNC, contested overall.
wedge_hints: Mid-volume (100-5,000 piece), mid-tolerance parts that Xometry's prototype model and Hadrian's defense-grade model both skip; shop-side ERP, quoting, scheduling and inspection-as-a-service (CMM and first-article reports); buy-and-automate roll-ups of non-defense shops; used-machine and tooling financing. Bottom-up check: $100M of software needs about 2,000 shops at $50k (12% of all shops), which is heroic; a marketplace or roll-up route needs about $1B of flow at a 10% take.
insider_roles: Shop owners and estimators; OEM sourcing and supplier-development engineers; NTMA and PMPA staff; CNC programmers; commercial and SBA lenders to shops; Haas and Mazak dealers.

name: US OEM and prime purchases of metal castings from foundries (defense-critical)
size_basis: AFS (American Foundry Society, July 2026): US metalcasting industry revenue about $53.7B in 2025, with casting sales projected +8.0% in 2026 (about $58B), up from a 4.2% January projection [primary]. Forgings are not included; the only FIA figure found was $10.6B of custom-forging shipments in 2012, too old to use. Foundry count not found.
money_flow: OEMs and defense primes (valves and fittings, pumps, heavy equipment, vehicles, rail, aerospace and defense) pay foundries for castings; foundries buy scrap, alloys, sand and patterns and do their own finishing.
shock: The Department of War's Manufacturing Technology Program Strategic Plan FY2026-2031 (published 2026-09-30) names castings, forgings and microelectronics as single points of failure and states the department lacks latent capacity to rapidly scale production of key systems and munitions in a crisis, citing offshoring, consolidation, qualification delays and small-supplier financing gaps (no new dollars attached). A Pentagon acquisition official is quoted saying the defense cast-and-forge supply chain has shrunk 80% (date unclear), with at least 122,000 more workers needed by 2028. AFS puts tariff cost to the industry near $1B to date; a June 2026 MxD roadmap cites aging equipment and offshoring.
incumbents: Thousands of small and mid-size foundries; large aerospace casting and forging houses (Howmet, PCC, Wyman-Gordon, Carpenter, from memory). About 377 foundries make valves and pipe fittings (narrower count).
incumbent_fragility: Capital-intensive, environmentally permitted, aging workforce, long pattern and tooling lead times, and NADCAP/AS9100 qualification that takes months to years, so customers cannot easily dual-source and capacity is sticky and cannot flex to surge demand.
funded_startups_already_here: Fabri (MIT spinout, investment casting, $13.5M total, backed by RTX Ventures and Lockheed Martin Ventures, second foundry targeted for 2027; one profile dates a seed to 2026-06, likely a data artifact); Foundry Lab (New Zealand, microwave casting, $8M Series A, date unclear). Adjacent: Hadrian (CNC, not casting). No funded foundry-sourcing marketplace or qualification-as-a-service company found.
wedge_hints: Casting and forging sourcing and qualification (RFQ routing, first-article, NADCAP-ready paperwork); pattern and tooling as-a-service (digital twin, 3D-printed sand molds); foundry capacity and utilisation data; casting-to-machining kitted supply for primes; foundry roll-up with software. Bottom-up check: a 3% take on $53.7B is about $1.6B of flow-based revenue, so $100M needs about 6% of the pool at 3% take; needs trust and qualification credentials first.
insider_roles: Foundry owners, melt and pattern-shop managers; prime supplier-quality engineers; DCMA reps; NADCAP auditors; AFS and FIA staff; metallurgists qualifying alloys.

name: DoD munitions and shipbuilding production-ramp dollars flowing to sub-tier suppliers
size_basis: My derivation. OBBBA (signed 2025-07-04) gave about $150B for defense with execution to 2029, reported lines $29B shipbuilding and $25B munitions: $54B over about 4 years is about $13.5B a year; FY2026 appropriations (topline $838.7B) added roughly $3B-$6.4B for munitions (sources differ) plus multiyear authority for 8 of 13 missiles. Gross new procurement about $17-20B a year; an Army official said subcontractors often account for 50-60% of weapon-system cost, so sub-tier flow is about $9-12B a year; I use $10B. Full base-budget flow is larger but not sourced here. Line items are secondary (law-firm alert, SOFREP, Breaking Defense).
money_flow: Congress funds the Department of War; primes (Lockheed, RTX, Northrop, General Dynamics, HII, L3Harris) pay roughly half or more of weapon-system cost to sub-tier suppliers for castings, forgings, machined parts, energetics and electronics.
shock: OBBBA reconciliation funding (2025-07-04) with reporting that the Pentagon planned to spend it in FY2026; FY2026 appropriations (2026-02) gave multiyear authority for PAC-3, LRASM, JASSM-ER, THAAD, SM-6, AMRAAM, Tomahawk and SM-3 IB; a 2026 Iran campaign reportedly cost $33.4B including $22.3B of expended munitions (secondary, unverified) and exposed rocket-motor, energetics and labor bottlenecks. Lockheed said in May 2026 it will invest $8-9B through 2030 including new second sources; GMLRS rose from about 8,000 to about 14,000 rounds a year and PAC-3 from 300 to 550 missiles.
incumbents: Lockheed Martin, RTX, Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, HII, L3Harris, Boeing and their tier-1s, who capture the money through cost-plus and fixed-price multiyear contracts.
incumbent_fragility: The Department of War itself says there is no latent capacity; supplier qualification cycles are long, many parts are sole-source, small suppliers face financing gaps, and primes cannot create sub-tier capacity by contract alone. The CMMC compliance route was reversed in July 2026 (Phase 2 suspended), showing small-supplier cost sensitivity.
funded_startups_already_here: Hadrian ($1.37B Series D 2026, $7.87B valuation); Isembard ($50M Series A 2026, unverified); Fabri ($13.5M, casting); from memory and not searched: Anduril, Castelion, Firehawk, X-Bow, Ursa Major, Saronic, Divergent. Crowded for capacity and hardware; open only for the support layer (supplier qualification, first-article inspection, special-process capacity).
wedge_hints: AS9102 first-article inspection automation; special-process capacity brokerage (NADCAP heat treat, plating, NDT; a known aerospace bottleneck, from memory); sub-tier supplier-development services sold to primes; working-capital financing for small defense suppliers; sub-tier supply-chain mapping for DCMA and program offices. Legal premise to check: DFARS specialty-metals rules, ITAR, cost-accounting rules for subcontract financing.
insider_roles: Prime supplier-development and supplier-quality engineers; DCMA industrial specialists; program-office industrial-base analysts; sub-tier shop owners with AS9100; NADCAP auditors.

name: US industrial plant maintenance, repair and millwright labor and outsourced machinery repair
size_basis: Outsourced: about $54.6B for NAICS 81131 (commercial and industrial machinery repair group), Economic Census 2022, as quoted by Vantage Insights [secondary, group-level; Census does not publish a separate 811310 total in what I could reach, and the Census API needed a key I did not register for]. In-house on top: BLS counts 547,300 jobs in 2025 (446,900 industrial machinery mechanics, 59,700 machinery maintenance workers, 40,700 millwrights) at median pay $64,100 [primary]; my derivation 547,300 x $64,100 = about $35.1B of direct wages before benefits and overhead.
money_flow: Plants pay their own maintenance staff and outsourced repair shops and contractors to keep production equipment (motors, pumps, gearboxes, conveyors, machine tools) running.
shock: BLS 2025-35 projections: +14% (78,900 jobs, to about 626,200), about 51,900 openings a year, much faster than average [primary; release month inferred]. Deloitte/Manufacturing Institute (April 2024): up to 3.8M manufacturing jobs needed by 2033 with 1.9M possibly unfilled. Reshoring and automation enlarge the installed base to maintain (North American robot orders 36,766 units in 2025).
incumbents: In-house plant maintenance departments (most of the money); OEM service arms (Siemens, ABB, Rockwell); regional motor, pump and gearbox rebuilders; maintenance contractors and industrial staffing firms (the latter from memory).
incumbent_fragility: Fragmented owner-led repair shops, technician scarcity, knowledge held by retiring workers, and OEM service lock-in on proprietary controls; none can scale labor quickly.
funded_startups_already_here: Sensing and AI is funded: Augury ($75M Series F, Feb 2025, valuation above $1B); Tractian ($120M Series C, late 2024); competitors named in lists include MachineMetrics, Falkonry, Uptake, Uptime AI; Fullbay (truck-shop software) is adjacent. No funded startup selling technician labor or repair capacity as a service to plants was found.
wedge_hints: Technician-as-a-service with an apprenticeship pipeline and dispatch; motor, pump and gearbox rebuild roll-up with rebuild-versus-replace software (tariffs make replacement costlier); spare-part reverse engineering and remanufacture (DLA is doing this for DoD); outcome-priced maintenance bundled with sensing. Bottom-up check: $100M of labor-as-a-service needs about 800 technicians at $125k revenue each, about 0.15% of the workforce; the hard part is gross margin and recruiting.
insider_roles: Plant maintenance managers; reliability engineers; maintenance planners and schedulers; motor-repair shop owners (EASA members); millwright union business agents; OEM field-service managers.

name: Owners' parts and service spend on heavy equipment (ag, construction, mining), opened by right-to-repair
size_basis: Floor figure: Caterpillar services revenues of about $24B in 2025 per Cat's 2026 proxy statement [secondary, via search summary; I could not reach the 10-K MD&A text to confirm, and I could not confirm a $28B 2026 services target]. Cat total 2025 sales and revenues $67.589B [primary, 10-K]. Deere, CNH, AGCO, Komatsu and Kubota aftermarket is on top; I did not retrieve Deere's parts-and-service total.
money_flow: Farmers, contractors and miners pay OEM dealer networks for parts, diagnostics and repair; software locks (diagnostic tools, component pairing, emissions limp mode) have kept independent shops out.
shock: On 2026-07-08 the FTC and five states (Illinois, Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin) announced a settlement with Deere: a 10-year order requiring the same repair resources Deere gives dealers (read, clear and reset fault codes, reprogram and pair components, restart after emissions shutdown, manuals and troubleshooting) to farmers and independent shops on fair and reasonable terms, with no dealer retaliation; no fee schedule; stipulated order filed in N.D. Illinois and pending judicial approval. Preceded by a $99M class settlement in April 2026 in which Deere also promised digital repair tools for 10 years, starting before end-2026.
incumbents: OEMs and franchised dealer networks (Deere, Caterpillar, CNH, AGCO, Komatsu); parts and service carry higher margins than new machines (from memory) and are captured through proprietary software and dealer exclusivity.
incumbent_fragility: Business-model conflict: dealer service departments are profit centers protected by franchise law, so an OEM cannot price tools low without cannibalising dealers, yet 'fair and reasonable terms' is now court-enforced for Deere. The order covers Deere ag equipment only; Cat and construction/mining brands are not parties.
funded_startups_already_here: None found. Searches for 2026 funding of multi-brand diagnostic or independent-shop software for ag and construction equipment returned nothing; the settlement is only three months old, so absence may reflect search limits. Adjacent but not equivalent: truck-shop software Fullbay.
wedge_hints: Multi-brand diagnostic hardware and software for independent ag and construction repair shops (the Snap-on/Autel-for-tractors analogy); mobile field-repair networks; remanufactured emissions and electronic components; shop-management and parts cross-reference software; extended warranty and financing for independents. Legal premise: order unapproved as of the FTC page, pricing not final, Deere-only; construction and mining depend on state laws and DMCA repair exemptions (from memory). Bottom-up check: 5% of a Cat-scale $24B pool at a 10% take is $120M, with heroic share-shift assumptions.
insider_roles: Independent ag and construction repair shop owners; former Deere and Cat dealer service managers; custom-harvester and large-fleet equipment managers; equipment auction appraisers; US PIRG right-to-repair staff.

name: North American manufacturers' spend on factory-automation and robot cells (robots plus integration)
size_basis: My estimate. A3: North American companies ordered 36,766 robots worth $2.25B in 2025 (+6.6% units, +10.1% revenue; 2024: 31,311 units). Using a rule of thumb that the robot is about 25% of installed cell cost (from memory), $2.25B x 4 is about $9B. Cross-check: Control Engineering's 2026 Giants list shows the top 75 integrators alone reporting $4.67B of integration revenue net of hardware, +18% year on year (secondary, voluntary self-reporting).
money_flow: Manufacturers pay robot OEMs (FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa, KUKA), controls vendors (Rockwell, Siemens) and system integrators for robot cells and automation projects.
shock: Commerce opened a Section 232 investigation into robotics and industrial machinery in September 2025; by mid-2026 the administration signalled new tariffs but no final action was found; a 2026-06-01 proclamation cut Section 232 rates on ag, mobile industrial and HVAC equipment (effective 2026-06-08 through 2027-12-31). Demand is rotating: H1-2026 North American robot orders were 17,995 units and $1.166B (+2.0% units, +6.6% value) with semiconductors/electronics +35%, pharma +32%, automotive components +24% and automotive OEMs -25%.
incumbents: Robot OEMs (FANUC, ABB, Yaskawa, KUKA), controls vendors (Rockwell, Siemens) and thousands of custom-engineering system integrators; integrators with over $100M gross revenue rose from 12% in 2021 to 24% in 2025.
incumbent_fragility: Integrators are labor-bound project shops with scarce controls engineers (average engineers per integrator 105 in 2021, 168 in 2025), quote each project by hand, and face tariff-driven equipment cost inflation and pricing pressure.
funded_startups_already_here: Standard Bots ($200M Series C June 2026, $1B valuation; Sacra estimates $24M ARR in 2025); Vention ($110M Series D, Jan 2026); Path Robotics ($100M Series D, Oct 2024); Bright Machines ($126M Series C, June 2024); Formic (tiny listed round); Hadrian for machining cells. Figures are from aggregators, not company releases.
wedge_hints: Integrator back-office and engineering tools (quoting, PLC and cell-code generation, commissioning); brownfield welding and machine-tending for small shops; used and refurbished robot resale; safety validation services. Watch the pending Section 232 robotics outcome.
insider_roles: Integrator project managers and controls engineers; plant automation engineers; robot-brand distributors; machine builders; safety assessors.

name: US importers' customs-duty payments on industrial inputs and the duty-mitigation services market
size_basis: About $214B of US customs duties over the trailing twelve months through July 2026, from a tracker of Monthly Treasury Statement data (secondary; I did not open the Treasury statement; net monthly figures can dip when duties are refunded). The capturable services fee pool (brokers, counsel, drawback, audits) is a small fraction and was not sized. Overlap flag: finance slice excluded IEEPA refund claims; this pool is duties on Section 232 and 301 goods and the mitigation services.
money_flow: Importers pay duties to CBP, and pay customs brokers, trade counsel and consultants for classification, valuation, origin, drawback and foreign-trade-zone work.
shock: Section 122 surcharge expired 2026-07-24; Section 301 duties (10% or 12.5%) on goods from 60 economies took effect 2026-07-23 with no statutory sunset and a pending court challenge; Section 232 stacks on top; the formal derivative-inclusions process ended 2026-04-06; IEEPA tariffs were struck down 2026-02-20 and the Court of International Trade ordered refunds with interest in early March 2026. Customs bonds, audits and enforcement are rising.
incumbents: Customs brokers (UPS, Expeditors, Livingston and others, from memory), Big Four and trade-law firms, and trade-software vendors (E2open and similar, from memory); a CBP trade-enforcement tool contract lists Altana as incumbent on the government side.
incumbent_fragility: Hourly-billing brokers and counsel are built for stable rules; tariff stacking changes monthly and classification and origin work is manual and error-prone.
funded_startups_already_here: Altana (about $323-337M total raised, $1B valuation July 2024); Tarifflo (YC S26; AuditLive recovers overpaid duty; $500K+ pre-seed); Tariff Sense (Canada, CAD 220k pre-seed Dec 2025); TariffLens AI (launched May 2026); traide AI (Berlin); Flexport is also active (from memory). Many AI classification entrants but little capital outside Altana.
wedge_hints: Post-entry audits and recovery of overpaid Section 232/301 duties on a contingency basis; first-sale-for-export and drawback programs for mid-market manufacturers; metals-content declarations for Section 232 derivatives (the 15%-by-weight carve-out and annex treatment make this a real data task); supplier origin evidence. Legal premise: contingency fees on duty recovery need a licensed customs broker or counsel in the loop; refund eligibility turns on the 180-day protest window and 2026 court orders.
insider_roles: Licensed customs brokers; import compliance managers at mid-size manufacturers; trade counsel; CBP import specialists; drawback specialists.

name: US medium- and heavy-duty truck parts aftermarket bought by independent fleets and shops
size_basis: IBISWorld: about $25.5B of 2026 sales through US heavy-duty truck parts dealers (dealers only, so a floor) [secondary]. Global heavy-duty aftermarket estimates range $93B-$158B, with North America about 36% of the heavy-duty automotive aftermarket, but definitions differ and no clean US independent-aftermarket figure was found.
money_flow: Fleets and owner-operators pay dealers, distributors and independent shops for engine, drivetrain, brake and chassis parts and repair.
shock: 25% Section 232 tariff on imported medium- and heavy-duty trucks and truck parts (Class 3-8, engines, transmissions, tires, chassis), proclaimed 2025-10-17 and effective 2025-11-01; USMCA-eligible goods are treated on non-US content; manufacturer offsets of 3.75% benefit domestic assemblers, not aftermarket importers. FreightWaves reports heavy-duty engine parts cost 20-30% more than two years ago and many small carriers have not changed how they buy parts (unverified).
incumbents: OEM dealers (PACCAR Parts, Volvo/Mack, Daimler Truck), national distributors (FleetPride, TruckPro and others, from memory) and independent repair shops.
incumbent_fragility: Price discovery is by phone and parts counter, sourcing is concentrated in imports now taxed, and small fleets buy through habit, so dealers and distributors cannot easily offer transparent multi-source pricing.
funded_startups_already_here: Fullbay (heavy-duty shop-management software, $23M growth round July 2024 from JMI Equity with Mainsail; reported acquisition of Pitstop in March 2026, unverified); Decisiv (service software, not researched). No funded heavy-duty parts-procurement startup found.
wedge_hints: Parts price transparency and sourcing for small fleets and independent shops, including tariff-avoiding sources; remanufactured and domestic alternatives to taxed imports; core-return and warranty-recovery services; parts availability for down trucks. Bottom-up check: 1% of $25.5B is $255M of parts flow, so $100M of revenue needs about 0.4% of dealer-channel flow at full pass-through or about 4% at a 10% take.
insider_roles: Parts counter managers at truck dealers and distributors; independent fleet maintenance managers; owner-operators; heavy-duty shop owners; Auto Care Association and HDMA staff.

name: US-owned and foreign OEM contract manufacturing in Mexico (IMMEX / maquila) under the USMCA review
size_basis: More than $300B of IMMEX goods shipped in 2024 (an export value, not a fee pool; value added in Mexico is lower and was not found). As of December 2025: 6,512 active IMMEX establishments, 3.15M workers, monthly revenues above 653B pesos [secondary, American Industries Group; sources disagree on IMMEX's share of exports, 40% of total vs about 80% of manufacturing exports].
money_flow: US and foreign OEMs pay Mexican export-manufacturing operations (their own plants, shelter operators, EMS firms) to build products under the IMMEX duty-deferral program; customs brokers, industrial-park developers and compliance providers earn fees around it.
shock: The first USMCA joint review closed on 2026-07-01 without the 16-year extension, moving the three countries to annual reviews (the agreement itself runs to 2036); US-Mexico bilateral rounds covered steel, aluminum, autos, labor and rules of origin (third round ended about 2026-07-23, fourth set for Washington in September 2026; auto rules of origin unresolved). TrendForce says nearshoring investment turned more cautious; the Wilson Center found most sourcing changes made to meet rules of origin raised cost.
incumbents: EMS and contract manufacturers (Jabil, Flex, Foxconn, Celestica, Plexus, from memory), shelter operators, industrial-park developers and customs brokers.
incumbent_fragility: Plants with multi-year paybacks now sit on a one-year political horizon; rules-of-origin changes can strand compliance work; many nearshore operations are limited assembly that the review will sort from genuine production.
funded_startups_already_here: None found. Searches for 2025-2026 funding of Mexico contract-manufacturing or USMCA rules-of-origin platforms returned only vendor marketing; incumbent software (E2open) and ERP add-ons (a 2026 NetSuite USMCA guide) cover part of the problem. Evidence of absence is weak.
wedge_hints: USMCA origin and regional-value-content evidence collection across supplier tiers (a data-chasing task that recurs with every annual review); shelter-as-a-service for mid-size US manufacturers; Mexico-side quality and inspection services; dual-footprint (Mexico plus US) planning tools. Payer and budget line are weakest here, so treat as the least promising of the ten.
insider_roles: Mexican customs brokers (agentes aduanales); IMMEX program administrators; maquila plant managers; USMCA compliance managers at OEMs; industrial-park brokers.

name: US homeowners insurance premiums in wildfire-, hail- and hurricane-exposed markets (California cat-model reform, Florida reinsurance reset)
geography: US, concentrated in CA, FL, TX, CO, LA
size_basis: S&P Global Market Intelligence on NAIC data: about $173.1B direct homeowners premium written in 2024 (+13.4%, combined ratio 99.3%); NAIC says 2025 growth slowed, so 173 is a floor. State Farm held about 19.4% of 2024 premium. Figure came via search summary of the S&P article, not read in full.
money_flow: Households (via mortgage escrow) pay carriers and residual plans (CA FAIR Plan, FL Citizens). Carriers pay claims, cat reinsurers, agent commissions and modelers. Residual plans assess the industry when they lose money.
shock: California Sustainable Insurance Strategy lets insurers price with forward-looking wildfire cat models and pass California-only reinsurance costs into rates in exchange for writing in distressed areas (85% of market share). CDI approved the Verisk wildfire model 2025-07-24; Mercury filed the first rate case by 2025-08-15. CDI's Aug 2026 brief: twelve insurer groups have filed under SIS, FAIR Plan growth under 2% in Q2 2026. FAIR Plan has about 668k policies and a roughly 30-35% rate hike for renewals from 2026-10-15 (secondary sources conflict). Opposite pole: Florida Citizens fell from about 1.4M policies (Sept 2023) to 293,772 (May 31, 2026) and June 2026 cat reinsurance fell 15-20%. NAIC: Palisades and Eaton were the costliest wildfires in world history.
incumbents: State Farm, Allstate, Farmers, Progressive, USAA, Chubb, Mercury, CSAA; independent agents; cat modelers Verisk, Moody's RMS, KCC. Carriers earn the spread between premium and modeled loss; modelers license by seat.
incumbent_fragility: State Farm General went to S&P CreditWatch Negative and sought an emergency 17% hike. California is prior-approval, so every change needs a filing and the regulator sets the pace. The 85% writing commitment must now be proven with data. Legacy policy and inspection workflows cannot ingest mitigation evidence at scale.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: RockRose Risk ($12.5M Series A, Aug 2026, vertically integrated wildfire mitigation plus insurance, plans to acquire tree-trimming and roofing firms); BurnBot (Mercury strategic investment, May 2026); BirdsEyeView (seven-figure round, Jan 2026, wildfire modeling); Zesty.ai (Series B 2022, CDI-accepted model, no 2026 round found); Kettle (wildfire reinsurance MGA, $25M Series A, older). From background knowledge, not re-verified: Kin, Openly, Hippo, Lemonade, Branch.
wedge_hints: 1) Verified-mitigation evidence layer: SIS forces discounts and published wildfire risk scores, but homeowners must prove work (photos, invoices, IBHS or third-party inspection; State Farm's 2024 version needed a $125 inspection fee) - a registry or inspection-and-repair network carriers accept. 2) FAIR Plan take-out tooling (policy matching, pricing, agent workflow) for the twelve SIS carriers; Florida's nine Citizens take-out approvals Feb-Apr 2026 are the template. 3) Wildfire rebuild and claims logistics (contractor capacity, permits) after Palisades and Eaton. 4) Parametric deductible top-ups sold through MGAs.
insider_roles: CDI rate-filing analysts and carrier actuaries who file SIS cases; independent agents in California WUI zones; wildfire claims adjusters from Palisades/Eaton; FAIR Plan underwriters; Fire Safe Council and mitigation contractors; mortgage servicers' hazard-loss departments; Florida reinsurance brokers.

name: Insurers' spend on property-catastrophe reinsurance and insurance-linked securities (cat bonds, collateralized re), now repricing down 12-25%
geography: Global (US and Florida set the price)
size_basis: WEAK BASIS, lower bound only. No sourced total of global property-cat reinsurance premium was found. Derived: ILS capital $144.5B at 6/30/2026 times a rate-on-line of about 8.5-12% (Florida Citizens' net ROL was 8.46% in 2026 and 11.95% in 2025) gives about $12-17B for third-party capital alone. Dedicated reinsurance capital is $648B (Gallagher Re, YE2025) to $790B (Aon, 3/31/2026), so the full premium pool including traditional reinsurers is several times larger but unquantified.
money_flow: Primary insurers, state funds (Citizens, FHCF, CEA) and some corporates pay reinsurers and cat-bond investors for catastrophe limit. Brokers (Aon, Guy Carpenter, Gallagher Re, Howden) take brokerage; modelers sell the risk view.
shock: January 1, 2026 renewals: Howden risk-adjusted property cat pricing -14.7% (largest drop since 2014), retro -16.5%; Guy Carpenter global property cat ROL index -12%, then -16% at mid-year, now 23% below the 2024 peak; Florida June 1 down 15-25%. Record $25.6B cat bonds issued in 2025, $63.4B outstanding mid-2026. Counter-signal: CDI's Aug 2026 brief warns cumulative losses point to higher reinsurance costs for 2027.
incumbents: Munich Re, Swiss Re, Hannover Re, SCOR, Everest, Arch, RenaissanceRe; four large brokers; ILS managers. Reinsurers earn the spread over modeled loss; brokers earn a percentage of premium.
incumbent_fragility: Only moderate. Falling rates shrink brokerage dollars while placement work stays manual (spreadsheets, bordereaux). A record capital glut means reinsurers chase large cedents and neglect the long tail of small insurers, public entities and corporates. Balance sheets are not fragile.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Kettle (wildfire reinsurance MGA, $25M Series A, older). Not verified: Reask, Oasis LMF, Fermat Capital and other cat-model and ILS tech names.
wedge_hints: 1) Repeatable small-ticket cat-bond or parametric shelf for regional insurers, municipalities and mid-size corporates (under about $50M limit) where reinsurer minimums bite. 2) Reinsurance procurement and bordereaux data tooling for the roughly 65 new E&S carriers and thousands of MGAs that each buy several treaties. 3) Collateral and trust accounting operations (LOCs, trusts). 4) Parametric top-ups attached to homeowners (Pool 1). Assume software or services to cedents, not capacity.
insider_roles: Reinsurance brokers who place treaties; cedent reinsurance managers and CROs at regional carriers; cat modelers; ILS portfolio managers; trust and collateral administrators in Bermuda; parametric calculation agents.

name: US commercial auto and trucking liability premiums
size_basis: About $72.2B direct premium written in 2024 (+12.1%), AM Best as summarized in search results (not re-verified at source). NAIC 2025 report: commercial auto premium has risen for 15 straight years, +6.6% in Q4 2025 (highest of any line); commercial auto liability pure net loss ratio 71%.
money_flow: Motor carriers and fleets pay carriers and MGAs, mostly through trucking-specialist agents. Carriers pay claims and defense counsel; verdicts above $10M ('nuclear') drive severity.
shock: Two federal changes rewrite driver-qualification risk. English-language proficiency out-of-service enforcement began 2025-06-25 (DOT says 26,000+ drivers sidelined). The non-domiciled CDL final rule is effective 2026-03-16; FMCSA estimates 194,000 non-domiciled CDL holders affected. Commercial auto and GL are the only major lines still above 100% combined (Triple-I/Milliman, May 2026); S&P projects commercial auto at 104.4% in 2026 rising to 106.3% by 2029. The premium link from the new rules is mostly forecast so far; one executive said capacity has not yet fallen.
incumbents: Progressive (among the largest trucking writers, background knowledge), Travelers, Liberty Mutual, Berkshire/National Indemnity, Old Republic, Sentry, Great West; specialty trucking agencies. They profit only if rate increases outrun severity, which they have not for years.
incumbent_fragility: Roughly 15 years of underwriting pain; loss data and driver files sit in incompatible systems (telematics per fleet, MVR per state, FMCSA CSA scores); verdict inflation outruns filed rates; small-fleet agents cannot verify driver status. States regulate rates and the line is unprofitable, so carriers cut appetite rather than innovate.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Nirvana Insurance ($100M Series D at $1.5B valuation, over $260M raised, telematics, single-truck to 500+ truck fleets); Cover Whale (MGA, $40M from Morgan Stanley Expansion Capital Jul 2025, $1.3B+ GWP since 2020); LEEO (telematics commercial auto product launched Mar 2026); HDVI ($16M Series A, Munich Re Ventures and 8VC); Humn.ai ($13.7M Series A, UK, undated).
wedge_hints: 1) Driver-qualification verification feed (CDL status, ELP out-of-service history, non-domiciled flags, chameleon-carrier detection) sold to carriers, MGAs and brokers as underwriting data, like MVR vendors. 2) Group captive or risk retention group formation for 20-100 truck fleets (see captive pool). 3) Post-crash evidence and rapid-response services to blunt nuclear verdicts, paid from carrier claims budgets.
insider_roles: Trucking insurance agents at large specialty agencies; fleet safety directors; trucking claims adjusters and litigation managers at Progressive or Great West; defense counsel who try nuclear-verdict cases; FMCSA compliance consultants; loss-control engineers; CVSA inspectors.

name: US workers' compensation system cost (medical, indemnity, claims administration, cost containment)
size_basis: NASI (Aug 2026, 2023 data): $64.1B total benefits paid (medical plus cash) covering about 150M jobs. NCCI: private carriers wrote $41.6B net premium in 2025; the rest is state funds and self-insured employers. Total employer cost exceeds benefits (admin, profit, taxes) but is not sourced here.
money_flow: Employers pay premiums (or self-insure) to carriers and state funds. Carriers and third-party administrators pay medical providers, injured workers and lawyers. Cost-containment vendors (bill review, PBMs, nurse case management) are paid per bill or as a share of savings.
shock: NCCI State of the Line 2026 (May 2026): private carrier premium fell 0.2% in 2025, the only major line to shrink; calendar-year combined ratio rose to 91% from 86%; accident-year 2025 combined ratio is 102%, so profit now depends on old-reserve releases; medical claim severity rose 6% (2024 data).
incumbents: Travelers, Hartford, Liberty, Zurich, Chubb, AmTrust; state funds (e.g., California SCIF); TPAs (Sedgwick, Gallagher Bassett, CorVel); medical cost containment (Enlyte, MedRisk, Healthesystems). Money is made on float, reserve releases and per-bill vendor fees.
incumbent_fragility: 50 different fee schedules force national vendors to rebuild logic per state; savings-based vendor fees reward inflated 'savings'; premium audits and class-code disputes irritate the paying employer; reserve-release earnings are shrinking. Boring and fragmented rather than weak.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: CompScience ($27.6M Series B, Feb 2025, safety video analytics plus MGA); Pie Insurance (over $615M raised, Series D 2021); Hourly ($27M Series A, undated); Insurate (2021 seed). No 2026 rounds found for workers' comp claims, medical or nurse case-management startups.
wedge_hints: 1) Employer-side premium audit and class-code correction on contingency (employers have a premium line and hate audit disputes). 2) Medical bill-review exceptions and pharmacy cost transparency for self-insured employers and TPAs. 3) Return-to-work and case-management coordination networks. Check state anti-kickback and percent-of-savings rules.
insider_roles: Workers' comp claims adjusters and nurse case managers; employer risk managers; applicant and defense attorneys; TPA operations heads; premium auditors; NCCI/WCIRB classification specialists; state fund underwriters.

name: US title insurance premiums (money mostly retained by title agents)
size_basis: NAIC 2025 full-year report (read as PDF): title direct premium written $18.6B in 2025 (+13.5%); ALTA says $18.5B (+13.8%). Settlement and escrow fees paid by buyers sit on top and are not counted. Non-affiliated agents handle 62.7% of premium; 72.6% of operating expenses are paid to or retained by agents.
money_flow: Buyers and refinancing borrowers pay a one-time premium at closing. Agents keep most of it, underwriters keep the rest and pay claims. Net loss ratio is only 4.4% and expense ratio 98.5% (combined 102.8%, third straight year above 100%); paid losses and expense average $51 per policy.
shock: FHFA/Fannie Mae title waiver pilot: Doma Title first vendor from Nov 2024, Westcor added Jul 2025; lenders can skip lender's title insurance on low-risk refinances and pay Fannie a $75 fee. In June 2026 FHFA director Pulte said Fannie was working to expand the pilot; KBW analysts called the earnings impact small and it is still refinance-only. Separately, 2025 premium jumped as refis revived when rates fell to about 6.5% in Sept 2025. ALTA argues fraud and forgery are about 40% of refi claim costs. Shock is real but small so far.
incumbents: First American 23.1%, Fidelity National 14.5%, Old Republic 14%, Chicago Title 13.1%, Stewart 10.9% (ALTA via Scotsman Guide; top five over 75%); thousands of agencies; county recorders and local title plants as data gatekeepers.
incumbent_fragility: Nearly all revenue is a one-time toll on a transaction while claims are 4.4% of premium, so the product is priced like distribution, not insurance. A federal buyer (Fannie/Freddie) can waive the requirement for loans it owns. But state statutes, the purchase-loan lender requirement and ALTA lobbying slow any bypass.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Qualia (closing platform; reported $50M round Aug 2026, sources conflict on series and valuation); Doma (first waiver vendor); Westcor (traditional underwriter, second waiver vendor); Spruce, States Title, JetClosing, Modus, Endpoint (named by Bain Capital Ventures, no 2026 rounds found); Blueprint Title ($16M Series B, 2021); Vestris (YC, end-to-end title processing).
wedge_hints: 1) Automated title-risk product for the GSE waiver (needs a licensed underwriter partner; the $75 flat fee versus 4.4% loss ratio shows the margin is in not paying agents). 2) Wire-fraud and forgery prevention at closing (identity, wire verification). 3) National standardized title-plant and recorder data across 3,000+ counties licensed to underwriters, lenders and GSEs. 4) Commercial real estate title review as volumes rebound.
insider_roles: Title examiners and underwriting counsel; escrow officers; title agency owners; county recorders; mortgage closers and post-closers; GSE seller/servicer relationship managers.

name: US annuity and life insurance distribution compensation (agent commissions and IMO/FMO overrides)
size_basis: DERIVED. LIMRA: 2025 annuity sales $461.3B (+6%), of which FIA $128.2B, RILA $79.6B, other about $253.5B. Assumed commissions (not verified at source; only Wink's 2017 average indexed-annuity commission of 4.96% found): FIA about 5% ($6.4B), RILA about 3.5% ($2.8B), other about 2.5% ($6.3B), total about $15.5B. A 3-5% blended range gives $14-23B. Life insurance commissions are extra and not counted.
money_flow: Carriers (Athene, Corebridge, Allianz Life, Jackson, MassMutual, F&G) pay commissions to independent agents, banks and broker-dealers, plus overrides to IMOs/FMOs. Consumers pay through spread and surrender charges.
shock: Record demand and a product mix shift: Q2 2026 was a record quarter at $123.9B and H1 2026 reached $231.3B (LIMRA); RILA +21%, FIA -5% as caps fell, fixed-rate deferred -7%. Mix shifts move commission dollars between channels. Hypothesis, unverified: surrender periods on 2022-2024 purchases are starting to end, creating a retention and rollover wave.
incumbents: IMOs and FMOs (e.g., Integrity, AmeriLife - background knowledge), independent broker-dealers (LPL, Osaic), banks, career agencies, carrier wholesalers. Money is earned as override percentages and carrier bonuses.
incumbent_fragility: Each carrier has its own application, illustration, suitability form and contracting process; best-interest rules add documentation burden; commissions compress as sales shift to lower-commission RILAs; overrides pay for manual back-office work. Lock-in is real though, since agents follow their IMO.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Ethos (term life, IPO Jan 2026 raising about $200M); DPL Financial Partners ($23M Series C, Dec 2024, RIA insurance marketplace); Annuity.com ($15.7M seed, May 2024); Axonic Insurance ($210M, Oct 2025, annuity issuer); Micruity ($5.1M seed, annuities in 401(k)s, undated); Blueprint Income (MassMutual subsidiary). Term life is crowded (Ladder, Bestow, Policygenius from background knowledge); annuity back-office is thin.
wedge_hints: 1) Best-interest documentation and suitability workflow for IMOs and carriers (compliance budget exists). 2) In-force book management for agents: maturity and surrender-expiry alerts plus 1035-exchange paperwork, if the 2022-24 purchase wave is maturing (needs verification). 3) Shared carrier contracting and licensing back-office network (agents wait weeks per carrier).
insider_roles: IMO/FMO compliance officers; annuity wholesalers at carriers; independent agents with 500+ clients; IMO new-business desk staff; state insurance department market-conduct examiners; annuity actuaries.

name: Wholesale, MGA and delegated-authority intermediation of US surplus lines (E&S) and specialty insurance
size_basis: DERIVED. AM Best: US surplus lines direct premium $143.3B in 2025 (+10.4%), 12.9% of all P&C premium, 27.5% of commercial lines; surplus lines wrote over $51B of GL (39% of industry GL). Conning via InsurTech NY (secondary): US MGA premium about $128B in 2025. Assuming roughly 15% intermediary take on $143.3B gives about $21B.
