Cross-check: Ryan Specialty 2025 revenue $3,051M (+21.3%), about $1.4B (47%) delegated authority, implying about 14% share of a $21B pool.
money_flow: Retail agents hand risks to wholesalers (Amwins, CRC/Ryan, Brown & Brown, Gallagher) and MGAs, who place with surplus lines carriers or fronting carriers supplying the balance sheet. Intermediaries are paid commission and fees by carriers out of premium.
shock: The E&S double-digit boom is ending: premium growth slowed to 9.7% through Q3 2025 from 13.5%; competition in cyber, property and D&O; admitted carriers returning to lines they left; AM Best cut the segment outlook to stable in Nov 2025 and flagged adverse-development risk at fronting carriers (accident years 2021-2024). About 65 carriers formed or refocused on E&S in the past decade hold about 26% of premium (ALIRT). AXA XL is forming a wholesale-only surplus lines carrier for 2027.
incumbents: Ryan Specialty ($3.05B revenue, #2 US wholesale, #1 delegated underwriter), Amwins, Brown & Brown, Gallagher, CRC; thousands of MGAs; capacity providers (Berkshire, Lloyd's, AIG, Markel, fronting carriers). Money is a percentage of premium.
incumbent_fragility: Commission is a percentage of premium, so falling property rates shrink revenue while submission handling stays manual (each carrier has a portal and ACORD forms). Roughly 65 new E&S carriers must audit, bordereau-check and police dozens of MGAs by hand. Capacity providers can pull an MGA's support overnight. Surplus lines tax and stamping rules differ per state.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Sixfold ($30M Series B, Jan 2026, underwriting AI); Kalepa ($14M Series A plus an SMB MGA buildout); Corgi (AI-native carrier for startups, reported $2.6B valuation and further raises); Federato (no 2026 funding found). Underwriting-workbench AI is crowded and excluded by round-2 rules; the delegated-authority plumbing has no funded entrant found.
wedge_hints: 1) Bordereaux and delegated-authority compliance infrastructure sold to capacity providers and fronting carriers (budget line in underwriting management; AM Best's fronting concern raises stakes). 2) Surplus lines tax, diligent-search and stamping compliance as a service for wholesalers and MGAs. 3) MGA-capacity marketplace and orphan-program transfer when a capacity provider exits.
insider_roles: MGA COOs and finance leads; bordereaux analysts; delegated-authority audit heads at carriers; wholesalers' submission-desk managers; program managers at fronting carriers; surplus lines compliance officers.

name: US P&C insurers' claims-handling (adjusting) and litigation-defense expense (LAE)
size_basis: DERIVED FROM PRIMARY DATA. Triple-I table (NAIC data via S&P): 2025 net premiums earned $959.5B; adjusting and other expense 5.3% (about $50.9B) plus defense and cost containment 3.7% (about $35.5B) = about $86.4B. 2024: 5.5% and 3.8% of $902.4B. NAIC separately reports $162.9B of unpaid LAE reserves.
money_flow: Insurers' claims departments pay independent adjusters, TPAs and in-house staff (A&O) and defense law firms, experts and court costs (DCC). Estimating, repair-network and photo vendors are paid per claim.
shock: 2025 Palisades and Eaton fires (costliest wildfires in world history, nearly half of 2025 insured losses in one state) plus severe convective storms of about $50B for the third straight year. AM Best says social inflation, nuclear verdicts and third-party litigation financing keep pressure on liability lines. CDI's Aug 2026 brief warns of a Super El Niño. Adjusting expense fell from 7.4% of premium (2021) to 5.3% (2025) in benign years, so surge capacity is thin.
incumbents: In-house claims organizations; Sedgwick, Crawford, Gallagher Bassett and other TPAs/independent adjusters; Verisk (Xactimate), CCC and Enlyte for estimating; panel defense firms under billing guidelines; e-billing platforms such as CounselLink and Mitratech (named from background knowledge). Money is earned per file, per hour and per estimate.
incumbent_fragility: Labor-intensive and volume-priced, so benign years cut staff and cat years overwhelm it. Panel-counsel bills are audited by hand. The payer (claims VP) is cost-pressured and no vendor owns litigation-spend intelligence.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session but funding is old: Five Sigma ($12M Series A 2021, $18M total), Snapsheet (over $100M raised, last round 2021). Named in a 2026 vendor guide with no 2023-2026 funding found: Tractable, CLARA Analytics, Hi Marley, Sprout.ai. Claims AI is a round-1 cliche and crowded; carrier-side litigation-spend intelligence has no funded entrant found.
wedge_hints: 1) Litigation-spend and panel-counsel performance intelligence (outcomes by firm and venue, not just bills) sold to claims VPs and litigation managers. 2) Credentialed catastrophe surge-capacity marketplace for adjusters and repair contractors, activated by event and paid per claim. 3) Subrogation and recovery services where insurers under-collect (needs sizing first).
insider_roles: Claims VPs and litigation managers; cat adjusters; TPA operations heads; panel-counsel partners who bill hourly; Xactimate estimators and public adjusters; subrogation specialists; repair contractors.

name: Cyber and liability premiums being carved out for generative-AI risk (cyber, tech E&O, D&O, GL)
geography: Global for cyber; US for the general liability base
size_basis: Munich Re: global cyber premium $15.3B in 2024, about $16.3B in 2025, about $29B forecast for 2027. Larger base affected: US general liability about $131B (my derivation: surplus lines wrote $51B+ of GL, which AM Best says is 39% of industry GL). AI-specific spend today is a small fraction of both; the point is that AI coverage is being removed from existing policies so buyers must buy it elsewhere.
money_flow: Corporates pay cyber, tech E&O, D&O and GL premiums; carriers pay claims and rely on Verisk/ISO form language shared across the market.
shock: Verisk/ISO generative-AI exclusions took effect January 2026 (CG 40 47 broad, CG 40 48 advertising injury, CG 35 08 products). W.R. Berkley filed an 'absolute' AI exclusion across D&O, E&O and fiduciary; AIG, Great American and Hamilton filed exclusions; Beazley and QBE use AI sublimits of about 10% of cyber limits. An unverified analysis counts 2,369 generative-AI exclusion records across 49 states by mid-2026.
incumbents: Chubb, AXA XL, Beazley, AIG, Travelers, Munich Re; cyber MGAs such as Coalition, At-Bay, Cowbell, Resilience (background knowledge); Verisk as form-maker; brokers Marsh and Aon.
incumbent_fragility: Carriers cannot price AI risk (no loss history, no testing standard), so they exclude. Broad 'arising out of' wording leaves enterprises with deployments their own customers' contracts require them to insure. Forms are shared by licensing, so everyone excludes at once.
funded_startups_already_here: Verified this session: Armilla AI ($25M, Jan 2026, first Lloyd's coverholder dedicated to AI liability); Klaimee ($5.5M seed, Jul 2026, YC, insurance-backed performance warranties and A-F certification for AI agents); Mount (YC Spring 2026, AI-liability carrier, seed size unconfirmed); Corgi (AI-native carrier). Not verified: AIUC, Testudo, Vouch, and the cyber MGAs above.
wedge_hints: 1) AI-system testing and certification standard that underwriters accept for pricing, paid by AI vendors because their customers demand insurance (Klaimee and Armilla already point here, so differentiate on testing depth and a shared standard). 2) M&A and renewal coverage-gap diligence, since acquirers inherit AI liabilities and see narrowed coverage only at renewal. 3) Pooled AI-incident loss-data consortium that gives actuaries something to price from.
insider_roles: Policyholder-side coverage counsel; cyber and tech E&O underwriters at Beazley, Chubb, AXA XL; Verisk/ISO form drafters; broker cyber and tech practice leaders; CISOs and general counsel negotiating AI vendor contracts; cyber reinsurance modelers.

name: Captives, group captives and fronting: corporate premium moving out of the commercial market
geography: Global (Vermont, Delaware, Bermuda, Cayman, Guernsey, Montana; 30+ US states have captive laws)
size_basis: Marsh Benchmarking Report (published 2026-06-01): Marsh-managed captives wrote $79.1B gross written premium in 2025 ($77B in 2024). Swiss Re Institute's older estimate for the whole world was $60-80B, so the true total is at least Marsh's slice. The fee pool inside this (management, fronting, letters of credit, actuarial, reinsurance placement) is much smaller: at an assumed 3-5% it would be $2-4B (hypothesis, unsourced).
money_flow: Corporates and groups of mid-size firms pay premium into their own insurance subsidiary instead of commercial carriers. Fronting carriers issue the policies and charge fees and collateral; managers (Marsh, Aon, WTW, Gallagher/Artex) charge management fees; reinsurers take the excess.
shock: Captives kept growing as commercial pricing fell: Marsh-managed captive premium rose while its commercial price index fell 4% in 2025; Marsh formed 118 new captives in 2025 versus 92 in 2024 and manages about 1,500; third-party-risk captives wrote $4.4B; protected-cell programs grew 47% by premium. Regulatory moves: IRS final rule of 2025-01-14 listing certain 831(b) micro-captive transactions was upheld by one court in March 2026 (CIC Services) and narrowed in April 2026 (Drake Plastics) per conflicting secondary reports; Montana passed a new captive law in May 2025.
incumbents: Marsh Captive Solutions, Aon, WTW, Gallagher/Artex; fronting carriers; group-captive specialists such as Captive Resources (background knowledge).
incumbent_fragility: Conflict of interest: brokers earning commissions on commercial placements run the captives that replace them, so they sell captives to large clients and under-serve mid-size ones. Fronting capacity and letters of credit are costly and slow; domiciles are fragmented; no standard 'captive in a box' exists for a 20-100 unit fleet or contractor group.
funded_startups_already_here: None found with 2023-2026 venture funding for captive management, fronting or group-captive formation. Searched: group captive, fronting fee, captive management, 831(b). One vendor guide says a 20-100 truck fleet needs about $50K-$250K initial capital (marketing estimate).
wedge_hints: 1) Group-captive formation for 20-100 unit fleets, contractors and dealerships with standardized fronting, reinsurance and actuarial work (links to the trucking pool). 2) Captive loss-data benchmarking and feasibility studies as a data asset. 3) White-label cells (protected cell or rent-a-captive) for associations wanting a risk pool without building one. 'Open' on the venture side does not mean easy: heavy capital and regulatory moat.
insider_roles: Captive managers; captive actuaries; Vermont, Delaware, Montana and Bermuda regulators; tax counsel from the 831(b) cases; fronting-carrier underwriters; group-captive agents; CFOs of mid-size trucking and construction firms.

name: US importers' IEEPA tariff refunds and pass-through recovery (one-time stock, mostly already certified)
size_basis: One-time stock, not an annual flow: about $166B of IEEPA duties plus interest expected to be refunded to roughly 330,000 importers of record (Fortune, Apr 2026; Penn Wharton says up to $175B; Reuters factbox says at least $133.5B). As of Oct 2, 2026 CBP had accepted about $136.6B for processing and certified about $126B to Treasury, so roughly 76% is already moving; remaining tail is finally liquidated entries (about $11.4B, 6.9%), non-plaintiff importers under Federal Circuit appeal, and downstream pass-through disputes.
money_flow: US Treasury (via CBP's CAPE portal in ACE) pays refunds plus interest to the importer of record or Form 4811 notify party. Importers then owe or fight over pass-through to those who actually bore the cost: customers of carriers that acted as importer of record (FedEx booked $749M of customer refund obligations at May 31, 2026), buyers charged tariff surcharges under DDP or B2B contracts, and consumers (14 nationwide class actions against FedEx alone). A secondary market (reported up to $100B) trades claims at roughly 50-75 cents on the dollar, with loans at about 50% LTV.
shock: Supreme Court invalidated the IEEPA tariffs on Feb 20, 2026 (6-3). CBP launched CAPE Apr 20, 2026; Phase 3 (finally liquidated entries) opened Oct 6, 2026 but only for CIT plaintiffs who gave CBP an importer-of-record number by Jul 30, 2026. DOJ has appealed on whether non-plaintiffs are entitled to refunds. As of Sept 11, 2026 more than 20,000 refunds (about $1.3B) were undelivered because importers had not enrolled in ACH. Section 232, 301 and AD/CVD duties are not refundable.
incumbents: CBP (CAPE), carriers and customs brokers filing as importer of record (UPS, FedEx, DHL), Big 4 and trade-law firms on contingency, and hedge funds / private credit buying or lending against claims. Plus niche platforms: Tariff Refund Agency and Capital Gurus 'IEEPA Recovery' (contingency). They earn contingency fees (filing) or spread (claim purchase).
incumbent_fragility: Filing is commoditizing fast and the window is closing. The fragility is in the leftovers: refunds go to the importer of record, not whoever bore the cost, so thousands of mid-market flows have no clear owner of the money. Carriers are pledging pass-through but face consolidated class actions (13 in Tennessee federal court). Legal authority for universal refunds is under appeal, and CBP said May 29, 2026 it cannot refund finally liquidated entries without a court order.
funded_startups_already_here: No venture-funded IEEPA-refund startup found (searched 'startup raises funding IEEPA tariff refund recovery claims platform'). Named players without disclosed rounds: Tariff Refund Agency (platform plus advance funding), Capital Gurus (IEEPA Recovery). Competing supply is law firms, Big 4, carriers, and claim-buying funds.
wedge_hints: Pass-through reconciliation for B2B buyers charged tariff surcharges where contracts were silent on refunds; settlement and claims administration for carrier/retailer class actions; ACH-enrollment and un-enrolled-importer tail (only about 8% of importers had enrolled by end of March per CBP); then roll the capability into a standing duty-recovery stack (drawback, post-summary corrections, valuation). Honest limit: pure refund filing is one-time and about 76% already certified, so a $100M business needs a recurring duty-recovery franchise (lesson 6 risk).
insider_roles: Customs attorneys litigating at the Court of International Trade; licensed brokers filing CAPE declarations; importer trade-compliance managers and controllers; distressed-debt and claims traders; class-action settlement administrators; drawback specialists.

name: US importers' spend on customs brokerage and trade-compliance services
size_basis: Mordor Intelligence estimates the US customs brokerage market at about $5.48B in 2026 (Deep Cognition: about $5.3B in 2025). Derived cross-check: roughly 35M formal entries a year (GII Research, undated pre-2020 figure of 35.5M) times an assumed average of about $150 per entry is about $5.3B. Sits right at the $5B floor; the leverage is the duty stream passing through it (about $281B gross tariff revenue in FY2026 through July, First Trust). Broker counts conflict (about 14,500 licensed individuals / 6,200 firms vs about 11,000 active per J.J. Keller).
money_flow: Roughly 330,000+ importers of record pay licensed customs brokerage firms per-entry fees, continuous-bond fees, classification, valuation and compliance advisory; brokers file entries in ACE and often advance duties on behalf of importers.
shock: Tariff-regime churn: IEEPA tariffs struck Feb 20, 2026; a Section 122 global tariff ran until Jul 24, 2026 and was replaced by new Section 301 actions; Section 232 derivative lists keep expanding; de minimis shipments now require formal or postal entry (two CBP interim final rules Jun 24, 2026); CAPE refund filings add work. Trade press and NCBFAA report filings that needed one HTS code now need three to five and sharply higher document load per agent.
incumbents: Integrator brokerages (UPS, FedEx, DHL), forwarders (Expeditors, C.H. Robinson, Kuehne+Nagel), thousands of small regional brokerages, and software vendors (Descartes, WiseTech CargoWise). They earn per-entry fees and bond/ancillary fees.
incumbent_fragility: Flat per-entry pricing breaks when each entry needs more skilled labor; licensed-broker labor is the scarce input. Small shops run legacy ABI/ACE integrations and lack capital to rebuild. The license (plus CBP responsible-supervision rules) protects incumbents from software-only entrants, but also means a buyer or licensee of a brokerage can be the vehicle.
funded_startups_already_here: Flexport (brokerage inside a forwarder; round history not re-verified), Zonos ($69M Series A 2021; selected by CBP Nov 2025 for a Commercial Solutions Opening pilot on classification and duty collection), Amari AI (about $4.5M seed Feb 2026, Pear VC and First Round, aggregator-reported), Alchemize (YC Spring 2026, amounts conflict), Nabu (France, seed May 2026 per aggregator), CustomsBridge (France, about $2.8M), KlearNow (Series A 2020). Raft also operates here but its funding was not verified.
wedge_hints: Buy or build a licensed brokerage as the regulated shell and run it with automation, rolling up small brokerages with retiring owners; tariff-stack-heavy verticals (auto parts under Section 232, steel/aluminum derivatives, e-commerce sellers moving to formal entry); non-resident importer-of-record services for foreign DTC brands; recurring duty-recovery on contingency (post-summary corrections, drawback, first sale, FTZ). Bottom-up: $100M is about 1.8% of the fee pool, roughly 650,000 entries a year at $150; software sold to brokers is far smaller (6,200 firms times $20-50k).
insider_roles: Licensed customs brokers at 20-100 person regional brokerages; ACE entry writers; trade-compliance managers at mid-market importers; former CBP import specialists; customs attorneys; customs surety/bond underwriters; drawback specialists.

name: Low-value cross-border e-commerce parcels into the US and EU: duty, clearance and rerouted logistics
size_basis: Derived and borderline, pre-shock flow. US: 1.36B de minimis parcels in FY2024 (CBP, widely cited); CBP collected over $1B on 246M shipments May-Dec 2025. EU: about 4.6B items under EUR 150 in 2024 (about 12M parcels a day, European Commission data); at the new EUR 3 per item that is up to about EUR 13.8B (about $15-16B) of duty a year if volumes held. Realized flow is lower: UPU reports small-parcel volumes into the US and EU fell about 70% by weight after exemptions ended. The capturable fee pool (clearance, duty collection, middle-mile) is a small fraction of the duty.
money_flow: Platforms (Temu, Shein, AliExpress, TikTok Shop) and SME sellers pay customs duty to the US and EU authorities and pay postal operators, express carriers, consolidators, customs brokers and DDP-tech vendors for carriage and clearance; money is migrating to bulk freight into local warehouses plus domestic last-mile.
shock: US de minimis ended for China/HK May 2, 2025 and for all countries Aug 29, 2025; suspension re-anchored by EO 14388 on Feb 20, 2026 and codified by two CBP interim final rules Jun 24, 2026 (postal entries via a spreadsheet process for shipments up to $2,500). EU temporary EUR 3 per-item duty from Jul 1, 2026, with a separate handling fee proposed (date provisional). UPU reports about 70% fewer small parcels by weight; Shein and Temu moved stock into US warehouses.
incumbents: Postal operators (USPS, Royal Mail, La Poste, Deutsche Post), integrators (DHL, FedEx, UPS), Chinese consolidators (Cainiao, YunExpress), customs brokers, and DDP/landed-cost vendors (Global-e, Zonos). They earn per-parcel carriage, brokerage and DDP fees.
incumbent_fragility: Postal systems were built for parcel-level exemption, not item-level formal entry; the interim US postal process is literally spreadsheet submission. Platforms are re-architecting from per-parcel postal to bulk-and-local-warehouse models, so volume and money move between payers faster than incumbents' contracts and systems adapt.
funded_startups_already_here: Zonos (CBP pilot award Nov 2025; $69M Series A 2021), Global-e (public), Amari AI and other customs-tech seeds (see customs pool), plus numerous landed-cost/DDP and cross-border fulfillment vendors. I found no credible cross-border logistics market-size figure and no new 2025-26 large rounds specific to this pool.
wedge_hints: Duty collection and IOSS-style intermediary services for EU sellers; middle-mile consolidation from China/SEA into US and EU bonded or domestic warehouses for mid-sized sellers; returns and re-export handling with duty implications. Honest limit: at about $0.10 per EU parcel for clearance/duty collection (4.4B parcels, about $440M), $100M would be about 23% share, and US volume is down about 70%. Best treated as a feeder to the customs pool.
insider_roles: Customs brokers handling Type 86/postal entries; postal-operator customs liaisons; platform logistics heads; IOSS intermediary compliance staff; cross-border 3PL ops managers; consolidators in Shenzhen/Yiwu.

name: US truckload freight brokerage gross profit (shippers to brokers to carriers)
size_basis: Market-research estimates of $19.5-20.1B for the US freight brokerage market in 2025 (methodology not shown, may be net revenue). Context: ATA puts total US trucking revenue at $906B for 2024; brokers handle about 30% of truckload spend (per Highway). Unverified: J.B. Hunt brokerage gross margin fell from 15.5% to 12.5% in Q2 2026 as purchased transportation rose 54% vs revenue up 49% (ARK TMS blog).
money_flow: Shippers pay brokers per load under contract and spot pricing; brokers buy capacity from carriers and keep the spread (gross profit), typically 12-16% of revenue.
shock: Driver supply cut and cost spike: non-domiciled CDL final rule effective Mar 16, 2026 (FMCSA estimates 194,000 holders lose eligibility; other estimates up to 437,000), English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement (more than 26,000 drivers sidelined per FreightWaves; codifying rule proposed Aug 10, 2026), plus record diesel. C.H. Robinson (Oct 1, 2026) forecasts 2026 dry van cost per mile +30% y/y, reefer +31%, flatbed +28%, route-guide failures peaked at 7.5% over the summer. Broker $75,000 financial responsibility rule fully effective Jan 16, 2026, letting FMCSA suspend authority if security falls short.
incumbents: C.H. Robinson, RXO, J.B. Hunt, Landstar, TQL, Echo, Coyote (UPS), Uber Freight, plus thousands of small brokers. Earn the buy-sell spread.
incumbent_fragility: Contract rates are fixed for months while carrier cost resets weekly, so margins compress when rates spike; small brokers are thinly capitalized and now carry a larger bond requirement and fraud exposure. Large brokers' scale helps but their margins are also falling.
funded_startups_already_here: Uber Freight, Loadsmart, Parade ($36M total), Highway (FTV Capital growth equity 2025; claims 1,050+ brokers incl. 70 of top 100), Freight Hero ($5-6M seed mid-2026, amounts conflict), Loop (freight audit/payment, $95M Series C Apr 2026 per aggregator), Triumph/TriumphPay (public). Convoy's 2023 collapse is the cautionary history.
wedge_hints: Credit, working capital and bonding products for small brokers under the $75k rule; rate-risk tools (indexed contracts, hedges) for shippers and brokers when spot-contract spreads blow out; outsourced broker back office. Avoid generic 'AI copilot for brokers' (round-1 cliche). $100M is 0.5% of the pool but only as a broker itself (about $700M gross revenue at 14%) or a finance/insurance layer.
insider_roles: Broker ops and carrier-sales leads; freight claims managers; BMC-84 surety underwriters; TMS implementers; 3PL CFOs; shipper transportation procurement managers.

name: US heavy trucking liability and cargo insurance premiums
size_basis: Derived, trucking split unverified. Verified: US commercial auto direct premiums written were $72.18B in 2025, up 12.1% (AM Best data via Beinsure). Trucking is the largest segment but no published trucking-only split was found; my estimate is about 40% of the total, roughly $30B. Cross-check: ATRI reports trucking liability premiums at a record 10.2 cents per mile.
money_flow: Motor carriers (about 500k authorities; the largest self-insure) pay premiums to admitted and surplus-lines insurers, mostly via retail and wholesale brokers (RPS, Amwins) and captives/RRGs.
shock: At the 10 largest public trucking companies insurance and claims cost rose 54.4% from $992M (2021) to $1.53B (2025) against revenue up 9.95%, and combined net profit fell 46.9% (Demotech analysis of 10-Ks). Median trucking nuclear verdict $51M in 2024 vs $21M in 2020 (Marathon Strategies). ATRI: liability premiums +18.6% 2021-2024 while crashes fell. AM Best: commercial auto's 14th straight underwriting loss in 2024 (about $4.9B), reserves short $4-5B (secondary); Q1 2026 broker survey shows commercial auto rates +5.8%, the largest of any line (Heffins summary, not opened). Umbrella buyers who bought $25M can often only get $10M. Month of shock is approximate.
incumbents: Progressive (about 15% of commercial auto DPW), Travelers, Old Republic, Liberty Mutual, specialty writers; wholesalers RPS and Amwins; captives and risk retention groups. Earn underwriting margin, commission and float.
incumbent_fragility: Fourteen years of underwriting losses, rate inadequacy versus loss trend, legacy class-code pricing that ignores telematics and driver quality, and retreating capacity at excess layers. Incumbents cannot easily re-underwrite a book they are losing money on without losing share.
funded_startups_already_here: Nirvana Insurance (about $262M raised; $100M Series D at $1.5B valuation late 2025; more than $100M premium by Mar 2025), Cover Whale ($27.5M debt and equity, Jun 2024), HDVI ($16M Series A, 8VC and Munich Re Ventures), Koffie ($4.5M seed).
wedge_hints: Excess/umbrella capacity for 50-1,000 truck fleets (MGA with reinsurer backing); group captives or RRGs for mid-size fleets underwritten on video telematics; pre-litigation claims handling and evidence capture aimed at nuclear-verdict exposure; driver-hiring risk scoring while tens of thousands of drivers are being removed. $100M of MGA commission at about 15% is roughly $670M of premium, about 2% of the pool; capital and licensing intensive.
insider_roles: Trucking defense attorneys; liability claims adjusters; wholesale brokers at RPS/Amwins; fleet risk managers; safety directors; plaintiff-side attorneys; casualty actuaries.

name: US heavy-duty (Class 6-8) truck repair, maintenance and parts aftermarket
size_basis: Stale but order-of-magnitude. MacKay & Co: aftermarket parts for Class 6-8 trucks, trailers and chassis were $31.6B in 2019 (forecast $37B by 2024); service labor $58.5B in 2015 and total aftermarket about $107B (Fleet Maintenance citing MacKay; assumes $100/hour and includes in-house fleet work). Verified (ATRI via FleetOwner): repair and maintenance was 21.5 cents per mile in 2025, up 8.6%.
money_flow: Fleets and owner-operators pay OEM dealers, heavy-duty distributors, truck-stop service chains and independent shops for parts, labor and tires; a large share is in-house fleet maintenance. Dealers took 49% of parts purchases and distributors 18% (MacKay 2019).
shock: Section 232 25% tariffs on imported medium and heavy-duty trucks and parts effective Nov 1, 2025 (proclamation Oct 17, 2025; USMCA content relief partial); FreightWaves cites an injector 20-30% pricier than two years ago (anecdote). Carriers keep older trucks longer (C.H. Robinson Oct 2026), driving repair load. ATRI-cited data: 65.5% of shops short-staffed in 2025 with nearly one in five technician slots unfilled (secondary). Record diesel and driver supply cuts squeeze fleet cash.
incumbents: OEM dealer networks, heavy-duty distributors (FleetPride, TruckPro), national service chains (TA, Love's, Pilot), and independent shops (9% of parts purchases). Earn parts margin and labor.
incumbent_fragility: Highly fragmented shops with weak procurement scale, opaque parts pricing, OEM control of fault-code data, and an aging technician workforce. Dealers cannot add technicians fast either, and tariffs hit their parts cost while fleets push back on price.
funded_startups_already_here: Fullbay (shop management software; $23M growth investment from Mainsail / JMI Equity, 2019 vs 2024 dates conflict; says its shops billed $5.04B in 2025, up 68% from 2023). No venture-funded heavy-duty mobile repair, parts marketplace or technician-staffing company found (searched; funded mobile-repair names were light-duty Wrench and RepairSmith). Fleetio-type fleet maintenance software exists but was not re-verified.
wedge_hints: Group purchasing and parts price transparency for independent shops in the tariff era (aftermarket and remanufactured alternatives); technician supply (training, staffing, shared mobile technicians for small fleets); warranty/recall/core recovery for fleets; payments and financing at the shop-to-fleet layer. Bottom-up: Fullbay's $5.04B of annual shop billings is about 5% of the pool; a 1-2% take on a similar flow is $50-100M.
insider_roles: Fleet maintenance directors; independent shop owners and service managers; parts counter managers; FleetPride/TruckPro branch GMs; OEM dealer warranty administrators; tire dealers; diesel technician instructors; owner-operators.

name: US trucking diesel purchasing (fuel cards, discount networks, surcharge pass-through)
size_basis: Derived. EIA: transportation-sector distillate consumption was about 2.94M barrels a day in 2025 (about 45B gallons a year). I assume heavy trucks are roughly 75-80% (about 35B gallons; an undated ATA figure cites 38.8B gallons) at an average 2026 price near $5.20, about $180B of purchases. The addressable intermediary margin is only roughly $4-9B (assumes 10-25 cents per gallon).
money_flow: Fleets and owner-operators buy diesel at truck stops and cardlock sites, mostly through fuel cards (Comdata, EFS/WEX, Fleet One) and discount programs; shippers pay fuel surcharges indexed to the weekly EIA average; intermediaries earn cents per gallon via interchange, network fees and retail margin.
shock: Diesel rose 89% from a January 2026 low to a record EIA national average of $6.529/gal for the week of Sept 21, 2026 (Iran conflict; California $8.18; some Pacific Northwest sites above $8). A 30-gallon fill-up went from about $113 to $191 in a year. Many surcharge tables step up near $6, and carriers say surcharges do not cover deadhead and downtime (C.H. Robinson). EIA expects distillate inventories below the five-year low through early 2027.
incumbents: Corpay (Comdata), WEX (EFS, Fleet One), TCS Fuel, truck-stop chains (Pilot/Flying J, Love's, TA), regional fuel jobbers. Earn interchange, network fees and retail fuel margin.
incumbent_fragility: Card economics are opaque to small carriers and fuel cards are credit products that small fleets often fail to qualify for; surcharge indices lag spot diesel; truck stops want volume commitments that aggregator apps can supply. A cash-strained small-carrier base at $6+ diesel is the opening.
funded_startups_already_here: Mudflap (fuel discount app plus fuel card; $50M Series B Aug 2022; 2,500-3,600 participating stops; no 2025-26 round found). Otherwise the big card networks. Searched for other 2025-26 fuel-card startups and found none with disclosed rounds.
wedge_hints: Working-capital fuel advances and credit for small carriers underwritten on load and payment data; surcharge auditing and indexed-contract redesign for shippers; IFTA and fuel-card fraud controls; forward-pricing/hedging for mid-size fleets. At 10 cents per gallon net, $100M needs about 1B gallons (about 3% of trucking diesel): plausible but fiercely contested, so the credit layer is the more defensible version.
insider_roles: Fleet fuel managers; truck-stop network GMs; fuel-card sales reps; fuel jobbers and distributors; owner-operators; shipper transportation procurement managers; IFTA auditors.

name: Airlines' and lessors' spend on commercial aviation MRO and aftermarket parts
size_basis: Estimates range $83-136B: Precision Aviation Group cites about $97B for 2026 (up from $91B in 2025), Spherical Insights $114B for 2025, Cassel Salpeter $136B for 2025 on a broader scope, Business Research Company $88.7B for 2026. Engine MRO alone about $50.7B in 2026 (Straits Research). Used serviceable material is a small sub-slice at about $6.2B (Business Research Company). I use about $100B.
money_flow: Airlines and lessors pay engine shops, component repair stations, airframe MROs and parts distributors; OEMs capture a large share via long-term power-by-the-hour agreements and proprietary parts.
shock: IATA/Emerton study (Jun 25, 2026): engine MRO bottlenecks are disrupting airlines; GTF-powered groundings peaked at 648 aircraft (28% of the GTF fleet) in March 2025; LEAP shop visits rise from about 600-800 (2025) to over 5,000 a year by 2040; GTF from about 1,000 to over 2,000. Secondary reports: more than 3,500 engines stalled awaiting castings and forgings; overhaul turnaround 180-240 days in 2026 vs 60-90 pre-2019. Tariffs (15% Section 301 on Chinese-origin parts, 25% on certain EU-origin parts per one analysis) raise costs. Airlines keep old aircraft and lease extra ones.
incumbents: OEMs (GE Aerospace, RTX/Pratt & Whitney, Safran/CFM, Rolls-Royce); MROs (Lufthansa Technik, AFI KLM E&M, ST Engineering, StandardAero, AAR, HAECO); parts distributors (Boeing Distribution, AJW, Satair). Earn long-term service agreement revenue, proprietary parts margin and repair labor.
incumbent_fragility: OEMs are constrained by supply of castings and forgings and cannot add shop capacity quickly; IATA and airlines are pushing for fair MRO market access, spare-parts price transparency and more PMA and used-parts channels. Counterfeit-document scandals push buyers toward traceable parts. OEM business models rely on parts exclusivity they cannot give up easily.
funded_startups_already_here: ePlane (B2B aerospace parts and repair marketplace; $9M round led by Marubeni Mar 2024, about $16.5M total then; a Series C reported Feb 2026 by one aggregator, unverified), plus marketplaces fipart, PartPilot, PartsBase, AeroParts Now, Honeywell GoDirect Trade, Locatory. AerSale and AAR are public. No 2025-26 venture rounds found for engine-MRO or PMA-development startups (searched).
wedge_hints: PMA and DER-approved repairs for high-failure rotables on A320/737 families and regional fleets (ATR, E-Jets); engine teardown and module-level used serviceable material trading; traceability and documentation verification for parts transactions; AOG parts logistics and lease-return inspection. $100M is 0.1% of the pool; a USM/PMA business at 10-20% gross margin needs roughly $0.5-1B of throughput, so inventory capital is the constraint, not demand.
insider_roles: Airline MRO procurement and technical services directors; engine shop planners; FAA DERs; USM traders; lessor technical reps (AerCap, SMBC); Part 145 repair-station quality managers; AOG desk coordinators.

name: Amazon's payments to third-party last-mile delivery partners (DSPs and rural program)
size_basis: Derived, low confidence. TechRadar (undated): 4,400 DSP owners, 390,000 driving jobs and $58B of cumulative revenue for participating companies; Amazon says it has invested $21.7B in the DSP program over eight years and announced another $1.9B for 2027 (Sept 2026). No published annual revenue figure; I infer roughly $13-20B a year from the cumulative number.
money_flow: Amazon pays about 3,000-4,400 small DSP businesses for last-mile delivery (DSPs employ the drivers), plus a smaller rural small-business delivery program, replacing volume that UPS is shedding.
shock: UPS said on Jan 28, 2026 it is in the final six months of its Amazon glide-down, will remove another 1M pieces a day in 2026, cut up to 30,000 more jobs and close 24 more facilities after closing 93 in 2025. Amazon is spending about $4B to triple its rural delivery network by end of 2026 (200+ new delivery stations) and keeps expanding the DSP program.
incumbents: Amazon Logistics (sole payer and rule-setter), UPS, FedEx, USPS. DSP owners earn per-route fees from Amazon.
incumbent_fragility: The fragility sits with UPS (shrinking), not with a startup-addressable payer. DSP owners are price-takers; Amazon supplies vehicles, cameras, insurance and coaching, leaving little room for outside vendors.
funded_startups_already_here: None found: searched 'startup serving Amazon DSP owners raises funding insurance payroll fleet software'. The absence likely reflects weak economics (single dominant payer, captive services) rather than opportunity.
wedge_hints: Insurance, driver payroll/benefits and van financing sold to DSP owners; adjacent: small regional carriers absorbing volume UPS and FedEx prune. Honest limit: 4,000 DSPs times $25k a year of third-party spend is $100M at 100% share; only an insurance or financing product with $1M+ of premium or balances per DSP could work. Likely dead as a standalone (wrong-payer, lesson 3).
insider_roles: DSP owners and station managers; Amazon last-mile program staff; UPS center managers; driver payroll providers; commercial auto brokers who write DSP fleets.

name: State Medicaid and SNAP agencies' eligibility and administration spend (work requirements, 6-month redeterminations, SNAP admin cost shift)
geography: US (43 expansion states + DC for Medicaid work requirements; all 50 states for SNAP)
size_basis: Derived. KFF: Medicaid administration is about 4% of total Medicaid spending; applying 4% to roughly $0.9T total spending (my assumption, verify vs CMS-64) gives about $35B. SNAP: USDA impact analysis (cited by CSPI/FRAC) shifts about $16.9B of admin cost from federal to states over FY2027-31 as the federal share drops 50% to 25%, implying total SNAP admin of roughly $13B/yr. Sum about $45-50B, order-of-magnitude. Only a fraction is outsourced to vendors; that share is not sourced.
money_flow: Federal match (generally 50% for admin, higher for some eligibility systems) plus state general funds go to state Medicaid/human-services agencies, which pay systems integrators (Deloitte, Conduent, Gainwell, Maximus, Accenture, GDIT, Optum, Acentra, RedMane, Curam/Merative), county eligibility workers and call-center/mail vendors. Managed-care plans separately pay for member outreach and retention (my inference).
shock: H.R.1 (July 2025) requires 80 hrs/month work or similar activity for Medicaid expansion adults from 2027-01-01 plus six-month renewals; CMS interim final rule issued 2026-06-01 (91 FR 33348), states had to send notices by 2026-08-31 and finish system changes by late 2026; CMS projects about 2.3M fewer enrollees in FY2027 and 3.1-3.3M later. SNAP: federal admin share falls to 25% on 2026-10-01 (about $16.9B shift to states over FY2027-31); from FY2028 states with error rates above 6% share benefit costs.
incumbents: Ten integrators pledged about $600M in discounted/free services to CMS in Jan 2026: Accenture, Acentra Health, Conduent, GDIT, Deloitte, Gainwell, Maximus, Curam by Merative, Optum, RedMane. They earn on long-term state system contracts and per-transaction operations. CMS also offers $200M in Government Efficiency Grants and a free federal toolkit (EMMY) of eligibility-verification APIs.
incumbent_fragility: Hard Jan 2027 deadline against slow state procurement; legacy integrated eligibility systems; political exposure (Senators Wyden, Warren, Sanders, Warnock wrote to Conduent, Deloitte, GDIT, Gainwell about payment structures and error handling); discounts signal pricing pressure. Caution: the free federal EMMY tooling is a public substitute, and states estimated only $3-10M each for work-requirement system changes (about $0.1-0.4B one-time across 43 states, derived), so the real money is recurring operations, not one-time build.
funded_startups_already_here: Fortuna Health (a16z, BoxGroup, YC; navigation/enrollment, Gainwell partner), Develop Health ($14.25M Series A Aug 2025; benefits verification, adjacent), Argyle (consent-based income data marketing to Medicaid verification), Ocrolus (2018 $4M Series A for Medicaid eligibility, precedent). No 2026 round found for a pure work-requirement verification company. Searched: startup raises funding Medicaid work requirements verification. Nonprofit/civic tech (Nava, Code for America) exist from background knowledge, not checked.
wedge_hints: (1) Retention services paid per retained member by managed-care plans (inference: 2.3-3.3M coverage losses at roughly $7k/yr capitation, an assumption, means $16-23B plan revenue at stake); (2) ex parte data-matching feeds (payroll, education, caregiver and medical-frailty exemptions) sold to states or sub-licensed to integrators; (3) notice, mailing and call-center overflow for counties; (4) SNAP payment-error-rate reduction, since states face hard-dollar liability from FY2028; (5) appeals/fair-hearing support.
insider_roles: State Medicaid eligibility policy directors; county eligibility supervisors; SNAP quality-control reviewers; managed-care plan member-engagement/retention executives; integrator program managers (Deloitte, Conduent, Gainwell); benefits legal-aid attorneys; state procurement officers.

name: Rural Health Transformation Program awards (CMS to 50 state agencies to rural providers and vendors)
size_basis: $50B over five years (FY2026-2030 per most sources), $10B/yr. First-year awards ranged $147M (New Jersey) to $281M (Texas), average about $200M. First-year funds spendable through 2027-09-30. Secondary source reporting the CMS announcement.
money_flow: CMS to state agencies (Medicaid agency or health department) to rural hospitals, FQHCs, EMS, universities, and technology/telehealth/cybersecurity vendors. States must pick from domains including technology and telehealth, health IT and cybersecurity, and behavioral health expansion.
shock: Brand-new time-limited federal money (created by the 2025 reconciliation law, my background knowledge); first-year awards announced 2025-12-29; state procurement windows reportedly open roughly Q3 2026 to Q1 2027 (vendor-authored estimate). Idaho, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee have posted RFPs/grants; Alaska portal ran June 2026; New Jersey published a vendor directory 2026-08-05; Colorado and Montana still awaiting CMS approvals.
incumbents: EHR vendors, telehealth companies and large consultancies will chase the money; state offices of rural health distribute it. No dominant captor yet because the money is spread across 50 separate state processes.
incumbent_fragility: State rural-health offices are small and must obligate money fast, so they lean on outsiders; procurement is uneven across states. Weakness for founders: it is a five-year program, not a permanent budget line, and each state buys differently.
funded_startups_already_here: none found tied to the program. Searched: Rural Health Transformation Program vendors startups states contracts Series A. Generic digital-health and telehealth vendors will all pitch; no named venture-funded startups with RHTP contracts surfaced.
wedge_hints: Sub-award administration for hundreds of small rural grantees (applications, scoring, payment tracking, outcomes reporting); program-management and CMS reporting tools for tiny state RHT offices; rural EMS staffing and billing; transfer and tele-specialty coordination; rural hospital workforce pipelines.
insider_roles: State Offices of Rural Health directors; critical-access-hospital CFOs; state hospital-association executives; Medicaid agency procurement officers; rural EMS chiefs.

name: US prison and jail health care (state corrections departments and counties paying contractors)
geography: US (state prisons, county jails, some federal)
size_basis: Derived, state prisons only. Pew: state prison health spending was $8.1B in FY2015 (about a fifth of prison budgets); grown about 3%/yr (my assumption) gives about $11B. Jails and the federal Bureau of Prisons would add more (not sourced; likely several billion). Cross-check: Maryland alone awarded $1.7B for five years of state-prison care, about $340M/yr.
money_flow: State corrections departments and county sheriffs/boards pay contractors fixed or capitated prices per facility; some states run care in-house. One analysis (unverified) says only 14 states still run prison health in-house and 36 outsource at least part.
shock: Wellpath (largest private provider) filed Chapter 11 on 2024-11-12 and emerged 2025-05-12 owned by its lenders; YesCare filed for bankruptcy 2026-05-08 and Polk County, Florida terminated its contract that day (CFG Health Systems took over); Doña Ana County, NM signed a roughly $4.5M emergency contract with Thrive Medical after YesCare missed payroll; Maryland dropped YesCare for Centurion ($1.7B state prisons, $723M pretrial, five years plus two-year option); Shasta County moving to Mediko ($25M/3 yrs); Medicaid reentry (90 days pre-release) waivers starting, with 12 states given CMS planning grants in Jan 2025 (Nevada's $5M for an EHR that can bill Medicaid).
incumbents: Wellpath, Centurion (Centene-linked, ownership unverified), YesCare/Corizon, NaphCare, plus regional firms (Mediko, CFG Health Systems, Thrive). They sell thin-margin fixed-price or capitated facility contracts.
incumbent_fragility: Heavy wrongful-death/civil-rights litigation, debt loads (Wellpath restructured about $550M), repeated payroll failures, and counties left with no bidder. Buyers (sheriffs, county boards) are risk-averse and procurement is slow, which also slows any newcomer.
funded_startups_already_here: none found. Searched: correctional healthcare startup raises funding jail telehealth reentry Medicaid 1115 waiver. Safety Net Connect (eConsult specialty referrals) announced a correctional-health expansion in July 2025 with no round named.
wedge_hints: Off-site specialty and hospital referral management (a major cost driver, not sourced here); Medicaid reentry enrollment and billing infrastructure for states and counties; pharmacy and formulary management; staffing and in-house program support for counties that fire a vendor; EHR plus billing for jails.
insider_roles: Jail health administrators; state DOC health services directors; NCCHC accreditors; county risk managers; correctional nurses and physicians; civil-rights litigators who sue these contractors.

name: FEMA disaster dollars to state/local governments and the recovery-administration layer (Public Assistance reimbursements, grant management)
size_basis: FY2026 Disaster Relief Fund appropriation of $26.367B (Senate Appropriations summary). The part paid to state/local governments as Public Assistance plus Individual Assistance has run about $7B/yr for hazard events 2016 to Sept 2026 per a third-party OpenFEMA tally (unverified). The vendor-capturable admin layer is much smaller; consultant share of grants is not sourced and is probably a few percent, so this pool may fail the $100M test.
money_flow: Congress to FEMA Disaster Relief Fund to states and localities (reimbursement of recovery projects), who pay consultants and engineers to prepare documentation and manage grants (ICF, Guidehouse, Tidal Basin, EY surfaced).
shock: FEMA Review Council final report (2026-05-07, nonbinding): raise the per-capita damage threshold from $1.94 to $2.99, require states to meet minimum annual disaster spending before federal aid, and send money to states within 30 days of declaration; about half of recommendations need Congress. EY (March 2026) reports steep cuts in federal grant capacity and a move toward a state-centric model.
incumbents: Disaster-recovery consultancies (ICF, Guidehouse, Tidal Basin, EY) and engineering firms earning on documentation-heavy reimbursement work; FEMA's own free Grants Portal.
incumbent_fragility: A direct-funding model would reduce documentation-heavy work but raise states' need for audit and fraud controls; state oversight capacity is weak (Vermont lost track of millions in FEMA funds under a consultant contract, per Grist). Caution: policy change is uncertain and nonbinding.
funded_startups_already_here: none found with 2023-2026 funding. Existing: Veoci (PA paperwork product), Tidal Basin (consulting plus OneCase software), FEMA's free Grants Portal. Searched: disaster recovery grant management software startup funding FEMA Public Assistance.
wedge_hints: State-level subrecipient monitoring and audit-readiness; deobligation-risk detection; recovery-fund fraud and oversight analytics sold to state auditors; mitigation grant administration for small counties.
insider_roles: State emergency-management finance chiefs; county emergency managers; FEMA public assistance officers; recovery consultants; state auditors.

name: US drinking-water utilities' pipe replacement and rehabilitation, including lead service lines
size_basis: Need, not actual spend. EPA's 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey: $625B over 20 years nationally, of which $422.9B is transmission and distribution pipes, about $21B/yr. Lead lines alone fail the $5B/yr test: at about 4M lines and $5-12k each, replacement is $20-48B over a decade, or $2-4B/yr (derived).
money_flow: Ratepayers, municipal bonds, state revolving funds and federal grants go to utilities, which pay engineers and contractors; pipe, valve and meter makers and distributors sell materials.
shock: EPA's Lead and Copper Rule Improvements require replacing all lead lines by 2037 (about 10% a year), with updated inventories due 2027-11-01. On 2025-11-25 EPA cut the estimated lead-line count from about 9M to about 4M and announced $3B in new state revolving fund money plus $1.1B reallocated; NRDC disputes the new count. No 2026 sign of the deadline moving was found.
incumbents: Municipal utilities (owners and payers), large engineers (Jacobs, Black & Veatch, Tetra Tech), utility contractors, and pipe/meter makers and distributors.
incumbent_fragility: Fragmentation: most systems are small, with unknown service-line materials and thin engineering staff; contractor crew capacity is limited. Revised inventories shrank the lead-line job, which lowers the lead-specific pool.
funded_startups_already_here: none confirmed in-session. From background knowledge, not verified here: BlueConduit (lead-line prediction), Fracta (pipe-failure AI), SewerAI. Searched for lead service line startups and found only vendor marketing pages.
wedge_hints: Verifying 'unknown' service-line materials with non-destructive testing; replacement-program management for small systems; contractor capacity (crews, trenchless methods); customer-side line records.
insider_roles: Utility distribution superintendents; state drinking-water program engineers; utility contractors; asset-management consultants; state revolving fund managers.

name: DoD depot maintenance and spare parts where OEMs hold the technical data (sole-source repair and parts)
size_basis: CRS defense primer: FY2025 operation and maintenance request of $40.6B for depot maintenance across all services (FY2024 estimate $38.9B). Spare-part buying through the Defense Logistics Agency and services is extra; I could not source a total. GAO says operating and support costs are about 70% of a system's lifetime cost. The share locked to OEM data rights is not quantified; a 2023 DoD assessment reportedly found about half of 100 fielded systems lacked adequate data rights (secondary).
money_flow: Congress funds O&M accounts, which pay government depots, OEMs/primes and DLA. Where DoD lacks technical-data rights it must buy repair and parts from the OEM or its authorized sources.
shock: Right-to-repair language was stripped from the final FY2026 NDAA in Dec 2025 after contractor lobbying; a revived version was added in the House Armed Services markup on 2026-06-04 and approved by the Senate Armed Services committee, but House floor action is stalled (July 2026). Hegseth and other leaders back moving data rights to the government. Marine Corps examples: antenna mast built for $10 in 10 hours versus up to $5,644 and seven months from the OEM. Feb 2026: two-year $1.8M reverse-engineering initiative. Shock is pending, not law.
incumbents: OEMs and parts specialists on sole-source repair and spares. DoD IG found TransDigm earned at least $20.8M excess profit on 105 parts across 150 contracts (2017-2019) and was sole source for 39 of 47 parts reviewed.
incumbent_fragility: Fragility is political, not structural: if the statute passes the data-rights moat weakens; if lobbyists win again it persists. Services (Marines) are already building their own parts.
funded_startups_already_here: Hadrian ($1.37B Series D at $7.87B valuation Aug 2026; automated factories for aerospace/defense including submarine spare parts), Firestorm (reported $82M, aggregator-sourced, unverified), Radian Forge ($2.5M seed, large-format metal printing), Velo3D (public; $32.6M DIU award), Parts Life (small, last raised $970K in 2020). Searched: startup raises spare parts reverse engineering sustainment.
wedge_hints: Not manufacturing. Auditing restrictive data-rights markings for program offices; rebuilding technical data packages and qualifying alternate sources; a source-approval and first-article qualification workflow for small shops; price-reasonableness analysis for sole-source commercial-item parts, sold to buyers and price analysts.
insider_roles: Depot industrial engineers; DLA item managers and buyers; DCMA price analysts; program-office product-support managers; DoD IG auditors; small machine-shop owners bidding on DLA parts; contract attorneys handling data-rights challenges.

name: German federal spend on Bundeswehr infrastructure, barracks and housing (construction and renovation)
geography: Germany (extension to Poland and the Baltics)
size_basis: Derived estimate, +/- 40%; I could not retrieve the Einzelplan 14 infrastructure line. TUV Consulting (citing internal estimates) puts renovation need above EUR 50B through 2031 and says over EUR 20B of the special fund is earmarked for infrastructure; 2025 project and construction volume was EUR 1.7B with 10-20% annual growth targeted (June 2025 infrastructure report via Heidelberg24); G-CAP Inland Stage 1 is EUR 4.6B over a 48-month framework (about EUR 1.15B/yr); a container program is about EUR 900M. Execution (EUR 1.7B) is far below need (EUR 50B+).
money_flow: Federal defense budget (Germany plans over EUR 108B for security and defense in 2026 and 3.5% of GDP core defense by 2029) goes to the Bundeswehr construction agency and state construction administrations (BLB NRW ran the G-CAP tender), then to regional general contractors and subcontractors.
shock: NATO's June 2025 Hague pledge of 3.5% core plus 1.5% broader security spending by 2035; the Bundeswehr planning and procurement acceleration act passed the Bundestag 2026-01-15 (runs to 2035, covers all Bundeswehr needs, removes the stop-work period after award challenges); G-CAP Inland Stage 1 signed 2026-08-27: about 300 buildings at about 130 sites, over 54,000 beds, seven contractors in regional lots, first call-offs September 2026, first 14 buildings by mid-2027.
incumbents: Understaffed public construction offices (average eight years from planning to completion per TUV), then large contractors and modular builders: a Wolff & Mueller/OBG/Lechner consortium among the G-CAP winners, Adapteo, and Rheinmetall (EUR 250M modular camp in Lithuania).
incumbent_fragility: The bottleneck is public-sector capacity, not money: EUR 1.7B executed against a EUR 50B+ backlog, thin construction-office staffing, tender thresholds, and skilled-labor shortages. Barriers for a newcomer: security clearances, German procurement law, language and local presence.
funded_startups_already_here: none venture-scale found. Quickblock (Scotland, about GBP 940k), KT-Shelter (acquired by W5 Solutions for EUR 22M, Mar 2026). Searched: modular military base barracks shelter startup raises.
wedge_hints: Prefabricated components and subcontract capacity for the G-CAP lots; building-condition surveys across roughly 1,500 properties; digital project controls and handover for the seven contractors; cleared trades labor; replicating the model in Poland and the Baltics.
insider_roles: Bundeswehr construction project managers; base commanders; state construction administrators; procurement-law attorneys; site managers at serial-construction firms.

name: European munitions, propellant and energetics procurement financed by EU SAFE loans and national budgets
size_basis: Annualized SAFE loan envelope: EUR 150B over about five years, all categories (ammunition, missiles and artillery are priority categories but their share is not sourced). Narrower derivation: the 2025 goal of 2M artillery shells times an assumed EUR 3-5k each is EUR 6-10B/yr (derived). Lithuania received EUR 956M as 15% pre-financing of a EUR 6.375B loan.
money_flow: EU loans to member governments go to joint purchases from European producers (Rheinmetall, Nammo, Eurenco, Explosia, Synthesia, MSM Walsrode, Nitro-Chem). A third-party tracker says Germany did not apply for SAFE (unverified).
shock: SAFE loan disbursement began in 2026; the EU's first energetic-components call under the defense industry programme closed 2026-06-16 with 83 proposals, over EUR 165M of EU money and up to EUR 470M total investment, results due September 2026. Bottlenecks are powder, TNT and nitrocellulose; Explosia called its propellant expansion a three-year project; Nitro-Chem's TNT doubling takes three to four years; one investigation put EU 155mm capacity near 580,000 shells/yr against a 2M goal; Rheinmetall is investing EUR 650M in propellant and Eurenco signed a EUR 300M loan in Feb 2026.
incumbents: Rheinmetall, Nammo, Eurenco, Explosia, Synthesia, MSM Walsrode, Nitro-Chem, largely state-supported and capital-heavy.
incumbent_fragility: Slow, licensed, capital-intensive expansion (multi-year) means they cannot respond fast to demand, but a small team also cannot enter explosives or chemical manufacturing without large capital and permits.
funded_startups_already_here: Cambridge Aerospace ($300M Series C at $3.4B Aug 2026; $200M Series B Apr 2026) and Frankenburg Technologies (EUR 30M Series A Feb 2026; plans solid rocket motors), both interceptors. No European energetics startup found; CellCore (nitrocellulose) is in Saskatchewan, Canada. Searched: European defence startups munitions energetics propellant explosives raises.
wedge_hints: Sub-tier parts (shell bodies, cartridge cases, fuzes); load-assemble-pack capacity; energetics process analytics and qualification testing; cellulose feedstock supply; plant permitting and engineering services. Capital and licensing barriers are high.
insider_roles: Plant managers at propellant makers; ordnance engineers; NATO support agency stockpile planners; defense-ministry procurement officers; explosives-safety regulators.

name: Japan, South Korea and Taiwan defense equipment acquisition (drones, counter-UAS, air defense, munitions)
size_basis: Derived. Japan FY2026 defense budget about 9.04T yen (about $58B, cabinet-approved draft). South Korea 2026 budget 66.3T won (about $46B) with acquisition near 30% (about $14B). Taiwan special budget NT$1.25T (about $40B) over 2026-2033, about $5B/yr if passed; stalled in legislature as of April 2026. I assumed about $10B of Japanese equipment spending without a source.
money_flow: Defense ministries to domestic primes and increasingly to drone startups; Japan's SHIELD coastal drone system has about 100.1B yen in FY2026.
shock: Japan's procurement agency received 38 bids for its interceptor-drone program; Terra Drone was selected in July 2026 as a test system, with Germany's Quantum Systems helping evaluate; Taiwan's legislature was deadlocked on the special budget (opposition proposed NT$380-400B); South Korea's budget rose 8.2%.
incumbents: National champions such as Mitsubishi Heavy, protected by local-content and security rules.
incumbent_fragility: Little evidence of fragility; the incumbents are protected rather than fragile.
funded_startups_already_here: Terra Drone, Eams Robotics and Quantum Systems (Germany) are active; no round sizes found. Searched: Japan Taiwan Australia defense startups funding 2026; found nothing on Taiwan or Australia startup rounds.
wedge_hints: None practical for a US-based small team; supplier roles to local primes at best. Included for completeness because the pool is large.
insider_roles: Defense-ministry acquisition officers; prime-contractor program managers; local drone-startup founders.

name: US farmers' annual purchases of fertilizer, lime and soil conditioners
size_basis: USDA ERS farm income forecast (page updated Sept 3, 2026): fertilizer, lime and soil conditioners about $34.6B in 2025 and about $39.9B forecast for 2026 (both backed out from stated changes, so approximate); earlier ERS vintage put 2025 at $29.2B. Midpoint used.
money_flow: Farmers pay ag retailers and co-ops (Nutrien Ag Solutions, CHS, independents), who buy from producers and importers (Nutrien, Mosaic, CF Industries, Koch, Yara, OCP).
shock: Early-2026 Iran war pushed nitrogen sharply higher (one farmer's reported price went from $530 to $950 a ton within days). DOJ was reported investigating fertilizer price coordination in March 2026, the FTC confirmed a probe in May, and 17 farm groups asked the Senate Judiciary Committee to press DOJ in July. Countervailing duties on Moroccan and Russian phosphate are in a five-year sunset review (a second source says the Moroccan duties were suspended; the reports conflict).
incumbents: A handful of producers (Nutrien, Mosaic, CF, Koch, Yara) supply most US nutrients; Nutrien alone makes about 20% of US phosphate. Retailers and co-ops add a margin on top (my recollection of high-teens to 20s percent gross margin, not verified).
incumbent_fragility: Weak on technology, exposed on politics and law: DOJ and FTC probes, farmer multidistrict litigation alleging coordination since 2021, and USDA's deputy secretary publicly criticizing Mosaic for idling two Brazil plants. Otherwise incumbents are strong, so this is a procurement and trust opening, not a technology one.
funded_startups_already_here: Pivot Bio ($430M Series D in 2021; laid off 62 and closed Berkeley in mid-2025), Nitricity ($50M Series B, Sept 2025), Atlas Agro (Macquarie up to $325M; final investment decision slipped to 2027), Farmers Business Network (FBN Direct input marketplace; restructuring reported, timing unverified).
wedge_hints: Buying groups or forward-purchase pools for mid-size farms; price-transparency and procurement tools for co-ops and retailers; nitrogen-rate reduction services paid per ton avoided; manure and biosolids to fertilizer marketplace; input prepay finance.
insider_roles: Co-op general managers, ag retail agronomists, fertilizer barge and terminal traders, Farm Credit input lenders, certified crop advisers.

name: US farm employers' spend on hired and H-2A labor
size_basis: USDA ERS cash labor of $44.3B in the 2026 forecast; the broader labor line was $54.3B in the Sept 2025 forecast and farmdoc daily puts hired labor near $49B in 2023. The H-2A slice is about $12B (my arithmetic: about 391,600 positions requested in FY2024 x about $18.12 an hour x an assumed 1,200 hours, plus about $10,000 non-wage cost per worker).
money_flow: Farm employers pay workers, plus recruiters, farm labor contractors, H-2A agents, housing and transport providers.
shock: DOL interim final rule of Oct 2, 2025 changed how the H-2A Adverse Effect Wage Rate is set, using BLS OEWS data with two skill levels and a housing adjustment, because USDA discontinued the Farm Labor Survey on Aug 31, 2025 and the 2023 AEWR rule was vacated on Aug 25, 2025. UFW sued Nov 21, 2025. The notice cites a study of a possible loss of about 225,000 farm workers from enforcement.
incumbents: Farm labor contractors, state grower H-2A associations, immigration attorneys and payroll providers capture the money through fees and markups on a paper-heavy process across about 2M fragmented farms.
incumbent_fragility: Fragmentation and manual compliance: most employers run H-2A on paper and agents, and the wage-setting rules just changed under litigation, so incumbents' playbooks are unsettled. No single incumbent controls the channel.
funded_startups_already_here: Seso ($25M Series A from Index in 2022; $26M Series B led by BOND in April 2024), Croft ($2.67M seed, Feb 2024). No 2025-26 rounds found.
wedge_hints: Employer-provided H-2A housing (the AEWR housing adjustment changes the economics); H-2A compliance and recruitment for mid-size growers; payroll, banking and remittances for farmworkers; ag workers' comp; harvest and packhouse automation sold as a service; wage benchmarking against the new OEWS-based rates.
insider_roles: Farm labor contractor owners, H-2A agent-association staff, farm bureau labor directors, state workforce agency job-order staff, HR managers at growers with 1,000+ workers.

name: US federal crop insurance premiums (farmer-paid plus taxpayer subsidy)
size_basis: USDA RMA Summary of Business, 2025 crop year, interim snapshot as of Apr 21, 2025: total premium $18.04B, subsidy $11.26B (farmer-paid about $6.78B, my subtraction), liability $177.0B, indemnity $17.66B. The administrative and operating reimbursement to insurers is not sourced for 2025 (CRS: $1.6B in 2009, scales with premium); my estimate is about $2B or more.
money_flow: Farmers pay about a third of premium; Treasury pays the premium subsidy and an administrative and operating reimbursement to Approved Insurance Providers, who sell through private agents. Treasury also reinsures losses and shares gains under the Standard Reinsurance Agreement; indemnities flow back to farmers.
shock: One Big Beautiful Bill Act raised buy-up premium subsidies 3-5 points (38-64% to 41-69%), lifted the Supplemental Coverage Option subsidy from 65% to 80%, adds 90% coverage via the Enhanced Coverage Option in 2026, extra beginning-farmer support, and an extra 6% reimbursement in high-loss states (farmdoc daily, dollar value unverified). RMA implemented it by bulletin on Aug 20, 2025, effective for sales closing dates on or after July 1, 2025. CBO scores +$4.4B over 10 years; farmdoc argues earlier RMA actions on ECO added $13.2B.
incumbents: About 16 Approved Insurance Providers (an older, roughly 2018-era count) sell identical federally priced policies through private agents; per a Watts analysis (2018) nearly all of the reimbursement goes to agent commissions.
incumbent_fragility: Moderate. RMA sets rates and subsidies, so AIPs compete only on service and distribution; agent books, paper-heavy claims and a thin adjuster workforce are soft spots. Barriers to entry are real: AIP approval, capital and reinsurance.
funded_startups_already_here: None found building a federally reinsured AIP or agency (searched Arbol, Descartes, Pula, Acre and general crop-insurance startups). Arbol (parametric, $60M Series B April 2024, about $250M gross written premium in 2023) is supplemental. Descartes, Pula and Acre returned nothing relevant for US farms.
wedge_hints: Remote-sensing and drone claims adjusting sold to AIPs; digital agency or agent-book roll-up; SCO/ECO decision tools; supplemental private coverage layered on federal policies; specialty-crop MGA. A $100M path needs roughly 5% of a ~$2B reimbursement pool, so it is a roll-up or digital-AIP outcome, not a pure software one.
insider_roles: Crop insurance agents with large books, AIP claims managers, loss adjusters, RMA compliance reviewers, farm lenders who require coverage.

name: US feedlot and packer purchases of cattle and calves (cattle cash receipts)
size_basis: USDA cattle and calves cash receipts of $134B in 2025, up 19% from $112B in 2024 (final figures, April 2026 summary, as relayed in search results; I did not open the document itself).
money_flow: Packers pay feedlots for fed cattle; feedlots pay cow-calf ranchers and auction barns for feeder cattle; Mexican feeder cattle historically filled part of the gap.
shock: Beef cow herd at 27.6M head in the Jan 2026 inventory, the lowest since 1951. New World screwworm closed the Mexican feeder-cattle trade (about $1.2B a year); 42 US cases as of about August 2026, nearly all in Texas; USDA announced a phased reopening on July 24, 2026 (Douglas, AZ from Aug 24 at 700 head a day, then 900, RFID required). Tyson announced closing its Lexington, NE plant in Nov 2025 (about 5,000 head a day, 7.5-9% of slaughter capacity) after a $1.135B FY2025 beef loss. USDA's Ranchers First Initiative (Aug 31, 2026) adds a heifer-retention insurance endorsement with no rollout date.
incumbents: A few large packers (JBS, Tyson, Cargill, National Beef), large feedlots, and tens of thousands of cow-calf operations and auction barns.
incumbent_fragility: Packers are losing money with excess capacity and a shrinking herd, and ranchers are undercapitalized to rebuild. The structural squeeze (cost of cattle versus slaughter capacity) is hard for incumbents to fix quickly.
funded_startups_already_here: None found in the US for herd-rebuilding finance, EID/traceability or screwworm compliance (searched cattle fintech, marketplace and traceability startups). Nearest is France's EDS (Bovicash, EUR100M cattle-leasing platform, launching autumn 2026). Public money dominates: USDA's screwworm grand challenge had about $105M against about $664M requested.
wedge_hints: Heifer leasing and herd-rebuild finance, possibly tied to the new heifer insurance endorsement; screwworm and EID compliance logistics at ranch and border scale; feeder-calf sourcing for feedlots; custom-grazing marketplace; brokerage of small regional packing capacity. Leasing carries mortality and regulatory risk.
insider_roles: Auction market owners, order buyers, feedlot risk managers, ag bank and Farm Credit lenders, accredited large-animal vets.

name: US electric utilities' spend on vegetation management (line clearance)
size_basis: Harris Williams (2022) put it at about $8B and a 2026 Power Magazine piece at about $7B; no government total exists. Cross-check: Davey Tree 2025 revenue was $1.95B with Utility Services up 5.4% (about $54M); Asplundh is private with a secondhand $5.7B revenue estimate that includes non-vegetation work.
money_flow: Utility operating budgets, recovered in rates, pay line-clearance contractors for trimming, tree removal, herbicide and work planning.
shock: January 2025 Los Angeles fires: investigators pointed to Southern California Edison equipment for the Eaton Fire and LA County and DOJ sued SCE; California inverse condemnation imposes strict liability; property insurers are retreating; industry argues for a move from fixed trim cycles to risk-based work. NERC FAC-003-5 has applied since Apr 1, 2024. Davey reported a 37.9% ($10.2M) decline in its Utility Resource Group in 2025 tied to vegetation management market challenges, so demand is not uniformly strong.
incumbents: Asplundh (private), Davey Tree (public), Wright Tree (employee-owned) and utility in-house crews, paid mostly by volume (miles cleared, trees removed) under unit-price contracts.
incumbent_fragility: Business-model conflict: contractors are paid by volume, so risk-based programs that cut billable work run against their revenue. Labor shortages and rising contractor costs are cited, and utilities increasingly need regulator-grade evidence of work done.
funded_startups_already_here: Overstory (satellite/AI vegetation intelligence; sources conflict, with a reported EUR14M round in 2023 and a $5.2M round led by Convective Capital), Pano AI (wildfire detection, $44M Series B reported June 2025), Vibrant Planet (about $45M raised in total).
wedge_hints: Independent post-trim LiDAR audit of contractor work for utilities and regulators; risk-based work planning sold with outcome data; hazard-tree prioritization; biomass disposal and wood utilization marketplace; contractor labor staffing.
insider_roles: Utility vegetation program managers, utility arborists, contractor general foremen, work planners, wildfire-mitigation-plan regulators.

name: US packaging extended producer responsibility (EPR) producer fees
geography: United States (California, Oregon, Colorado, Maine, Minnesota, Maryland, Washington)
size_basis: BORDERLINE against the $5B bar. California's first Circular Action Alliance program plan (filed June 15, 2026) projects a 5-year budget of $9.3-17.2B, about $1.9-3.4B a year (my division). Oregon is reported at about $100M a year (one weak guide). No sourced national total exists; my estimate at maturity across the seven states is $4-7B a year, dependent on plan approval and the federal challenge to SB 54.
money_flow: Consumer packaged goods brands and retailers pay annual fees to a producer responsibility organization (Circular Action Alliance), which funds municipal collection, MRF upgrades and recycling targets.
shock: California's first EPR program plan was filed June 15, 2026 under SB 54 (litigation pending in federal court); Oregon sent first invoices in Jan 2026 (another guide says the program went live July 1, 2025, so dates conflict); Colorado's program starts in 2026; the next fee cycle, based on detailed 2026 supply reports, begins in 2027.
incumbents: Circular Action Alliance (the dominant producer responsibility organization), haulers and MRF operators, and the CPG brands that pay. Cities currently carry much of the cost.
incumbent_fragility: CAA is new and building data and payment systems from scratch; CPG brands lack SKU-level packaging data; haulers have a conflict between collection and landfill revenue and recycling goals.
funded_startups_already_here: ForSURE (Utrecht, EPR compliance software, $3.6M total, seed Sept 2024); on the sorting side AMP Robotics ($91M Series D, Dec 2024) and Sortera. No sizable US producer-side EPR compliance round found.
wedge_hints: SKU-level packaging data and fee reporting for CPG companies; eco-modulation optimization (redesign to lower fees); audit and dispute of producer-organization invoices; reuse and refill systems paid with fee credits; financing for MRF upgrades; recycled-content resin sourcing.
insider_roles: CPG packaging engineers and sustainability directors, MRF operators, Oregon DEQ and Colorado CDPHE program staff, municipal recycling coordinators.

name: US farmers' spend on equipment repair, maintenance and parts
size_basis: USDA NASS Farm Production Expenditures lists 'farm supplies and repairs' at $24.0B for 2024; repair and maintenance alone was $18B in 2023 (a Senate Agriculture deck citing ERS, not checked against the ERS table). Lower figure used. PIRG separately estimates repair restrictions cost farmers $4.2B a year (advocacy estimate).
money_flow: Farmers and custom operators pay equipment dealers, and a minority independent shops, for parts, labor and diagnostics.
shock: FTC and five states (IL, AZ, MI, MN, WI) settled with Deere on July 8, 2026: 10 years of dealer-equivalent repair tools and software for farmers and independents, including parts pairing, and no retaliation. Deere also agreed in April 2026 to a $99M class settlement for repair payers since Jan 2018. Iowa's House passed a farm right-to-repair bill 70-18 in April 2026.
incumbents: Deere, CNH, AGCO and Kubota dealer networks. One dealer anecdote: parts about 20% of revenue at about 35% margin, service about 10% at about 70% margin.
incumbent_fragility: Business-model conflict: dealer profit is concentrated in service and parts, and the settlement removes the diagnostic-software moat that protected it. Manufacturers earn thin margins on equipment and rely on the aftermarket.
funded_startups_already_here: None found for independent farm repair or parts marketplaces in 2025-26 (searched marketplace, used-parts and right-to-repair startups); an established used-equipment and parts ecosystem exists.
wedge_hints: Dealer-equivalent diagnostics and subscription tools for mixed fleets; mobile technician network; independent shop parts procurement; remanufacturing; technician training; downtime insurance. Actual tool access is unproven until the order is entered and tested.
insider_roles: Independent ag repair shop owners, dealer service managers, custom harvesters, large-farm shop managers, former OEM service engineers.

name: US community water systems' mandated lead service line replacement and PFAS treatment capex
size_basis: DISPUTED. On the AWWA basis: PFAS compliance $3.8-5.5B a year (relayed by secondary coverage) plus lead line replacement of $46B to over $90B nationally over about 10 years (about $4.6-9B a year), giving about $8-15B a year. On EPA's own basis: PFAS about $1.5B a year plus the LCRI at $1.47-1.95B a year in total, about $3B, which is under the bar. Midpoint of the AWWA range used.
money_flow: About 50,000 fragmented community water systems pay engineering firms, contractors, treatment media and equipment suppliers, funded by ratepayers, state revolving funds and federal infrastructure money.
shock: EPA announced May 14, 2025 that it would keep the 4 ppt PFOA and PFOS limits, rescind four other PFAS limits and extend deadlines; the formal proposal of May 20, 2026 would move PFOA/PFOS compliance from April 26, 2029 to April 26, 2031 for systems that ask. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements date stays Nov 1, 2027; oral argument in the AWWA v. EPA challenge was Sept 30, 2026, with a decision likely in 6-12 months.
incumbents: Engineering and design firms, utility contractors, and treatment media and equipment makers; utilities themselves buy through slow municipal procurement.
incumbent_fragility: Fragmented buyers and incomplete service line inventories. Deadlines and rules are moving under litigation, so incumbents face demand-timing risk, not a technology threat.
funded_startups_already_here: BlueConduit (predictive lead-line identification; $2.25M across 5 rounds per an aggregator, last seed July 2023). No 2025-26 rounds for lead or PFAS water startups found in search.
wedge_hints: Turnkey lead-line replacement programs for small and mid utilities that solve homeowner consent and access; inventory verification data; state revolving fund grant and loan navigation for small systems; PFAS treatment sold as a service (media change-out and regeneration). Timing risk from the PFAS delay and LCRI litigation.
insider_roles: Utility water-quality managers, state SRF program managers, GAC and ion exchange media suppliers, public works directors.

name: US biofuel producers' purchases of fats, oils and grease feedstock
size_basis: EIA July 2026 monthly feedstock use (million lb): soybean oil 1,687, corn oil 453, canola 330, tallow 771, poultry fat 34, yellow grease/UCO 610, other 101, about 3,990 total, or about 48B lb a year at that run rate. At an assumed $0.50-0.60 a lb (my assumption; current prices not verified) that is about $24-29B.
money_flow: Renewable diesel and biodiesel producers buy soybean oil, tallow, used cooking oil, corn oil and canola oil from crushers, renderers, collectors and importers.
shock: EPA finalized 2026-27 Renewable Fuel Standard volumes in late March 2026 (published Apr 1): 9.07B gallons of biomass-based diesel for 2026, about 60% above 2025 (one source gives 8.95B for 2027, so figures conflict).
