From 2026 the 45Z credit applies only to North American feedstocks, and from 2028 imported feedstock and fuel get half the RFS value. UCO imports fell 38% year on year (China-origin down 67%), and biofuel's share of US soybean oil use is about 54%, up from 40% two years earlier.
incumbents: Large renderers, crushers (ADM, Bunge, Cargill), thousands of fragmented UCO and grease collectors, and the refiners that buy.
incumbent_fragility: Supply of domestic fats is inelastic in the short run and collection is fragmented, so scarcity rent goes to whoever controls domestic collection and origin documentation; imported-feedstock fraud and certification burdens favor traceable supply.
funded_startups_already_here: None found in feedstock sourcing or traceability (searched renderer, UCO collection and feedstock traceability startups). Capital-heavy at scale, with strong incumbent renderers.
wedge_hints: Grease route-density consolidation with software; origin and carbon-intensity documentation for 45Z and ISCC audits; waste-oil brokerage with North American origin certification; carbon-intensity measurement for soybean growers; offtake for new oilseeds (camelina, carinata, pennycress).
insider_roles: Renderer procurement managers, UCO route collectors, refinery feedstock buyers, RIN traders, carbon-intensity auditors.

name: US purchases of metal scrap by mills, smelters and foundries (ferrous and copper)
size_basis: USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026: domestic purchases of iron and steel scrap $19.7B in 2025 ($20.4B in 2024). Copper: 160kt from old scrap plus 760kt from new scrap, about 920kt contained copper at 490 cents a lb (about $10,800 a ton), about $9.9B (my arithmetic). Total at least $29B, before aluminum and other metals.
money_flow: Generators (auto shredders, demolition, fabricators) sell to dealers and processors, who sell to mills, brass and rod mills, foundries and exporters.
shock: Section 232 copper proclamation of July 30, 2025: 50% tariff on semi-finished and derivative copper from Aug 1, 2025 (scrap, cathode and concentrate exempt) and a direction to Commerce to pursue domestic sales requirements, including 25% for high-quality copper scrap (no implementing rule found; no scrap export controls imposed). A phased refined copper tariff (15% from Jan 1, 2027, 30% in 2028) was tied to a Commerce report due June 30, 2026. Refined copper imports jumped to about 1.7Mt in 2025 from 0.9Mt, with year-end stocks of 450kt and net import reliance of 57% (USGS).
incumbents: A few large processors (USGS: five leading processors handled 26M tons through 354 facilities in 2023) plus a long tail of independent yards; exporters and domestic buyers have opposed interests in any sales mandate.
incumbent_fragility: A possible domestic sales mandate and tariff-driven shifts in demand pit exporters against domestic mills; the long tail of independent yards runs thin, mostly manual operations with little software.
funded_startups_already_here: Sortera ($30.5M Series C, alloy sorting), AMP Robotics ($91M Series D, Dec 2024), Redwood Materials ($350M, Nov 2025, battery materials), Metaloop (EUR16M, 2023), ScrapAd (Spain, EUR6M Series A, Dec 2025, B2B scrap marketplace). No dominant US B2B scrap marketplace found.
wedge_hints: B2B marketplace and price discovery for fabricators selling new scrap; chain-of-custody and grading certification if a domestic sales mandate is implemented; yard software (weighing, ID checks, payments); alloy-sorting as a service; fabricator scrap financing and hedging.
insider_roles: Scrap yard general managers, mill scrap buyers, brass mill metal managers, metals brokers, shredder operators, customs brokers.

name: US state governments' spend on Medicaid and SNAP administration (eligibility determination, enrollment and verification systems, outsourced operations)
geography: US (50 states; counties administer SNAP in 10 states)
size_basis: Medicaid FY2024 administrative spending $41.3B federal+state (MACPAC Exhibit 31, parsed from PDF: eligibility systems $9.9B, MMIS $5.9B, other 50%-match functions incl. eligibility workers $23.0B; excludes managed-care plan admin). SNAP admin ~ $13B/yr derived [my estimate]: USDA regulatory analysis puts federal-to-state shift at ~$16.9B over FY2027-31 (CSPI), and the shift is 25 points of total admin cost. Addressable core (eligibility systems + operations) probably $15-25B [my estimate].
money_flow: Federal government and states split admin cost (50% baseline, 90% federal match for system build, 75% for operations); states/counties pay system integrators and operations vendors (Maximus, Conduent, Gainwell, Deloitte, GDIT) plus their own and county caseworkers.
shock: H.R.1 (P.L. 119-21, signed 2025-07-04): Medicaid work-requirement verification for expansion adults from 2027-01-01 (CMS interim final rule issued 2026-06-01, effective 2026-07-31; data-first verification, 6-month or quarterly checks); SNAP federal admin share cut from 50% to 25% on 2026-10-01 (~$16.9B shifted to states FY27-31; Maryland alone +$57.5M/yr); only $200M federal Medicaid implementation grants vs. states' costs; SNAP benefit cost-share tied to error rates starts FY2028.
incumbents: Maximus (named by CMS as one of 10 existing E&E vendors pledging support), Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, GDIT, Accenture; earn on large implementation builds plus long operations contracts. CMS-brokered vendor deals: fixed fees for upgrades, discounted licenses, free fraud monitoring (claimed $600M savings through 2028).
incumbent_fragility: States run patchwork legacy eligibility systems that cannot pull cross-agency data; vendors are under Senate scrutiny (Wyden/Warren letters to Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, GDIT, Maximus) and forced to discount; states are budget-squeezed by the SNAP cost shift and want per-verification pricing. Counterpoint: Jan 2027 go-live is so tight that first-wave money flows to existing vendors; newcomer window is 2027-2029 re-procurements and the verification data layer. Open-source/nonprofit tooling (Nava/APHSA) and USDA grants are free substitutes.
funded_startups_already_here: Fortuna Health ($18M, July 2025, Medicaid enrollment/recertification); Nava PBC / Nava Labs ($1.2M grant, open-source AI verification for SNAP/Medicaid with APHSA and Maryland); Code for America (nonprofit); Equifax The Work Number (incumbent income verification). USDA FY26 SNAP earnings-verification grants up to $38M. Propel, Truv, Pinwheel not verified this session. No venture-scale direct attacker found.
wedge_hints: (1) Per-verification employment/income data-matching for state agencies against 6-month and quarterly cycles; (2) exemption-evidence and document-capture tooling for county caseworkers in county-run SNAP states; (3) managed-care plans (capitation reasons to retain members) as payer for re-verification help, subject to outreach/marketing rules; (4) SNAP payment-error reduction before the FY2028 benefit cost-share. Payer who signs: state Medicaid or SNAP director via MES/human-services IT procurement.
insider_roles: State Medicaid eligibility directors; county SNAP directors; state E&E/MMIS integration leads; MES procurement officers; managed-care plan enrollment and retention heads; Maximus/Conduent contract and site managers; legal-aid benefits attorneys; APHSA staff.

name: US federal agencies' spend on management advisory and professional support services (consultants and support contractors)
geography: US federal government (shock concentrated on civilian agencies)
size_basis: Bloomberg Government (Jan 2026, paywalled, secondary): FY2025 management-advisory obligations fell 19% to a five-year low, civilian down one-third to $26B and DoD down 1% to $24B. GAO FY2025 snapshot (total contract commitments ~$793B; professional support services ~$26B at DoD and ~$18B civilian, a narrower category).
money_flow: Agencies pay labor-hour/time-and-materials fees to primes (Booz Allen, Deloitte GPS, Accenture Federal, SAIC, CACI, Leidos) and to small-business subcontractors via GSA schedules and IDIQs.
shock: Feb 2025 GSA memo told agencies to review and justify contracts with the 10 highest-paid consulting firms (>$65B in fees in 2025 and later); Bloomberg reported ~1,700 GSA consulting terminations claiming $4.5B savings, then a second phase pushing outcome-based restructuring ($8.9B immediate savings claimed). Deloitte at least 127 contracts cut or modified, Booz Allen ~61, Accenture at least 30 ($240M).
incumbents: Booz Allen (almost all of ~$11B revenue is public sector), Deloitte Government and Public Services, Accenture Federal (federal ~8% of global revenue FY2024), SAIC, CACI, Leidos; revenue depends on billable headcount.
incumbent_fragility: Labor-hour model conflicts with outcome-based buying and AI productivity; civilian demand down by a third and agencies must defend spend. Counterpoint: DoD contract spend is growing ($491.6B FY2025 vs $445B), so the shock is civilian-only; moats are past performance, set-asides and clearances.
funded_startups_already_here: No funded AI-native delivery firm selling services to federal civilian agencies found. Funded players are software for contractors: NationGraph ($18M Series A, Feb 2026), Vultron ($22M Series A, 2025), Ask Sage ($17M Series A, Dec 2024), Procurement Sciences AI ($10M Series A, 2024). Real competitors are mid-size GovCons with set-aside status; big firms repositioning toward agent delivery.
wedge_hints: Fixed-price, outcome-priced work replacing terminated time-and-materials contracts at civilian agencies (claims backlogs, grants management, FOIA, IT modernization); subcontract slots with primes that must reprice; small-business set-aside entry (status of SBA 8(a)/set-aside programs in 2026 not verified, check). Payer who signs: contracting officer with agency CIO/program office as sponsor.
insider_roles: GSA FAS contracting officers and CORs; agency CFO/CIO staff; capture and pricing leads at primes; small-business subcontractors; OIG and GAO auditors; former DOGE/GSA acquisition staff.

name: US employers' commissions and fees paid to benefits brokers and consultants for group health plans
size_basis: [my estimate, +/-40%] ~150M Americans have employer coverage (Insurance Business, Sept 2026); KFF 2025 avg single premium $9,325, family $26,993, implying roughly $1.2-1.4T of employer premiums/claims at ~$8.7k per covered person; Form 5500 analysis (2022-24) found median broker commission 6.8% for smallest employers (<$500k premium) falling to 2.3% for the largest; blended 2.5-3.5% gives $33-45B. Excludes TPA and carrier fees.
money_flow: Carriers pay brokers commissions (percent of premium, or $25-40 PEPM for small groups) or employers pay consulting fees; self-funded employers also pay stop-loss placement and consulting fees.
shock: ICHRA rebranded 'CHOICE Arrangements' by SBA/CMS (announced ~2026-09-09); employers offering ICHRA grew 99% from 2025 to 2026 to >500,000 covered lives, two-thirds of small adopters never previously offered coverage; Peterson-KFF (Jan 2026) found ICHRA administrators taking over agent-of-record at renewal; small-group premiums heading into 2027 with national median +14% (KFF). Weak shock: 500k lives vs 150M, so erosion is slow.
incumbents: Marsh McLennan Agency, Gallagher, Aon (incl. NFP), WTW, USI, Alliant, Brown & Brown, HUB plus thousands of small agencies, many PE-backed roll-ups (background knowledge, not verified here). Paid by carrier commission as percent of premium.
incumbent_fragility: Percent-of-premium pay rises with cost inflation, conflicting with the buyer's goal; ICHRA breaks the carrier-commission flow because employees buy individual plans, and brokers resist selling it (54% of surveyed brokers never sold one, per TASC, a vendor with a stake); fragmented so no player can reprice.
funded_startups_already_here: Corridor ($25M seed, Bain Capital Ventures, AI + licensed advisors for 1-500 employee firms, ~2026-09); Gyde ($60M launch, Lightspeed, Jan 2026, AI-native brokerage platform); Harper ($46.8M Series A+seed, P&C brokerage, Emergence); Nayya ($55M Series C, $106M total, benefits navigation). Thatch, Take Command, Ease: no 2026 rounds found.
wedge_hints: (1) Flat-fee, comp-transparent advisory for 20-200 employee firms where median commission is highest (6.8%); (2) first-time-offer ICHRA/CHOICE enrollment with broker-agnostic comp; (3) mid-market self-funded stop-loss and pharmacy-benefit auditing where fees are 2-3% of a larger base. Check state broker licensing and ERISA compensation disclosure. Payer who signs: CFO or head of HR (budget line exists but is paid indirectly by carrier today).
insider_roles: Account managers and producers at mid-size agencies; carrier small-group underwriters; TPA operations leads; stop-loss MGUs; HR and finance leaders at 50-500 employee firms; ERISA litigators.

name: Enterprises' spend on outsourced customer-service BPO (Concentrix, TP and peers; Philippines, India, nearshore)
size_basis: [my estimate, low confidence] Concentrix FY2026 revenue guidance $9.83-9.88B (Oct 1, 2026 release); TP (Teleperformance) H1 2026 revenue EUR 4.88B (~EUR 9.8B annualized); those two alone ~$20B; Philippines IT-BPM export revenue >$40B in 2025 per IBPAP (not all customer service). No source gave the global CX-outsourcing total.
money_flow: Enterprise customer-care budgets pay per seat-hour or per transaction to BPOs, which employ offshore agents.
shock: Concentrix cut FY2026 guidance on 2026-06-29 (to $9.925-10.025B; shares -21%, TP -11-13% in sympathy), cut again on 2026-10-01 (Q3 revenue $2.45B, -1.2%; $1.05B goodwill impairment; Q4 guided -3% to -5% constant currency); TP H1 2026 like-for-like -1.7% with Trust and Safety sharply down on AI automation and offshoring, restructuring raised to EUR 120-140M; Concentrix healthcare vertical -14% in Q2.
incumbents: Concentrix, TP, Genpact, TaskUs, TTEC, Foundever, Alorica; billed per seat-hour. Both leaders are repositioning (Concentrix: ~50% of revenue from business won in the last 3 years).
incumbent_fragility: Per-seat billing conflicts with AI that removes seats; market punishing them (impairment, guidance cuts). But they have scale, compliance infrastructure and client relationships, and AI-led deflation is still gradual.
funded_startups_already_here: Sierra ($950M at $15B+, May 2026), Decagon ($250M Series D at $4.5B, Jan 2026), Parloa ($350M Series D, ~$3B, Jan 2026); aggregator data conflicts in places. Crescendo not found.
wedge_hints: Only if taking the services P&L: health-plan member services and prior-auth phone work (HIPAA and human-in-the-loop protection while Concentrix healthcare shrinks); rolling up small regional BPOs and applying AI to cut seats; collections and dispute handling priced per resolution. Payer who signs: VP customer experience or head of vendor management. Generic AI support agent is a round-1 cliche.
insider_roles: BPO site directors and workforce-management planners; QA leads; client-services VPs at BPOs; enterprise CX procurement leads; contact-center platform admins; Manila/Pune labor relations.

name: US enterprises' spend on offshore-delivered IT services (application development and maintenance, testing, infrastructure from Indian IT majors and captives)
size_basis: [my estimate] Nasscom FY26: IT services ~$149B, total exports ~$246B; India GCC ecosystem >2,000 centers and ~$100B revenue (headline only). North America share not found; assumed ~two-thirds of IT-services exports from background knowledge, giving ~$100B.
money_flow: US enterprises pay time-and-materials or multi-year fixed-price fees (3-5% annual escalators) to Indian IT providers and captives; work done largely by H-1B and India-based staff.
shock: 2025-09-19 proclamation imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions; Bloomberg found ~90% of new H-1B hires at TCS, Infosys, Cognizant were approved at consulates (fee-exposed), >$1B of fees for Infosys alone on historical volumes; H-1B demand plummeted after the fee. AI deflation: TCS passes ~10-15% of AI productivity gains to clients, ICICI Direct estimates 2-3%/yr deflation, NIFTY IT -39% from Dec 2024 peak to May 2026 (Bessemer). Counterpoint: TCS Q2 FY27 (2026-10-08) revenue Rs 73,188 crore, +11.2% YoY in rupees but +0.5% QoQ constant currency, AI revenue $3.1B annualized; eroding, not collapsing.
incumbents: TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, Accenture; pyramid-leveraged time-and-materials billing and visa dependency.
incumbent_fragility: Pyramid billing conflicts with AI productivity; visa fee raises the cost of the onsite model; multi-year fixed-price contracts with escalators slow repricing; clients push for pass-through of AI gains. They are large, profitable and adapting, so the window is slow.
funded_startups_already_here: Kodesage ($6.6M seed, June 2026, legacy knowledge extraction); Hypercubic (~$5M seed, COBOL modernization, single aggregator); Rhino.ai ($50M, Jan 2025); Bessemer publicly backing AI-native services challengers. Cognition and Factory not verified this session.
wedge_hints: Fixed-price COBOL/mainframe modernization for mid-market banks and insurers below the minimum ticket of Accenture/TCS; per-ticket outcome-priced application maintenance; 'captive as a service' in India for US mid-market firms that cannot build a GCC now that H-1B import is costly (check transfer pricing and permanent-establishment rules). Payer who signs: CIO or head of IT sourcing.
insider_roles: Delivery heads at Indian IT majors; client-side vendor management office leads; sourcing advisors (ISG, Everest, Gartner); GCC leaders in Bengaluru/Pune; immigration counsel; mainframe/COBOL architects.

name: Corporate clients' fees to large US law firms for associate-leveraged work (diligence, drafting, document review, regulatory research)
size_basis: Am Law 100 aggregate gross revenue was $178.95B for 2025, +13.0% (Kirkland $10.56B, Latham $8.3B). Leveraged associate-work share assumed 35-45% [my estimate, no source], giving ~$60-80B.
money_flow: Corporate legal departments and sponsors pay hourly or fixed fees to firms; firms bill associates at a multiple of pay.
shock: Weak shock: 2025 was a record year (profit +13%, worked rates +7.3%) but Thomson Reuters/Georgetown 2026 report flags 'fault lines'; smaller firms took most growth as clients shifted to lower-cost alternatives; tech spend +~10%, talent cost +8.2%. The real disturbance is legal AI capital: Harvey $200M at $11B (Mar 2026), Legora $550M Series D at $5.55B, Crosby $60M Series B (Mar 2026), >$5B into legal AI in 2025 (PitchBook via vendor blog).
incumbents: Kirkland, Latham, DLA Piper and the rest of the Am Law 100; billable-hour pyramid.
incumbent_fragility: Low near-term. Billable hour conflicts with AI efficiency, but partners currently capture gains as margin and buy the tools (Harvey). Fragility is latent, not realized.
funded_startups_already_here: Harvey, Legora, Crosby (AI-native fixed-fee contract review firm), Eudia (Series A up to $105M, Feb 2025), plus many others.
wedge_hints: Only owning a law-firm P&L in a niche is open (fixed-fee contract review for mid-market), and Crosby leads there. Check unauthorized-practice-of-law and Arizona ABS-type ownership rules; 2026 status of non-lawyer ownership not verified. Payer who signs: general counsel or head of legal operations. Generic legal copilot is a round-1 cliche.
insider_roles: Law-firm pricing directors; practice-support partners; corporate legal-ops leaders; outside-counsel billing auditors; legal malpractice insurers; bar ethics counsel.

name: US households' and small businesses' fees for tax preparation and accounting (paid preparers and CPA/EA firms)
size_basis: Census Services Annual Survey NAICS 5412, 2022 (via FRED): tax preparation for corporate/other clients $30.6B + individuals/unincorporated $25.3B + general accounting $11.1B. Excludes audit/assurance $42.4B, payroll $29.0B, tax planning $7.8B. 2022 is the latest annual found.
money_flow: Households and small firms pay H&R Block, Jackson Hewitt, independent preparers and CPA/EA firms; NATP 2025 base Form 1040 averaged $280 (CPA), $228 (EA), ~$185 (non-credentialed).
shock: IRS Direct File not offered for the 2026 filing season; paid preparers filed 54.7% of e-filed returns through 2026-04-10 (61.4M of 112.2M, secondary); CPA pipeline shrinking (first-time candidates 48,004 in 2016 to 32,188 in 2021); private equity now behind most fast-growing firms (23 of 26 in Accounting Today's 2026 list; roughly half of the 20 largest firms PE-backed per a June 2026 count) pushing work offshore and to AI.
incumbents: H&R Block, Intuit, regional CPA firms (many PE-backed), thousands of sole practitioners.
incumbent_fragility: Partner retirement cliff, staff shortage, seasonal capacity, PE margin targets; Intuit lobbied against Direct File so its incentive is to keep the paid path. Not collapsing: demand for paid preparers is rising.
funded_startups_already_here: Basis ($100M Series B at $1.15B, Feb 2026), Rillet ($100M Series C at $1B), Accrual ($75M launch, Feb 2026, individual returns, General Catalyst), Juno ($12M seed, Apr 2026), Filed ($17.2M, 2025), TaxGPT; Black Ore no funding found.
wedge_hints: Software layer is crowded; open space is buying retiring sole-practitioner books and running them AI-native (PE is also doing this), and high-volume IRS/state notice response (neither sized). Payer who signs: household or small-business owner; practice owner for software.
insider_roles: Managing partners and operations directors at CPA firms; enrolled agents; H&R Block franchisees; state CPA society executives; PE operating partners in accounting; offshore tax-prep managers in India.

name: US financial institutions' spend on BSA/AML/KYC compliance operations (alert triage, investigations, SAR filing, onboarding diligence)
geography: US (LexisNexis figure covers US and Canada)
size_basis: June 9, 2026 House Financial Services Republicans letter cites ~$59B/yr (attributed to Forrester; derivation unverified). LexisNexis True Cost of Financial Crime Compliance: $61B for US+Canada (2024), survey of 1,181 decision-makers with only 160 in US/Canada.
money_flow: Banks, broker-dealers, MSBs and fintechs pay in-house analysts, offshore BPOs and software vendors for monitoring, investigations and onboarding.
shock: FinCEN NPRM of 2026-04-07 rewriting AML/CFT program rules toward risk-based programs; Oct 2025 SAR FAQs easing continuing-activity review and documentation; Congress floating higher SAR/CTR thresholds; House Republicans urging AI-driven monitoring (June 2026). This shock can shrink the pool by cutting low-value filings.
incumbents: Bank in-house ops teams, BPOs (Genpact, Accenture, Cognizant, Capgemini), vendors (NICE Actimize, LexisNexis Risk, Fenergo, Quantexa); headcount-priced.
incumbent_fragility: Headcount-based cost structure is exposed if regulators reduce required volume and endorse AI monitoring; banks are budget-sensitive. Regulatory-risk aversion keeps humans in the loop, so change is gradual.
funded_startups_already_here: Bretton AI ($75M Series B, Sapphire), Norm Ai (~$136M total per Owler, unverified), Greenlite (Series A ~$15M, entity unconfirmed), Sardine ($70M Series C, Feb 2025), Seon ($80M Series C), Steward ($5M, Mar 2026), Diligent AI (~EUR 2M), Marble (EUR 6.5M Series A, Sept 2026). Hummingbird and Persona not verified.
wedge_hints: Outsourced BSA-officer and AML operations for community banks and credit unions (one-person compliance teams unable to afford Bretton-class software); sponsor-bank oversight of fintech programs. Number of institutions not counted. Payer who signs: BSA officer or chief compliance officer; exam-driven mandated spend. Overlaps the financial-services slice.
insider_roles: BSA officers at community banks; FIU investigators; sponsor-bank compliance leads; former OCC/FinCEN examiners; AML BPO site managers.

name: Global buyer spend on translation, localization and interpreting delivered by language service providers
size_basis: Nimdzi 2026: $72.6B in 2025 (revised down from $75.7B), $73.4B in 2026, <1% CAGR to 2030. CSA Research's narrower scope gives $51.9B (2024). Interpreting $11.7B (2024) growing to $17.1B by 2029 (8% CAGR), too small alone for the $15B global bar. Figures comparable only within one source.
money_flow: Enterprises, hospitals, courts and governments pay language service providers per word or per minute; LSPs pay freelancers.
shock: Executive Order 14224 (2025-03-01) made English the official language and rescinded EO 13166; DOJ rescinded its LEP guidance (April 2025) and a 2025-07-14 DOJ memo ordered an audit and reallocation of multilingual services; DOGE cancelled at least 10 language/translation contracts; Nimdzi cut its 2025 estimate citing US budget freezes, English-only rhetoric and tariffs; CSA Research predicts AI-driven translation price compression. Floor under interpreting: Section 1557 and Title VI still require meaningful access, but HHS enforcement status of the 2024 rule not verified.
incumbents: LanguageLine, TransPerfect, RWS, Lionbridge, Welocalize and thousands of small LSPs; per-word pricing and freelancer pass-through.
incumbent_fragility: Fragmented; per-word pricing compressed by machine translation; federal demand cut. Interpreting is partly protected by legal qualification requirements in healthcare.
funded_startups_already_here: No 2026 rounds found in this session's searches. From memory, not verified here: DeepL, Lilt, Smartcat and several AI-interpreting and interpreter-dispatch firms.
wedge_hints: Healthcare qualified-interpreter dispatch plus AI-assist where law requires human qualification; court interpreter scheduling in shortage states; regulated-content translation for pharma and devices; Section 1557 language-access compliance audits for hospitals. Payer who signs: hospital language-services director, court administrator, or localization lead.
insider_roles: Hospital language-services directors; court interpreter coordinators; LSP vendor managers; certified medical interpreters (CCHI, NBCMI); HHS OCR staff; pharma localization leads.

name: AI labs' and enterprises' spend on expert human data and evaluation labor (contract professionals paid to train and grade models)
geography: Global buyers (mainly US frontier labs), mostly US expert supply
size_basis: [secondary, self-reported or estimated, gross of contractor pay] Mercor ~$2.0B annualized gross (June 2026; $760M at end of 2025); Scale AI ~$1.5B; Handshake AI ~$1.1B (Apr 2026); Surge AI >$1B trailing ($1.2B in 2024); Turing $300M (2024); Invisible $134M (2024); sum ~$6.2B, rounded up for others. Contractors receive 60-70% of gross, so the labor pool is ~$4B. No credible market-wide total found.
money_flow: Labs and enterprises pay vendors, which pay lawyers, doctors, quants and engineers hourly to write, grade and verify model outputs; the counter-flow to 'AI displaces professionals'.
shock: Meta's investment in Scale AI (valuing it above $29B) pushed labs to diversify vendors; Mercor grew ~2.6x in H1 2026 ($614M gross in H1 2026 vs $760M for all of 2025 end run rate); March 2026 Mercor data breach led Meta to pause its contract. (June 2025 date for the Meta-Scale deal is from memory.)
incumbents: Scale AI, Surge AI, Mercor, Handshake AI, Turing, Invisible; Appen and TELUS Digital in decline; Amazon Mechanical Turk fading.
incumbent_fragility: Buyer concentration (a handful of frontier labs), 30-40% gross margins, insourcing and synthetic-data substitution, breach risk, worker-classification exposure.
funded_startups_already_here: Mercor ($350M Series C at ~$10B, Oct 2025; talks near $20B), Surge (reported raise at $15-25B), Turing ($2.2B), Invisible ($2B), Handshake; valuations press-reported.
wedge_hints: Vertical expert networks and RL-environment building for enterprise (non-lab) buyers deploying agents in law, finance, accounting and medicine; expert-quality certification. Check 1099 vs W-2 classification. Payer who signs: head of data or post-training at a lab; AI platform lead at an enterprise.
insider_roles: Data-operations leads at frontier labs; vendor managers for data procurement; expert contractors (lawyers, doctors, quants); QA reviewer leads at Surge and Mercor; employment-classification counsel.

name: US farm employers' H-2A guest-worker wage bill and the recruiter / farm-labor-contractor / compliance layer around it
size_basis: FY2025 H-2A wage bill $6,935M (FY24: $6.5B) on ~398,000 certified positions, from UC Davis Rural Migration News built on DOL OFLC data. 44% of jobs certified to farm labor contractors (FLCs); 7 of top-10 H-2A employers are FLCs; agents filed 56% of applications; ~9,700 registered FLCs/employees (~4,000 active businesses, Mar 2026). Total US farm labor ~$53B/yr (Farm Bureau/ERS forecast). Service-fee layer (FLC markups, agent fees, housing, transport) is additional and not sized in sources. Path to $100M revenue needs ~15% of a ~$700M fee pool at 10%, i.e. heroic share, or a gross-billing employer-of-record model.
money_flow: Growers pay AEWR-floor wages plus free housing, transport and visa costs. FLCs act as employer of record and bill growers wages plus markup. Agents recruit abroad (mostly Mexico) and file ETA-790 job orders and visa paperwork.
shock: DOL interim final rule (published Oct 2, 2025) replaced the USDA-survey AEWR with a two-tier OEWS-based AEWR plus a $1-3/hr housing adjustment for H-2A workers only; mode AEWR fell from $17 to $14/hr in FY26 Q1; DOL projects >$2B/yr employer savings, EPI estimates $4.4-5.4B/yr lost wages. On Aug 26, 2026 the E.D. Cal. (UFW v. DOL) held the rule unlawful but declined to vacate, ordered DOL to produce a new methodology 'promptly' (no deadline) and to notify employers they may owe backpay. Wage regime is now legally unsettled with retroactive true-up risk.
incumbents: ~4,000 active FLCs (half of H-2A jobs), foreign recruiting agents (56% of filings), regional grower associations, ag-labor law firms. Nobody owns payroll + housing + recruiting + compliance end to end.
incumbent_fragility: Thousands of small FLCs/agents on paper-heavy compliance (ETA-790, housing inspections, wage records), thin working capital and joint-employer liability, and now a wage rate in legal limbo with possible backpay. Fragmentation prevents a coordinated response.
funded_startups_already_here: Seso (SF): $25M Series A 2022 led by Index; $26M Series B 2024 led by Bond (Mary Meeker) with Index/NFX; H-2A compliance, payroll, HR, worker banking. Croft (Indianapolis, seed Feb 2024, ~$2.7M per Caplight). Yadag (Toronto, ~$0.8M per CB Insights). H2 Organizer (Austin, product launch Sep 2024). No 2025-26 round found, but only one search run.
wedge_hints: Backpay-exposure modeling/escrow/insurance by job order; FLC back office (payroll, wage statements, worker banking); working-capital/factoring for FLCs who pay weekly and collect late; employer-provided housing at scale (modular or leaseback); monitoring foreign recruiters for banned worker-paid fees; H-2B (non-ag) adjacent program.
insider_roles: FLC owners/operators; grower-association H-2A managers; ag-labor attorneys; farm HR/payroll managers; labor recruiters in Mexico; former DOL Wage and Hour investigators; farmworker-housing inspectors.

name: Private-school-choice money: state ESAs, vouchers, tax-credit scholarships, plus the federal tax-credit scholarship starting 2027
size_basis: EdChoice 2026 Spending Share Rankings: private school choice programs allocated $10.6B in the latest year, +29% from $8.2B. Florida $3.7B, Arizona $1.06B (prior-year ranking). Texas TEFA ESA ($1B initial, up to ~90,000 accounts, run by contractor Odyssey) began paying Jul 1, 2026. Federal credit from Jan 1, 2027: $1,700/taxpayer; Education Reform Now (cited by Third Way) estimates $1.6B/yr at 2% participation to $8B at 10%. SGOs must spend >=90% of income on scholarships, so operator take is thin (3-5% of $10.6B = $300-500M sector-wide).
money_flow: States (and from 2027 donors via SGOs) fund family accounts or vouchers; families spend on private-school tuition, homeschool vendors, tutors and therapists; a platform vendor runs applications, payments and audits for a fee.
shock: Federal tax-credit scholarship enacted in the July 2025 reconciliation law; Treasury/IRS opt-in notice Dec 12, 2025; program launches Jan 1, 2027; IRS announced 27 states opted in as of Jun 8, 2026. Texas $1B ESA launched Jul 2026. Arizona treasurer issued a June 2026 RFI to replace/upgrade its ESA platform with fraud detection after the Auditor General found as few as 6.5% of purchases audited.
incumbents: ClassWallet (Arizona and other states; ~$102.6M raised incl. $95M growth round Mar 2023), Odyssey (Texas turnkey ESA admin), state education agencies/treasuries, nonprofit SGOs.
incumbent_fragility: Vendors are being audited and re-bid (Arizona). ECCA SGO infrastructure does not exist at scale; Treasury rules not final, including whether the 90% test covers all income and how the 300%-of-area-median income eligibility is verified.
funded_startups_already_here: ClassWallet (Guidepost Growth Equity-led $95M, Mar 2023; ~$102.6M total per CB Insights); Odyssey ($10M Series A led by Tusk Venture Partners). No other funded ESA/SGO platforms found.
wedge_hints: Risk-based audit/fraud analytics for state treasuries; ECCA SGO operating platform (donor portal, income-eligibility checks, 90% accounting, state-list compliance) for the many new SGOs; microschool/small-private-school back office that bills ESAs; provider onboarding for ESA-eligible therapists and tutors.
insider_roles: State ESA program directors; treasury/comptroller staff; SGO executive directors; private-school business managers; microschool founders; state auditor staff.

name: US graduate-school borrowing displaced from Grad PLUS (private lending gap)
size_basis: NBER WP 35683 (Turner, Aug 2026): financing gap ~ $8B/yr across ~370,000 borrowers. Grad PLUS was ~$14B/yr across 440,000 students in AY2023-24 (Bloomberg Government). Parent PLUS ($11B in 2022) now capped at $20k/yr, $65k lifetime. Sallie Mae CEO cites potential +$4.5-5B/yr originations for itself. NOTE: this is loan volume; lender revenue is spread/fees, a small fraction of $8B.
money_flow: Students borrow capped federal Direct Unsubsidized loans ($20,500/yr graduate, $50,000/yr professional) and fill the rest with private loans, savings, employer aid or forgo enrollment; private lenders earn spread/fees and sell or securitize; schools are paid upfront.
shock: Grad PLUS closed to new borrowers on Jul 1, 2026 under the 2025 reconciliation law; new annual/aggregate caps on graduate and professional loans and Parent PLUS; current students grandfathered up to 3 years.
incumbents: Sallie Mae (Q2 2026 originations +4.5%, net charge-offs $113M vs $94M), Navient/Earnest, SoFi, banks and credit unions.
incumbent_fragility: NBER: private grad lending collapsed after Grad PLUS expanded in 2006 and never recovered; capital constraints; legal limits on using program-level outcomes data in underwriting; fields with flat earnings gradients (social work, counseling, PT) cannot carry private loans; incumbents are credit-conservative.
funded_startups_already_here: GradBridge ($20M Series A, Acorn/Oaktree; second-look lending; date conflicts Oct 2025 vs Jun 2026). Climb ($50M Goldman UIG, 2019). Prodigy Finance (international-student lending, 2017). Searches for Juno, Mos, Stride, Edly returned nothing (not proof they don't exist).
wedge_hints: School-sponsored or risk-shared lending in law/MBA and other steep-earnings programs (NBER notes institutions emerging as intermediaries); warehouse/ABS capital plumbing for new originators; programs just outside the 'professional' $50k cap; outcomes-based underwriting that survives fair-lending review.
insider_roles: Grad-school financial aid directors; law/medical school CFOs and enrollment deans; consumer-lending credit-risk heads; ABS structurers; fair-lending counsel.

name: International students' tuition and living spend at US colleges
geography: United States (inbound from India, China, Nigeria, Vietnam and others)
size_basis: NAFSA/JB International: international students contributed $42.9B and supported 355,736 jobs in 2024-25 (2023-24: $43.8B). Includes tuition and living; a tuition-only split was not found in sources opened. Moving portion: NAFSA projects -$1.1B for fall 2025 and up to -111,000 students (-9.5%) and -$3.4B in 2026-27.
money_flow: Families, loans and sponsors pay tuition (net of aid) to US universities and living costs to local economies; schools pay recruiter commissions and pathway-partner revenue shares; lenders finance part.
shock: IIE Fall 2025 snapshot (828 institutions, 63% of international students): new international enrollment -17%, graduate -12%, 96% cite visa problems, 72% offered deferrals to spring 2026 and 56% to fall 2026. Fitch warns ending 'duration of status' would hurt tuition-dependent colleges. Students are shifting to Germany, France, Korea, Japan while Canada caps.
incumbents: University international offices, recruitment agents, pathway providers (Shorelight, Navitas and others), ApplyBoard.
incumbent_fragility: Tuition-dependent privates and regional publics with large one-year master's programs; agent-commission and revenue-share models misalign when demand falls; Fitch notes domestic recruiting cannot replace the revenue quickly.
funded_startups_already_here: ApplyBoard (earlier round at $1.4B valuation, undated), Edvisor ($13M pre-A per Signalbase), Adventus (~$12M), Concourse Global ($2M seed), Leap Finance (India, $165M in 2025), Prodigy Finance (financing). Dates from aggregators, rough. No 2025-26 rounds found for Shorelight, Navitas, Mpower.
wedge_hints: Deferral and hybrid first-semester programs delivered with partners abroad; visa-risk scoring for admissions; financing for students rerouted to third countries; compliance tooling for SEVIS/I-20 management.
insider_roles: International admissions directors; designated school officials (DSOs); immigration attorneys; recruiters in India/China; university CFOs/treasurers; higher-ed rating analysts (Fitch/Moody's).

name: K-12 special-education related services (speech, OT, PT, psychology, nursing), contract staffing and school-based Medicaid
size_basis: DERIVED, soft. 8.2M IDEA students in 2024 (CEC) x $13,127/student (Bellwether FY2020, 24 states covering 41% of students) = ~$105B total special-ed spend. UNVERIFIED ASSUMPTION: related services are 10-15% of that, giving $10-16B. Federal IDEA Part B is $14.2B (FY23/FY24). School-based Medicaid was nearly $4B in 2015 (CBPP); no current national figure found. Contract rates ~$50/hr vs ~$30 staff in one district.
money_flow: Districts pay salaries or contract rates to staffing firms, teletherapy providers and nonpublic agencies, funded by local/state/IDEA dollars plus Medicaid reimbursement; billing intermediaries historically took up to 25% contingency (CRS).
shock: Oct 10, 2025 Education Department layoffs (415 staff, 121 in OSERS; court blocked them Oct 15, 2025); Jun 16, 2026 interagency agreement under which HHS supports OSERS (statutory IDEA unchanged; Senate Democrats called it illegal); ESSER-funded staffing positions ran out. No 2025-26 reporting found linking Medicaid changes to school billing, and none on contract-therapist cuts tied to ESSER, so the financing shock is partly inferred.
incumbents: AMN Healthcare ($3.045M Cumberland County NC 2026-27), CompHealth, TherapyTravelers (Oakland USD vendor), PresenceLearning (1,000+ clinicians, $71.5M VC), Medicaid billing intermediaries.
incumbent_fragility: Procurement is bid-by-bid across ~13,000 districts; contract clinicians cost ~60% more than staff and are often part-time; Medicaid billing rules and consent requirements vary by state; federal oversight capacity is shrinking.
funded_startups_already_here: Parallel Learning ($20M Series B Dec 2025 led by Valspring; $28.9M total since 2021), PresenceLearning ($27M Series D 2020, Bain Capital Double Impact), TeleTeachers (small), Expressable (direct-to-family, $26M Series B May 2024). No school-Medicaid-billing startup raise found in 2025-26.
wedge_hints: Clinician network bundled with Medicaid claiming in states that just expanded school billing (Illinois districts got an extra $23.4M in year two; Oklahoma state plan amendment; Washington modernizing, target summer 2027); cross-district sharing of scarce clinicians; IEP-service delivery tracking that feeds claims.
insider_roles: District special-ed directors; school-based Medicaid coordinators; contract SLPs/OTs; state Medicaid school-health program managers; school business officials.

name: K-12 student transportation (district fleets, contractors, special-ed and choice-student rides)
size_basis: DERIVED. NCES Digest Table 236.90 shows $24.3B total transportation expenditures in 2015-16 (last row available). Roughly a decade of cost growth gives ~$30B (plus or minus 15%); a 2026 HopSkipDrive job listing also cites $30B, unsourced.
money_flow: State transportation aid and local dollars pay district-run fleets or contractors (per route/day), plus ride-network vendors for special-ed, homeless and charter students; some states mandate transport for private/charter/ESA students.
shock: School bus drivers fell from ~223,000 (Aug 2019) to ~202,000 (Aug 2025) per EPI; 71% of districts report an operational consequence of driver shortages (HopSkipDrive 2026 report, vendor-sponsored; AP-NORC found 80% affected); AASA May 2026 survey has diesel 6-20%+ over budget; some Texas districts' state allotment covers as little as 12% of costs; Ohio fines districts that don't transport private/charter students; EverDriven charter partnerships +31% 2024-25.
incumbents: District fleets, large contractors (First Student, Student Transportation of America, National Express: known to me but not verified in this research), routing software vendors, Zum, HopSkipDrive, EverDriven, Via, GoKid.
incumbent_fragility: Fixed-price contracts against diesel and wage inflation; routing built for neighborhood schools, not choice; many districts cannot serve private/charter/ESA students; driver supply is structurally short.
funded_startups_already_here: Zum: $140M Series E Jan 2024 (GIC), EPA Clean School Bus grants $26.58M and $32M (2024), $100M TPG Rise Fund Apr 16, 2026 at $1.7B valuation, ~$333M revenue 2025 (aggregator; TPG release not opened). HopSkipDrive ($37M Series D 2022; 13,500 schools, ~1,300 partners, 21 states). EverDriven (no 2025-26 equity found; reports 94% new-business surge, Oct 2025 headline). Via (NYC contract $36M/5 years, 2019). GoKid (carpooling, 10 states).
wedge_hints: Cross-district brokerage for charter/ESA/microschool students; non-bus alternatives where states allow them (Virginia since Jun 2025 for districts under 4,500 students; nine other states similar); driver pipeline (CDL P/S endorsement training and retention); electrification financing.
insider_roles: District transportation directors; contractor general managers; state pupil-transportation directors; routing coordinators; fleet mechanics; special-ed transport coordinators; district CFOs.

name: Trucking driver slots being re-sourced after the non-domiciled CDL and English-proficiency crackdown (recruiting, training, onboarding, compliance)
size_basis: SOFT, borderline vs the $5B bar. FMCSA estimates ~194,000 of ~200,000 non-domiciled CDL holders lose eligibility as licenses expire over ~5 years. 194,000 slots x $58,640 BLS median driver pay (May 2025) = $11.4B of annual payroll carriers must re-source, but exits are phased so the annual flow is closer to $2.3B. Vendor-addressable layer is smaller: replacement cost $8,234 (UGPTI) to ~$13,000 (PDA) x 194,000 = $1.6-2.5B one-time. Driver iQ claims $10.6B/yr truckload turnover cost (undated). BLS: 2.22M jobs, 214,500 openings/yr.
money_flow: Carriers pay drivers plus recruiting/orientation costs; students and carriers pay CDL schools (3-6 months); entry-level training must come from a school on the federal Training Provider Registry.
shock: FMCSA final rule (reported Feb 2026) restricts non-domiciled CDLs to H-2A, H-2B and E-2 categories; 28,000+ already revoked by states; English-proficiency out-of-service enforcement resumed Jun 25, 2025 (28,000+ drivers sidelined); Aug 31, 2026 DOT ordered 110 truck-driving schools shut and flagged ~160 more (counts vary); July 2026 DOL notice says CDL demand remains steady.
incumbents: Carriers' in-house recruiters; Tenstreet (driver recruiting/management software; CB Insights shows it investing in/acquiring DriverReach 3/31/2025); private, community-college and carrier-sponsored CDL schools.
incumbent_fragility: Fragmented training market now losing schools; 50-94% turnover at large truckload carriers; no standard way for carriers to verify English proficiency, license status and training-provider eligibility at scale.
funded_startups_already_here: YouCruit/Lanefinder ($11.5M, undated), DriverReach ($7.5M, Fulcrum), Drive My Way ($4.4M Series A Oct 2022), Spotter AI (Sentinel hiring/compliance launch Feb 2026), Call2Action.ai ($500K, Jul 2026). None found focused on English-proficiency verification.
wedge_hints: Driver-qualification file automation covering English-proficiency evidence, CDL status and training-provider checks; carrier-sponsored CDL academies to replace closed schools; tuition financing tied to placement.
insider_roles: Carrier safety/compliance directors; driver recruiters; CDL school owners and instructors; state CDL examiners and third-party skills testers; drug and alcohol program managers.

name: Craft labor spend on US data-center construction (electricians and allied trades)
geography: United States (Texas, Virginia, Ohio, Indiana, Louisiana and others)
size_basis: DERIVED. Data-center construction was $50.7B annualized in Apr 2026, +~28% YoY (Census as reported by AGC/Electrical Marketing; a single unconfirmed source cites $84.95B for Aug 2026). UNVERIFIED ASSUMPTION: labor ~35% of construction cost gives $17.7B; plausible range $15-23B. ABC puts the 2026 need at ~349,000 net new construction workers.
money_flow: Hyperscalers/developers pay general contractors, who pay electrical and mechanical subcontractors, who pay union or open-shop craft labor; hyperscaler philanthropy funds training pipelines.
shock: AI infrastructure capex: electricians earn up to double wages on large projects; one Texas builder reported two-month delays after data centers hired its electricians; BlackRock $100M (Mar 2026), Meta $115M workforce academy, Google ~$50M trades-training grants; BLS projects ~81,000 electrician openings/yr and McKinsey says 130,000 more electricians needed by 2030.
incumbents: Electrical contractors and GCs, union JATCs (IBEW-NECA), trades staffing firms. Specific names not verified in this research.
incumbent_fragility: Apprentice-to-journeyman ratios and state licensing cap supply; labor sourcing is local and relationship-driven; travel/per-diem logistics are manual; union training capacity is slow to scale.
funded_startups_already_here: Buildforce ($10M Series A, Jul 2026, led by Saepio; 2M+ hours across 2,000+ commercial projects). Corporate training pledges (Google, Meta, BlackRock) are grants, not startups. Only one search run, so others likely exist.
wedge_hints: Travel-crew logistics (housing, per diem, multi-state payroll, license reciprocity); prefab electrical assemblies that move labor offsite; foreman/supervisor upskilling; labor-capacity forecasting for developers' site selection.
insider_roles: IBEW business managers; NECA contractor project managers; GC labor superintendents; JATC training directors; electrical foremen; data-center developers' construction VPs.

name: School food service: federal child-nutrition programs (NSLP, breakfast, CACFP, summer) and the district / contractor kitchens that spend them
size_basis: USDA ERS FY2024: four child-nutrition programs cost $28.2B for 9.3B meals; NSLP alone $17.7B (4.83B lunches; $16.15B cash + $1.56B commodities per FNS data); CRS puts federal child nutrition at ~$32B. State, local and student payments are additional.
money_flow: USDA reimburses per meal and supplies commodities; student payments add; districts either self-operate or hire management companies, which buy from distributors and processors and employ kitchen labor.
shock: California AB 1264 signed Oct 8, 2025 (first US statutory definition and phase-out of 'ultraprocessed foods of concern' in schools; regulations due Jun 1, 2028, district phase-out from Jul 1, 2029, vendor ban from 2032, though some sources say 2035). USDA added-sugar limits began SY2025-26 with a weekly limit in 2027-28; sodium cuts delayed to 2027-28; whole milk allowed again in 2026; USDA drafting a new meal-pattern rule. Operative dates are 2029+, so the why-now is real but slow.
incumbents: Sodexo, Compass (Chartwells) and Aramark dominate the contracted segment; Cenavera (Nautic Partners investment, about Oct 2025, date unconfirmed; 350+ districts in 33 states); most districts self-operate.
incumbent_fragility: Fixed federal reimbursement cannot cover scratch-cooking labor; kitchens were built to reheat; the definition of ultraprocessed foods of concern does not exist yet; ~13,000 small buyers.
funded_startups_already_here: The Yay Company ($12M Series A Nov 2021, $15.5M total), Ordo (Series A Oct 2022), Revolution Foods (debt Oct 2023). No new venture rounds found for 2023-2026 (aggregator data, may be incomplete); recent capital is private equity (Cenavera).
wedge_hints: Shared central kitchens/commissaries across small districts; ingredient and label compliance data mapped to state definitions; purchasing co-ops for small districts; scratch-cooking labor and training models.
insider_roles: District child-nutrition directors; food-service management company general managers; state child-nutrition agency reviewers; school dietitians; K-12 food distributors' reps; commodity processors.
